en: The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara:
The Section on Vows (Vratākāṇḍa)
[1] [Invocation] The wish-fulfilling gem of skill, shining beautifully through the investigation of various tantras;

In this sixth book, the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, whose conduct is wondrous, joyfully and clearly expounds the vows that pacify the manifest transgressions of the *vrātyas* and others, which are endowed with their constituent parts and, when performed with devotion, yield the fruits desired by the hearts of the virtuous.

I shall describe, according to my own inclination, the various vows and observances pertaining to the days of the week and the lunar dates, as taught in the scriptures at length— vows that yield abundant fruit and are pleasing to the heart.
[Virtue of Vows] Vow alone is the supreme means for accomplishing the world and the means for attaining enjoyments;
since victory comes through vow alone, therefore everyone should practice vow.
[2] By means of his vow, King Sujoya became a sovereign ruler in the Kṛta age;
in the Tretā age, it was the righteous Rāma; but in the Dvāpara age, it was Dhanañjaya.
In the Kali age, King Vikrama [attained] great fruit from that vow;
for human beings, O Great-souled One, the vow alone is the singular dharma.
This was proclaimed by Śaṅkara to Hari through various tantras;
for although there are many dharmas in the world throughout the various ages.
Nevertheless, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the vow’s dharma;
for by means of that vow, the deer-eyed Vasuṃdharā attained liberation.
The virtuous daughter of Vikrama, who dwells in Daśārṇa,
[is honored by] the gods, the sons of Diti, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras.
[Padma Purāṇa] There is nothing more purifying than Brahmins, both in heaven and here on earth;
likewise, no ascetic practice is found equal to fasting.
For a thousand divine years, the wise Viśvāmitra alone subdued himself through austerity, and he attained the status of a brahmin.
Having observed the fast according to the rules, the gods attained the third heaven;
and the seers achieved supreme perfection through their fasts.
Likewise:
Hunger seizes both the perception of reality and the vital breaths, as well as fortitude;
he who conquers those which are difficult to conquer has thereby conquered heaven.
[3] In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "The dwelling together with virtues by one who has turned away from faults is to be understood as 'fasting' (*upavāsa*), which is devoid of all enjoyments."
“Faults” (*doṣāḥ*) are passion, hatred, and so forth; “virtues” (*guṇāḥ*) are compassion and so forth.
After fasting comes the food obtained by alms; after alms, that which is unasked for;
after that which is unasked for, the night-meal (*nakta*); therefore, one should subsist on the night-meal.
One who eats at night should practice these six: eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire-rites, and sleeping on the ground.
"The fire-rite" here consists of an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *mahāvyāhṛti* mantras. Likewise:
"Some men desire [the rite] at night, from the time the stars appear."
Some wise men declare that a day is less than a muhūrta.
"O Lord of Men, because the stars are visible, I consider it night;
'the day minus a muhūrta'—a *muhūrta* is two *ghaṭikās*, and by that [measure], it is 'the day minus [one]'.
[This is stated] in the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*."
When the sun stands at a distance of twice one's own height, one should know that it is a solar night; this is not the "night" for eating at night.
[4] Now, regarding the duties of the vow (*vratadharma*), they are found therein in the *Mahābhārata*.
Holding an udumbara vessel filled with water and facing north,
the wise man should either undertake the fast or make his formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
"Or else," [it refers to] another [time], such as at night and so forth.
Devala says: "Having eaten his morning meal, having bathed and sipped water, being composed in mind—"
And having offered it to the deities such as Sūrya, one should observe the vow.
Chāgaleya said:
Having previously taken a vow, if one does not practice it because of being deluded by desire,
he becomes a Caṇḍāla while living and is born as a dog after death.
Devala says: Fasting is destroyed by sleeping during the day, eating unwholesome food, and sexual intercourse;
even drinking water at the time of extreme distress causes the fast to be defiled.
"In *atyaye* means in the case of extreme suffering. Likewise:
'Fear of all beings, disease, negligence, and the teacher's instruction.'"
These are recited from the scriptures as acts that do not destroy one's vows, provided they are performed only once.

“Fear of all beings” means fear arising from all living creatures. By that [fear], even from the threat of snakes and the like, there may be a physical impairment; the meaning is that by this, a failure of the vow occurs. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: “Perfumes, ornaments, garments, flower garlands, and ointments...”
On a fast day, one does not incur fault by using a tooth-stick or applying collyrium.
Having observed the fast, the twice-born man should then provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa;
in this way, his fast indeed becomes complete in its merit.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Therefore, O King, by one who has observed a fast, bathing preceded by an oil massage must be diligently avoided, for that is supreme destroyer of beauty."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of the gods, offering oblations into the fire, contentment, and avoidance of theft.
This common dharma, established in ten ways, applies to all vows.
[6] Likewise:
"The sixth lunar day should be joined with the seventh, and the seventh should not be joined with the eighth;
for the worship of the Sun here, they prescribe fasting on the sixth."
Just as wise men observe a fast on the eleventh day for the purpose of worshiping Viṣṇu on the twelfth day, so too is this [practice].
Now, regarding incenses,
it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Agallochum, sandalwood, nut-grass, storax, and likewise vṛṣaṇa."
The incense produced from ambrosia (amṛta) should be prepared with equal parts.
O Lord of Beings, one should burn sandalwood with knots, agallochum, storax, nut-grass, camphor, and sugar for three days.
Thus, O best of gods, this "Infinite Incense" has been described.
"Granthi" is *granthiparṇa*; "Indu" is camphor;
as well as *palāśa* flowers, *dhava*, and *yakṣacandana*.
Camphor, sandalwood, costus, uśīra, and likewise sīlha;
O Bhīma, sa-granthi, vṛṣaṇa, kuṅkuma, gṛñjana,
and likewise harītakī— this, O Bhīma, is called the "limb of the Yakṣa."
[7] The meaning is that it is called "yakṣacandana. Black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*), *silhaka*, *vālaka*, and likewise *vṛṣaṇa*;
sandalwood (*candana*), *tagara*, *mustā*, and *prabodha* combined with sugar (*śarkarā*).
Camphor, sandalwood, flowers, aloe-wood, and likewise tagara;
gṛñjana, sugar, kuṣṭha, mahāṅga, and likewise silhaka.
This incense known as *mahāṅga* is always dear to the Lord.
*Mahāṅga* is *māṃsī* (nard).
[The other ingredients are: *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *mustā*, *aguru*, *silhaka*, and *śaśī*.
And likewise, O Brahmin, sugar is known as the "Great Incense."
Aloe-wood, *śilhaka*, and incense are known as the *prājāpatya* [vow].
Next are the vows pertaining to the days of the week (*vāravratas*).
[The Vows of Sunday] Regarding this, in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*,
Dindi said:
O Brahmin, tell me: what would be the fruit for those who worship the Sun on Sunday through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts?
Brahmā said:
Those men who perform a śrāddha when the day of the Sun has arrived become afflicted with disease for seven births.
But those men who take refuge there perform their rites at night,
reciting the supreme mantra to be recited, the *Ādityahṛdaya*.
Having indeed attained health in this world,
those who always observe a fast on Sunday go to the world of the Sun.
[9] And those who recite the Mahāśvetā mantra obtain their desired object—
whether by day and night, by night alone, or by the discipline of a three-night fast.
One who recites the Mahāśvetā obtains the fruit they desire.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one who performs japa especially on a Sunday for the six-syllable mantra of Mahāśvetā shall go to the realm of Vairocana.
The mantra is "Ādityahṛdayam. The mantra "Mahāśvetā" is "hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ. Some say the "six-syllabled" mantra is "sarolkāya namaḥ. The mantra is also "hrāṃ hrīṃ sūryāya. Likewise:
"He who, indeed, on a Sunday, having worshipped the Sun with devotion and faith..."
The person who performs this at night goes to the world of the immortals.
Āditya said:
"The man who, for one year, observes the *nakta* fast on my day, remaining celibate, conquering anger, and always intent upon my worship; [he shall attain my world]."
Having reached the end of the year, one should feed my devotees and indeed the twice-born; then one should say: "May the Sun-god be pleased with me."
[10] Thus, endowed with devotion, he goes to my world;
that man does not return to the unstable human world.
Thus [are described] the vows for Sundays, such as the Nakta-vrata and others;
now follows the procedure for the Nandā and other [vows] on Sundays,
according to the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
The day of the week belonging to the high-souled Āditya is known as Dvādaśāha;
it is Nanda, Bhadra, Saumya, Kāmada, and likewise Putrada.
Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, and likewise Ādityābhimukha; Hṛdaya, Rogahā, Mahāśvetāpriya, and Vara.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, he who exists on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha shall become Nanda, the remover of all sins and fears.
In that regard, bathing the Sun with ghee at night is remembered as meritorious;
furthermore, Agasti flowers here bring satisfaction to the Sun.
The unguent should be fragrant and the finest white sandalwood;
the incense should be the excellent guggulu resin, and the food offering should indeed be cakes.
[11] Having first given to a brahmin, one should then eat while restraining one's speech;
the cake made from wheat should be of the measure of a *prastha* and of the highest quality.
Or one may prepare a dish made from barley, combined with jaggery and clarified butter.
"A measure of a *prastha*" refers to sixteen cakes and grains.
This, along with gold, should be given to a Brahmin who is well-versed in the Itihāsas;
or it may be given on the earth or in the sky, or one should place it before the Sun.
The divine *brāhmaṇa* is the *gama*. Other *brāhmaṇas* than him are "terrestrial" (*bhauma*).
This *maṇḍaka* must indeed be given according to the mantra and accepted with devotion; likewise, cakes and other offerings should be presented slowly to the one who has Āditya as his supreme deity.
O Brahmin, accept this supreme cake for my welfare; it was produced from the splendor of the sun and fashioned by the Sun-god himself for kings.
I always accept this *maṇḍaka*, beloved of the Sun, which grants desires, bestows happiness, confers merit, and likewise grants sons and wealth.
These two great mantras, dear to Ravi, are for giving and receiving the cake, O best of the Gaṇas; they lead to welfare, of this there is no doubt.
[12] This very procedure for Nanda has been proclaimed, O Lord, for the welfare of men;
he who worships the Sun at Nanda according to this rite—
With his soul liberated from all evil, he is glorified in the world of the Sun;
neither poverty nor diseases shall afflict the family of that great-souled one.
Whoever should worship this Sun, for him there is never any decline in his lineage;
having gone to the world of the gods, he becomes a king upon the earth,
endowed with many kinsmen and equal to a twice-born in splendor.
“Resembling a twice-born” means equal to the sun.
Thus, O Hero, is the procedure for Nanda; it occurs in the month of Bhādrapada during the bright fortnight.
On the sixth [tithi], O best of the Gaṇa clans, he is proclaimed as Bhadra.
In that regard, whoever should observe a fast at night, or even during the day,
ascends upon the swan-vehicle and goes to the same world as the swans.
Mālatī flowers here, as well as white sandalwood,
Vijaya incense, and likewise excellent milk-rice (pāyasa).
[13] “Vijaya-dhūpa” is described in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*. It is as follows: “O Brahmin, [take] vṛṣaṇa, silhaka, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise aguru;
O twice-born one, [add] karpūra, mustā, sugar, and bark.”
Thus, this victorious incense was created by the Lord himself.
“Vṛṣaṇam” refers to musk;
O Destroyer of Tripura, one should employ it here in the worship of the Sun.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods at midday, O ruler of men.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, and then, restraining one's speech,
eat milk-rice with jaggery and ghee, O tiger among the Gaṇas.
Having obtained all desires here through sons, wives, wealth, and so forth,
and being liberated from all sins, one shall go to the world of the Sun.
O lord of men, this very rule has been proclaimed with great effort:
by performing it and hearing it, a man on earth is liberated from his sins.
Thus is the procedure for Bhadra.
O Hero, when the lunar mansion is Rohiṇī and it falls on its [the Moon’s] day, it attains gentleness;
O Hero, that is proclaimed as Saumya.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, performing fire oblations, and the worship of ancestors and gods—these shall become inexhaustible on the day of that Great-Souled One; of this there is no doubt.
The man who, established here at night, worships the Sun,
goes to the world of the high-souled god Bhāskara.
In that very place, there are red lotuses as well as red sandalwood;
the incense here is fragrant, and the supreme food offering is milk-rice.
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise one should eat it oneself;
whoever thus worships the gentle Citrabhānu, the Lord of Cows.
"Being thus liberated from sins, he shall attain the splendor of Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter.
Such is the Saumya rite; it occurs on the sixth day of the bright fortnight when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived.
That should be known as the boon-granting period of the Sun, and it is indeed his favorite.
He who worships the three-fold Sun with devotion, endowed with purity,
is liberated from all sins and shall attain the One of Fierce Rays.
O observer of noble vows, O hero, one should offer karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood,
as well as incense and oblations of ghee, to Bhāskara.

“Incense and an oblation of ghee”—this means incense produced by the casting of ghee. And as for the food offering (*naivedya*), it should be *kāsāra*, fragrant, and indeed pungent. O Destroyer of Tripura, one should then observe a fast or eat only at night.
For when the Sun, the illuminator of the world, is thus worshipped here,
and when Ravi is fully honored there, he grants abundant desires.

Thus ends the procedure for the Kāmada [rite]. O Bull-bannered One, that lunar mansion which possesses five stars, when it falls on the day of the God of Gods, that day is remembered as bestowing sons.
“Pañcatāram” refers to Rohiṇī and Hasta. Regarding the phrase “where”: in the rite for the birth of a son, there should be fasting, and the śrāddha should be performed as prescribed;
furthermore, the consumption of the honey-ball (madhumat-piṇḍa) is also proclaimed.
Having observed a fast, one should indeed worship the Lord of Cows there with devotion,
using incense, garlands, and offerings endowed with divine fragrances.
Having thus worshipped Vivasvat, O high-minded one, one should sleep on the ground at night in his very presence, while reciting the Śvetā Devī mantra.
"Having worshipped Vivasvat"— the word "on Sunday" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Then, having bathed at dawn and offered the supreme *arghya*,
O Lord of Gaṇas, with *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood...
Having worshipped the three-eyed Aṃśumat, the lord of planets and spirits,
and having likewise worshipped that day of the week, one should then perform the śrāddha.
O God of excellent vows, with five divine and terrestrial Brahmins,
one should designate those two Brahmins known as Gama as divine there.
O slayer of Andhaka, O beloved of the Sun, one should designate three Brāhmaṇas as representing the earth;
then, O friend of the Sun, one should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha in this manner.
[16] But when the śrāddha ceremony is completed, having consumed the middle piṇḍa,
O observer of excellent vows, one should stand before the God of gods while reciting the mantra.
O Lord of Gods, this is that very lump which is always desired by you;
behold it as we eat, so that through it there may be offspring for me.
"O Lord of Gods, my mind has been inspired by your grace;
thus worshipped, Bhāskara shall grant me a son."
Therefore, this day is proclaimed as the king’s turn for the granting of a son.
Thus ends the rule for the son.
That which occurs during the southern solstice is proclaimed as *japa*.
In this regard, fasting, eating at night, bathing, giving gifts, and likewise recitation (*japa*) [are prescribed].
O Lord, that which is performed for the pleasure of the Sun becomes a hundredfold more meritorious;
therefore, one should perform the rite at night and so forth, for that procedure shall be a hundredfold effective.
Thus is the procedure for victory;
it should be known as "Jayantī" during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), O Leader of the Gaṇas.
Wherever the abode of the God may be, there the Sun-god (Divākara) is to be worshipped.
O tiger among gods, when the Lord of Gods is worshipped there during rites such as bathing and giving gifts, he bestows a thousandfold fruit.
Where bathing with ghee, milk, and sugarcane juice is performed,
and where saffron unguent is applied, it is praised as dear to the Sun-god.
The incense rite is performed with guggulu resin, and the preferred food offering is sweetmeat (modaka).
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins with sweetmeats, sesame cakes, and *śaṣkulī* pastries;
he who worships the Sun in this manner on a Sunday, O Lord of Gaṇas.
O Lord, the God indeed bestows upon him a thousandfold fruit for his bathing,
giving, vows, and fasting.
Thus is the procedure for Jayantī.
That [tithi] occurring on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, is known as Vijayā; it removes all sins and fear.
In that regard, the Blessed Lord, the God who is the Master of the Gaṇas, when worshipped, bestows the entire fruit of meritorious action multiplied ten millionfold.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of the ancestors and the gods;
[18] as well as eating only at night or fasting—one should fully honor the Sun-god here.
And sovereignty over the seven worlds is attained for seventy-seven [kalpas].
Thus ends the procedure for victory. Now listen to the supreme rite concerning him who is born on the seventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, facing the Sun.
O Destroyer of Tripura, having observed a single meal on a Sunday,
one should then perform the morning bath and worship the Sun.
Facing the sun, the one of firm vows should stand until the setting of the sun,
reciting the Mahāśvetā mantra while leaning against a pillar.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should fashion a pillar from red sandalwood wood, four cubits long, soft, smooth, even, and firm.
Taking refuge in that god Divākara with devotion, O mighty-armed one,
one should remain standing while beholding and reciting the Mahāśvetā [hymn] until the setting of the sun.
Having worshipped the Sun with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
the Brahmin, having first offered food [to the deity], should then eat while maintaining silence.
[19] Indeed, if a man should act in this very manner for the pleasure of the Sun, Bhānumat will be pleased with him; and being pleased, he indeed bestows his favor.
O King, wealth, grain, sons, and health come from Bhārgavī;
therefore, one should worship Hari, the lord of the gods, on this day.
“Bhārgavī” refers to Lakṣmī. This is the procedure for facing the Sun. O Lord of Gaṇas, on the occasion of the sun’s transit (saṃkramaṇa), whatever day of the week it may be for the Sun...
He should be known by the name Hṛdaya, for he is dear to the Heart of the Sun (Ādityahṛdaya).
There, having relied upon the night and having worshipped the God according to the true principle,
one should go to the temple of the Sun and stand facing the Āditya.
The wise one should recite the Ādityahṛdaya eight hundred times,
or otherwise, he should contemplate the Sun within his heart until its setting.
Then, having returned home, O Śiva, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability;
and having eaten the milk-rice (pāyasa), the wise man should then sleep upon the ground.
Whoever worships the Sun here with devotion, endowed with faith,
shall obtain all desires offered within the Ādityahṛdaya.
Thus is the procedure for the heart [mantra].
When the day of Mars falls on a Sunday, which is the day of the deity Bhaga,
that day is declared to be a destroyer of disease, removing the fear of all ailments.
“Bhagadaivata” refers to Pūrvaphalgunī; some say it is Uttaraphalgunī.
Whoever worships the Sun here with auspicious perfumes and ointments, being liberated from all diseases, goes to the abode of the Lord of Consciousness (the Sun).
O observer of noble vows, having placed the flowers within a cup made of *arka* leaves,
a man should worship them with devotion before the deity at night.
Having worshipped that Sun-god with *arka* flowers, which are always dear to the Sun,
and having consumed an *arka* flower himself, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
Having eaten the milk-rice, O hero, he sleeps upon the ground at night;
indeed, he who worships a brahmin here according to this procedure [attains the fruit].
[21] Released from all diseases, he shall go to the abode of the Sun;
from there, he shall proceed to the world of the one who knows the sound of the syllable *huṃ*.
“Those who know the sound of the syllable *huṃ* are the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the ritual for the offering to the disease.
Now, O observer of good vows, the day of the Lord who is the master of the planet Āditya—
O Gośrutibhūṣaṇa, you are beloved in the world according to the teachings of your own branch of scripture and are renowned therein.
But whoever always worships Pataṅga, who is dear to the serpents, with perfumes, flowers, incense, or various abundant offerings;
Fasting and pure during a solar eclipse, O best of the Gaṇas,
he should mutter the Mahāśvetā mantra as prescribed in his own Vedic branch, or otherwise.
One should worship the Lord of the worlds, the destroyer of darkness, who moves swiftly;
having worshipped the Maker of Day, one should then worship Mahāśvetā.
Having worshipped Mahāśvetā, one should then worship the god Ravi;
having installed Mahāśvetā and well-adorned her with perfumes and flowers.

Furthermore, having worshipped Mahāśvetā and the presiding deity of the planets as prescribed in his own Vedic branch, he should, with a concentrated mind, perform the fire-ritual for that very same [goddess].
O Destroyer of Tripura, having caused the Brahmins to recite the benedictions, one should then eat while restraining one's speech on this day, which is conjoined with the Sun and the planets.
O Bull-bannered Lord, whatever meritorious action is performed— such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation— all that shall be conducive to auspiciousness.
O best of assemblies, there is no doubt that for those who have performed these acts, the fruit is infinite, just as the word of the Sun-god declares.
Therefore, on the day of the Sun, wise men should perform meritorious deeds,
such as eating once a day, eating only at night, or even fasting.
But those who perform [this] on the day of the Sun go to the supreme state;
it is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to fame, beneficial for obtaining sons, and likewise grants all desires.
In that [month], a gift of a cake is considered equal to the gift of a cow;
O mighty-armed one, these are the twelve days of the high-souled Sun.
These [rites] have been described to you as bestowers of contentment and removers of all sins and fears;
O Bull-vehicled One, by performing even one of these according to the rule.
[23] Then he goes to the supreme world of the great-souled one whose banner is a bull.
[Thus ends the ritual for the beloved of Mahāśvetā.
Thus ends the ritual for the days of the week beginning with Sunday according to the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
[The Divākara-vrata] Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having prepared the ground, one should draw a beautiful lotus adorned with a pericarp."
It was endowed with twelve petals, beautiful and delightful.
In the midst of those, however, one should place the Sun in the center of the four.

"Among them, four [are in the center]" means that four petals belonging to those twelve petals should be made attached to the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in the middle of the lotus; however, eight are outside of that. Thus, the meaning is "having made it twelve-petaled. One should place Sūra on the eastern petal, Divākara in the southeast, Vivasvant in the south, and Bhaga one should place in the southwest.
One should place Varuṇa on the western petal, Indra in the north-western,
Āditya in the northern, and Savitṛ immediately beyond that.
[24] One should place the horse of the Sun upon the eastern petal of the pericarp;
the thousand-rayed Mārtaṇḍa on the southern, and on the western petal.
Having thus placed the god Ravi in the north and Bhāskara in the center,
the worship of Sūrya shall take place in all directions.
With *karavīra* and *arka* flowers, with sandalwood, agallochum, and *campaka*,
I worship you, O Soul of Time, Soul of all beings, facing in every direction.
"O glorious Divākara, destroy birth, death, old age, sorrow, and the fear of saṃsāra; bring about the destruction of poverty and calamity!
[He should be addressed] with the mantra of salutation, the vyāhṛtis, the praṇava, and so forth.
“I praise Agni; homage to you! O Jātavedas, let there be homage to you!”
For food, to you, homage; for food, for strength, homage, homage!
O Agni, come hither for the feast; O you who contain Agni within, let there be homage to you!
"May the Goddess be auspicious to us; salutations to you, the eye of the world, salutations, salutations!
O Pāṇḍava, first seize [the day] on a Sunday when the moon is in the Hasta constellation."
[Then, for seven days starting from the day of the sun, one should perform worship.
Eating but a single meal and fasting at night, one should feed Brāhmaṇas during the day.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
standing before him, one should say: "May Bhāskara be pleased."
Whether born of desire, or anger, or intoxication, or likewise pride—
even the sin arising from thousands of lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Dadru, kīṭaja, and kuṣṭha; asthma, gaṇḍa, and bhagaṃdara; as well as malignant anal ulcers, fistula-in-ano, and carmakīlaka.
Even throughout thousands of births, he shall have no fear of disease;
endowed with wealth and grain, that man shall attain good fortune.
For thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons,

free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoted to the Rāmāyaṇa;
O Brahmin, he never experiences separation from his wife; nor does that woman become a widow as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Nowhere is a couple born deformed or afflicted by grief;
nor, O Grandfather, do their sons, cattle, or jewels ever go to ruin.
For seven thousand and seven hundred kalpas,
by making his bed never empty, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Aśūnyaśayana-vrata. [47] [The Kānti-vrata]
In the Varāha Purāṇa,
Agastya said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Kānti-vrata (the vow for beauty)."
But on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, O Indra among kings, [one should perform the rite].
At night, one should diligently worship Bala and Keśava;
one should worship the feet for Baladeva and the head for Keśava.
Having thus worshipped the supreme form of Viṣṇu, the wise man should worship on that day the highest essential nature known as Soma, which consists of two kalās.
The wise one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra of the Parameṣṭhin:
“Homage be to the one whose form is nectar, and who bears all medicinal herbs.”
"O King, having offered the *arghya* to the Moon, the Supreme Self and Lord of the world of sacrifice, with this very mantra..."
O King, during the night he should eat barley-food with ghee along with a Brahmin;
however, during the four months beginning with Phālguna, being pure, he should eat milk-rice with ghee.
One should perform the *tilahoma* (sesame oblation) during the month of Kārttika, and likewise with barley;
however, during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should have the *ghṛtahoma* (ghee oblation) performed.
One should eat sesame and rice at night; this is the sequence of the preliminary ritual.
Then, when the year is complete, having fashioned a silver image of Soma, [one should proceed].
Covered with a pair of white garments and anointed with white flowers and unguents,
having thus honored the twice-born, one should then bestow [the gift] upon him.
“O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to you! By your grace, may I be radiant in the world of the Aśvins, omniscient, pleasing to behold, and possessed of the form of the Moon.
Having recited this mantra and given [the gift] to a Brahmin while remaining silent, [one attains the fruit].
As soon as that is performed, the man becomes radiant with beauty.
O King, this was also performed in ancient times by Soma, the son of Atri;
at the conclusion of his vow, Janārdana himself was personally gratified with him.
[Thus ends] the Kāntivrata; these are the second vows.
Now, the third vows.
[The Vow of the Saltless Third Day] Regarding this, in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa,
Sumantu said:
Devoted to her husband, regarding him as her very life, and intent on serving him— even such a virtuous woman, though disciplined and pure in her diet, [is not exempt].
Fasting on the third lunar day, she should avoid salt.
Regarding the phrase "fasting" (*sopavāsā*): the meaning is that having observed the fast on the second day at the commencement of the vow, she should avoid salt on the third day.
She should indeed undertake this vow with devotion until the end of her life.
When satisfied, Gaurī bestows beauty and good fortune, as well as charm,
grace, and a heart-pleasing loveliness that is praiseworthy and captivating to the minds of men.
O King, by means of the Gaurī-vrata through the avoidance of salt, a man obtains a beautiful wife, and a husband becomes pleasing to his wife.
Listen to me as I relate that speech which was spoken by Umā in the past,
O Lord, concerning this vow while Dharmarāja was listening.
This vow of mine is supreme, bringing good fortune to men;
a woman who is disciplined by her husband shall likewise practice this vow.
And she shall rejoice with her husband as long as my husband Hara lives—
she who, being a beautiful and virtuous woman, finds a noble husband.
But she, with reference to this vow, should eat food that is not pungent;
with her mind fixed on me, her thoughts centered on me, devoted to me, and accepting me as her refuge, she should perform it.
Having established a golden image of Gaurī, adorned with perfumes and ornaments,
clothed in very fine garments, and decorated with floral embellishments;
O Bhārata, one should offer salt with jaggery and oil during the bright fortnight,
and present pungent tubers, cumin, conch-shell, and leaves.
“The white fortnight,” this is the ellipsis. “Kaṭukanda” is ginger.
O King, balls of molasses (*guḍapūpa*), as well as *pūpa* cakes and *khaṇḍaveṣṭa* sweets, should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is perfected in his vows and deeply learned in the scriptures.
After eating, an image should always be offered according to one's ability;
it may be made of gold, O King, but for those lacking wealth, it should indeed be made of honey and milk out of devotion.
O Hero, he eats food free from pungent condiments and salt at night while remaining restrained in speech;
Gaurī is ever present with him as he sleeps upon a bed of grass spread on the ground.
A maiden obtains a husband who is pleasing to her mind and desired by her;
having sported with her husband for a very long time, she shall indeed remain right here.
Having established his continuity, he goes along with that very [continuity] from this world to the next world, [attaining] the enjoyments of the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
But when the queen was a widow, O King, she remained devoted to her vows,
constantly self-restrained toward her husband, and always intent upon his worship.
Having cast off her own body right here and beholding her beloved in the city of Hara,
she shall draw him away from all beings and rejoice in heaven together with her husband.
Having enjoyed herself for ten times ten million years, she has come here;
together with her husband, she obtains the desired fruit previously described.
Thus, this lunar day is indeed the third, honored by the world;
it is especially meritorious whenever it occurs in the month of Vaiśākha.
The month of Bhādrapada is meritorious, as indeed is Māgha; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, for women, the month of Bhādrapada under the asterism Maghā is considered auspicious and praiseworthy.
But the third day of the month of Māgha, O Bhārata, is common to all the world; on that day, [offerings] of jaggery and salt [should be made].
O King, giving gifts brings about the highest welfare for both women and men;
the Goddess is satisfied with molasses, while Śaṅkara is satisfied with salt.
On the third lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada, she should give molasses cakes;
furthermore, she should offer milk-rice for the pleasure of Vāmadeva.
The gift of water is praised, O Bhārata, as is the gift of sweetmeats;
and in the month of Vaiśākha, O King of kings, so too is the gift of sandalwood on the third lunar day.
The Goddess is indeed satisfied with water, and Bhava himself with sweetmeats;
there is no doubt in this matter that one born in a grove [is pleased] by the gift of sandalwood here.
But this lunar day in the month of Vaiśākha, O tiger among the Kurus,
which is the third, is praised here by the gods as one that is inexhaustible in its merit within the world.
The wise man who gives water-pots provided with water-vessels in this world goes indeed to the realm of Hemamālin.
Thus, O hero, this third lunar day has been described as most excellent;
by fasting upon it, O King, a man shall attain an increase of intelligence and prosperity.
Thus ends the vow of the Saltless Third Day (alavaṇatṛtīyāvratam), also known as the Ārdrānandakarī-tṛtīyāvratam,
in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
In the same way, I shall describe another third [lunar day] that destroys sins,
which is renowned in the world by the name Ārdrānandakarī (the Delighter in the Ārdrā Nakṣatra).
When, on the third day of the bright fortnight, the asterism Āṣāḍhā should occur at any time,
or likewise Rohiṇī, Śatabhiṣaj, Hasta, or Mūla;

“Āṣāḍharkṣam” refers to Uttarāṣāḍhā; “brahmarkṣam” refers to Abhijit; and “āpyam” refers to Pūrvāṣāḍhā. At that time, one should properly perform the ritual bath with darbha grass and scented water, wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes.
One should worship Bhavānī with devotion using fragrant white flowers,
and likewise Mahādeva, seated upon a single seat.
"Salutation to Vāsudevī for the feet; then [salutation] to Hara for Śaṅkara.

Regarding "Salutation to Vāsudevī for the feet," one should worship the feet of the Goddess with "Salutation to Vāsudevī. One should worship the feet of Hara with "Oṃ, salutation to Śaṅkara. The same should be understood for what follows. "Salutation to Śokavināśinī for the shanks; salutation to Ānanda, O Lord."
One should worship the thighs with "To Rambhā" and those of the wielder of the Pināka bow with "To Śiva";
the waist of the Goddess with "To Ānandinī" and that of the trident-bearer with "To Śūlapāṇi."
Likewise, he offered his navel to Mādhavī and to Śambhu for the sake of Bhava;
his two breasts to Ānandakāriṇī and to the moon-bearing Saṅkara.
Salutation to Utkaṇṭhinī at the throat; salutation indeed to Nīlakaṇṭha, O Hari, at the neck; salutation to the lotus-bearing [goddess] at the hands, and to Rudra, the Lord of the worlds.
And the two arms to Parirambhiṇī; to Nṛtyaśīlā, O Hari, the face of the Goddess; and again to the Lord who bears the bull-emblem, to Vilāsinī.
And he offered a smile to Smaraśīlā; his face to Viśvavaktrā, who is intent upon that [Smaraśīlā];
his eyes to Mandanivāsinī; and [his gaze] to Viśvadhāmnī of the Trident-bearer.
The two eyebrows [are for] Nṛtyapriyā and for Śūlin’s Tāṇḍaveśa;
the forehead of the Goddess [is for] Indrāṇī, and that of the Lord [is for] Havyavāha.
To Svāhā belongs the crown of the Goddess; indeed, it belongs to the All-pervading One who bears the Gaṅgā.
Śiva and Śivā are the foremost in the universe, whose bodies are the universe, and whose feet and hands are the universe.
I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, whose faces are serene;
having thus worshipped them according to the rules, one should again [proceed] in front of the two Śivas.
One should have lotuses and water-lilies made of various colors with powder;
as well as a conch, a wheel, a crown, a swastika, and the svabhaṭāmara.
As many particles of dust as fall from that cloud of dust upon the earth,
for so many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
According to one's ability, one should give to a twice-born man four vessels of clarified butter along with gold, as well as a water-pot provided with water and food.
During the four months of the rainy season, one should offer barley food;
then, for the next four months, as before, [one should offer it] over a water-pot.
And having immediately given bowls of barley meal and bowls of sesame seeds,
[he offered] scented water, flower-water, sandalwood, and saffron water.
Unripe curd and milk, as well as water from a cow's horn, and likewise water mixed with the powder of kuṣṭha; again, [water] mixed with flour.
Likewise, having obtained water with uśīra root, water filled with barley,
and water with sesame seeds, one should sleep during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
Within each month, two fortnights are prescribed for consumption;
all white flowers are always recommended for worship.
And at all times during the giving of gifts, one should recite this mantra:
"May Gaurī, who is eternally blameless and the source of all auspiciousness, be pleased with me."
"Lalitā is for good fortune, and Bhavānī for the attainment of all perfections. At the end of the year, [one should offer] salt together with a jar of molasses.
Then, one should offer sandalwood paste and a cloth for the eyes along with a golden lotus;
likewise, a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara accompanied by stalks of sugarcane and fruits.
One should offer an excellent bed with a fine coverlet and a place for rest to a Brahmin together with his wife, saying: "May Gaurī be pleased with me."
This third [tithi], eternal and named Ārdrānandakarī,
is that by fasting upon which a person goes to the supreme abode of Śambhu.
In this world, one attains constant bliss, of this there is no doubt;
through long life, health, and progeny, no one shall encounter sorrow.
Whether it be a woman, a maiden, or even a widow who performs [this],
she too attains that fruit, cherished by the grace of the Goddess.
Having observed the fast as an antidote, one who knows the ritual procedures for the worship of the mantra attains the world of Rudrāṇī, from which rebirth is difficult to obtain.
Thus ends the Ārdrānandakarī Tṛtīyā vow [also known as the Nāmatṛtīyā vow] from the Devīpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
[One should worship] Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Bhadrā, Durgā, Kānti, Sarasvatī,
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī in due order.
Beginning with the third day of the month, one should perform worship; thus one shall become a partaker of heaven.
[One should worship Rudra as Ardhanārīśvara, or else Umāśaṅkara.]
A woman who worships according to the prescribed rite shall attain freedom from separation [from her husband].
Alternatively, she should always worship the Lord Śaṅkara in the form of Viṣṇu;
by means of the left-hand path (vāmabhāga), she shall obtain all her desires.
Thus ends the vow of Nāmatṛtīyā. [The Saubhāgyaśayana-vrata] from the Matsya Purāṇa.
Matsya said:
Having reached the month of Vaiśākha, on the third lunar day dear to the people,
during the forenoon of the bright fortnight, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds.
On that day, it is said, that goddess of excellent complexion was wedded by the Universal Soul with the mantras used for taking the hand in marriage.
Likewise, on the third lunar day, one should worship the Lord of Gods together with [the consort] using various kinds of fruits, incenses, lamps, and offerings of food.
Having bathed the image with the five products of the cow as well as with scented water, one should worship Gaurī together with Candraśekhara.
Homage be to Pāṭalā at the feet of the Goddess Śivā;
and having proclaimed "To Śiva," [homage is paid] to Jayā at both the secret places.
[57] Two pairs of shanks belong to Rudra and Bhavānī;
the two knees belong to Rudreśvara and Vijayā.
Having thus proclaimed [the mantra] for Harikeśa, likewise "Obeisance to the Giver of Boons" for the thighs;
"To Īśā" for the excellent hips; and "To Śaṅkara" for Śaṅkara.

And on the two sides of the belly, one should worship Koṭavī with "Obeisance to the wielder of the trident" and "To the trident-handed one"; and one should worship the abdomen with "Obeisance to you, Maṅgalā."
One should worship Rudra as the Self of All with the two breasts,
and likewise Śiva as the Divine Self with Bhadrāṇī at the throat;
one should worship Viśveśa as the Destroyer of Tripura with Anantā at both hands.
To Trilocana for Hara, and to Bāhū Kālānalapriyā.
One should worship the ornaments on the feet with "To Saubhāgyabhavana," the face of the Trident-bearer with "To Svāhā, Svadhā, and Bhāsvara."

The two lips, which grant desires, should be worshipped with the mantra "to her who dwells in the honey of the Aśoka tree," and likewise the mouth with "to Sthāṇu" and "to the beloved of the moon-faced one."
Homage to Ardhanārīśahara, [worship] Asitāṅgī on the nose;
homage to Ugra, [worship] Lokeśa on the eyebrows, and again Lalitā.
One should worship the destroyer of cities for Śarva, likewise Alaka for Vāsudevī;
one should worship Hara for the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, and likewise worship those with glossy hair.

Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite— [him] who is Bhīma yet possesses a gentle form— with the mantra "Salutation to the Head, the Soul of All," one should place the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) in front.
One should set out these eight items: ghee, parched grain, safflower, milk, cumin, *tavarāja*, sugar-cane juice, salt, and coriander.

Since this bestows good fortune (*saubhāgya*), it is called the "Eightfold Good Fortune" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*). Here, ghee and milk constitute a single category; for they are mentioned together earlier in the *Matsyapurāṇa* itself within the midst of the Eightfold Good Fortune, stating: "cow’s milk is a derivative [of water]. "Kustumbaru" is coriander (*dhanyāka*). "Tavarāja" is a specific kind of sugar.
Having thus offered all of that before the two, Śiva and Śivā, once again—
O subduer of enemies, having consumed the water from the horn in the month of Caitra, one should sleep on the ground;
then, rising again at dawn, pure and having performed his ablutions and recitations.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
[one should give] two golden images accompanied by the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka).
"May Lalitā be pleased here"—thus one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.
In this manner, for as long as a year, one should always perform the rite on the third lunar day with a focused mind.
Listen to me regarding the specific details concerning the consumption [of the substance] and the mantra for the gift:
in the month of Vaiśākha, it should consist of water from a cow's horn, and furthermore, cow dung.

In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the mandāraka flower is prescribed; in Śuci, the bilva leaf is remembered [as the offering]; in Śrāvaṇa, one should consume curd; and in Nabhasya, water infused with kuśa grass.
[59] In the month of Āśvayuja, one should consume milk; in Kārtika, *pṛṣadājya*—that is, ghee mixed with curd;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, cow’s urine; and in Pauṣa, one should consume ghee.
Likewise, in Māgha, one should offer black sesame seeds, and in Phālguna, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
[the goddesses are] Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, and Śivā.
At the time of giving the gift, one should recite: "May Vāsudevī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī, and Umā be pleased."
Mallikā, aśoka, lotus, kadamba, blue lotus, mālatī, kuluttha,
karavīra, vāṇa, mandāra, and paṅkaja.
And the sinduvāra is prescribed for all months in succession;
likewise the japā, the kusumbha flower, the mālatī, and the śatapatraka.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rule for as long as one year, using whatever is available— provided it is recommended— and always including the *karavīra* flower, a man [attains the fruit].
Whether it be a woman or a maiden, having worshipped Śiva and Śivā according to her ability with devotion,
she should, at the conclusion of the vow, give a bed furnished with all its appurtenances.
Having established a golden image of Umāmaheśvara along with a bull and a cow upon a bed, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
“Utensils” refers to pillows and the like. The pair of cows should also be made of gold, since it is impossible to place the primary [image] upon a bed.
Other pairs as well, according to one’s capacity, should be honored with garments and other items, along with offerings of grain, ornaments, gifts of cows, and stores of wealth.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoid of pride,
he who properly performs the Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata in this manner should worship.
One attains all desires and enjoys supreme bliss;
performing this, one should practice the renunciation of even a single fruit.
O lord of men, by exerting effort month after month, one attains fame, as well as good fortune,
health, beauty, long life, clothing, ornaments, and decorations.
O King, he who performs the Saubhāgyaśayana-vrata for twelve years shall not remain unliberated for three hundred billion years.
In the abode of Śrīkaṇṭha, being worshipped by the immortals, he shall remain perfectly for as long as three hundred kalpas, performing [his duties] seven and eight times over.
Whether it be a woman or even a maiden who performs this, O Lord of Men,
she obtains that fruit, cherished by the grace of the Goddess.
Whoever should even hear it, or should bestow it, or should direct their mind toward it,
shall also become a Vidyadhara and dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the Saubhāgyaśayana-vrata. [The Anantatṛtīyā-vrata] according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
Īśvara said: Listen attentively, O Goddess, likewise you who have performed infinite merit,
to this unsurpassed means of propitiation for both men and women.
In the month of Nabhasya, or Vaiśākha, or Puṣya, or Mārgaśīrṣa,
having bathed with white mustard seeds on the third day of the bright fortnight;
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead consisting of gorocanā with cow’s urine, mustā, and cow dung, mixed with curd and sandalwood.
Therefore, for the sake of good fortune and health, a man should always offer garments dyed with yellow pigment to Lalitā on the third lunar days of every fortnight.
If a woman is united with her husband, she should wear red garments;
a widow should wear those dyed with mineral pigments, and a maiden should wear white clothes.
Then one should bathe the image of the Goddess with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with milk alone,
likewise with honey, and with water scented with flowers.
One should worship with white flowers and also with various kinds of fruits,
accompanied by coriander, cumin, salt, jaggery, milk, and ghee.
One should always worship that goddess with white unbroken sesame seeds;
"white unbroken" refers to white rice grains, and "arcā" means an image.
O fair-faced one, one should perform the worship of her feet every fortnight.
Salutation to Varadā for the feet; likewise, salutation to Śrī for the ankles;
salutation to Aśokā for the shanks; and likewise, salutation to Pārvatī for the knees.
Salutations to the thighs for Māṅgalyakāriṇī, likewise to the waist for Vāmadevī;
salutations to the belly for Padmodarā and to the chest for Kāmaśrī.
Salutations to the hands that bestow good fortune; to the arms, the beauty of Hara’s face;
to the face that dwells in the mirror; and to the smile that grants the fulfillment of desire.
Salutation to Gaurī for the nose, and to Utpalā for the eyes;
salutation to Tuṣṭi for the forehead, and likewise to Kātyāyanī for the head.
Homage to Gaurī, homage to Tuṣṭi, homage to Kānti, homage to Śrī;
homage again and again to Rambhā, to Lalitā, and to Vāsudevī.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should draw a lotus in front,
provided with twelve petals and a pericarp made of saffron.
One should place Gaurī to the east, and after that Aparṇā;
likewise, Bhavānī to the south, and after that Rudrāṇī.
One should always install Saumyā, who dwells in Madana, in the west;
Pāṭalā, the fierce one, in the northwest; and then Umā in the north.
In the center, one should likewise install Umā, Śāntā, Maṅgalā, Kumudāsanī, and Bhadrā;
and having placed Lalitā in the middle, she should be situated upon the pericarp.
One should perform worship with flowers and unbroken grains, concluding with a prostration.
And having caused the auspicious sound of songs to be made by a married woman whose husband is living;
One should worship them with red garments and red sandalwood unguents;
one should also scatter the powder for the vermilion bath upon their heads.
“Bathing powder” refers to the powder of substances used for bathing.
Since vermilion and saffron are exceedingly desirable for the bath,
one should therefore also diligently worship the Guru who provides such instruction.
Where the guru is not honored, all ritual actions bear no fruit;
one should always worship Gaurī in the month of Nabhasya with blue lotuses.
In Āśvayuja, one should worship with bandhujīva flowers; in Kārtika, with śatapatra;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, with jasmine (jātī) flowers; and in Pauṣa, with yellow kuraṇṭaka flowers.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship the Goddess with *kundapuṣpa* flowers that shine like gold;
or in Phālguna, one should also honor Umā with *sinduvāra* or *jāti* flowers.
In Caitra, one should worship with *mallikā* and *aśoka* flowers; in Vaiśākha, with fragrant *pāṭala*;
in Jyeṣṭha, with lotuses and *mandāra*; and in Āṣāḍha, with *japā* buds.
Then, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should always worship with Kadamba and Mālatī flowers;
[one should offer] cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with Kuśa grass.
One should likewise bind [the patient] in sequence with bilva leaves, arka flowers, barley-water, cow-horn water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and bilva.

This is declared to be the commencement of the month of Bhādrapada and the ceremony of first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana); O fair-faced one, there is a pair [of lunar days] on the first and third of each fortnight.
One should designate a Brahmin and a Brahmin woman as Śiva and Gaurī;
then, having fed them with devotion, one should honor them with garments, garlands, and ointments.
One should give yellow garments to a man and saffron-dyed clothes to a woman,
along with flat beans, cumin, salt, sugarcane stalks, and molasses.
To him one should give a fruit joined with a golden lotus, [with this prayer]:
"O Goddess, so that the Lord of Gods does not depart, abandoning you."
"In that way, may my husband not go elsewhere after having completely abandoned me;
likewise, rescue me from the entire ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra."
Kumudā, Vimalā, Nandā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā,
Śivā, Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā, and Pārvatī.
In the months beginning with Nabhasya, one should utter the words, "May [the deity] be pleased.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should worship twenty-four pairs, or indeed twelve;
or one should worship eight pairs at the end of each month, or eight pairs during the Cāturmāsya.
Having given everything to the preceptor, the wise man should worship the remaining [deities];
this third [method] of Ananta, which has been described, always bestows infinite fruit.
The Goddess is the remover of all sins and the increaser of good fortune and health;
one should never transgress this [injunction] through stinginess regarding wealth.
Whether it be a man or a woman, from whatever curse one falls downward—
whether pregnant, recently delivered, a maiden, or afflicted by disease— at night [one should perform the rite].
When she is impure, then, being purified herself, she should have it performed by another;
whoever observes this third [lunar day], which bestows infinite fruit.
For more than a hundred billion eons, one is honored in the world of Śiva;
even one devoid of wealth should perform this for every year through fasts.
By means of the ritual procedure for the flower-mantra, even she shall obtain that fruit—
whether it be a woman, a maiden, or a widow.
She too, cherished by the grace of Gaurī, attains that fruit.
Thus ends the Ananta-tṛtīyā-vrata. [The Rasakalyāṇinī-vrata]
Īśvara said:
I shall also proclaim another third [vow], which destroys sins;
those who know the ancient kalpas recognize this as Rasakalyāṇinī.
Having reached the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
one should perform a bath in the morning with cow’s milk and sesame seeds.
One should bathe the Goddess with honey and likewise with sugarcane juice;
her worship is indeed performed with fragrant water, honey, and saffron.
Having worshipped the right limbs, one should then worship the left ones;
one should likewise worship the feet and the ankles of the Goddess with the mantra "Salutation to Lalitā."
Salutation to the shanks and knees for peace, and likewise to the thighs for prosperity;
salutation to the waist for Madālasā, and likewise to the belly for Amalā.
[67] One should offer the breast to Madanavāsinī and the neck to Kumudā;
the arm and the tip of the arm to Mādhavī, and the smile on the face to Kamalā.
The eyebrows and forehead to Śāntā, and likewise the hair-locks to Śaṅkarā;
the crown to Vindhyavāsinī, and again the hair-locks to Kānti.
To Madanā, the forehead; to Mohanā, the eyebrows;
to Candrārdhadhāriṇī, the eyes; and to Tuṣṭi, the face.
Salutation to Utkaṇṭhanī for the throat; salutation to Amṛtā for the breast;
salutation to Rambhā for the left arm; and salutation to Viśokā for the hand.
The heart [is offered] to Mandagāminī, the belly likewise to Pāṭalā;
the waist to Suratavāsinī, and the thighs to Campakaśrī.
Salutation to Gaurī for the knees, shanks, and feet; salutation to Gāyatrī for the ankles;
salutation to Dharādarā for the feet; and salutation to Viśvakā for the head.
Homage to Bhavānī, to Kāminī, to Kāmadevī, to Jagacchrī;
homage, repeated homage to Ānandā, Sunandā, and Subhadrā!
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one who is free from envy should honor a Brahmin couple by feeding them with sweet food and drink.
Having given a water-pot with a ladle and a pair of white garments,
one should then worship a golden lotus with perfumes and garlands.
[68] May Kumudā be pleased here; one should observe the salt-vow.
By this procedure, one should worship the Goddess month after month.
One should avoid salt in the month of Māgha, molasses in Phālguna,
sugar-candy in Caitra, and likewise honey in Mādhava.
One should avoid the *pāṭala* flower in the month of Jyeṣṭha, likewise cumin in Āṣāḍha;
one should avoid milk in Śrāvaṇa, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada.
Likewise, clarified butter is to be avoided in Āśvayuja;

in Kārtika, known as “Ūrja,” one should avoid *marjikā*—that is, *rasālā*, commonly known in the world as *śikhariṇī*. However, in Mārgaśīrṣa one should avoid coriander (*dhānyaka*), and in Pauṣa, sugar (*śarkarā*) is to be avoided.
At the conclusion of the vow, month after month,
one should give a full water-pot at the time of twilight, accompanied by food placed in a vessel.

Regarding the passage beginning with “at the end of the vow, a water-pot (*karaka*)...,” the meaning is that at the conclusion of the vow for whichever month any of these— salt, jaggery, and so forth— were renounced, one should give a “pot full” of that salt or other substance, along with a vessel containing the *laṭṭuka* and other foods to be described:
“sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*), white cakes (*śvetavatī*), *saṃyāva* cakes, then *pūrikā*s, *ghārtika*s, *ghṛtapūra*s, flour-cakes (*piṣṭāpūpa*), and *maṇḍaka*s.”
One should offer milk-vegetables, rice with curd, and likewise vegetable-rice-balls,
placing these in turn upon the water-pot starting from the month of Māgha.
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Rambhā, Bhadrā, Jayā,
Śivā, Umā, Rati, Satī, as well as Maṅgalā and Ratilālasā.
In this [rite], one should recite "May [the deity] be pleased" during the months beginning with Māgha in their proper sequence;
and in every case, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed.
One who is constantly observant of the fast, or if unable, is expected to eat only at night;
furthermore, when the month of Māgha has arrived, one should place sugar upon a water-pot.
Having fashioned a golden image of Gaurī endowed with the five jewels,
as well as a golden image the size of a thumb, together with a rosary and a water-pot;
Four-armed, joined with the moon, and covered by a white eye-cloth;
likewise, a pair of white cows, richly adorned with gold and clad in white garments.
One should give a vessel together with cloth, saying, "May Bhavānī be pleased.
Whosoever performs the Rasakalyāṇinī vow according to this rite, [attains the fruit].
He shall perform [this]; from all sins he is liberated at that very moment, and for thousands of billions of existences he will never again be born into suffering anywhere.
O lady of beautiful countenance, whether it be a woman or a maiden who performs this, she shall obtain that fruit which is gained by a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Whether she be a widow or a wretched woman, she too partakes in that fruit;
endowed with good fortune and health, she is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Thus ends the Rasakalyāṇinī-vrata.
[70] [The Aviyoga-tṛtīyā-vrata]
In the Kālikā Purāṇa,
Anilāda said:
"When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived and the moon is pure, O lady of radiant smiles..."
But having reached the second [lunar day], one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) at night.
Having sipped water and become pure, one should prostrate like a staff before Śaṅkara;
having offered salutation with the appropriate mudrās and made a formal request, one should touch the guru.
Then, having taken an udumbara twig, one should use it as a tooth-cleanser;
it should come from the northern direction, be with its tip intact, still possessed of its bark, free from blemishes, and auspicious.
On the third day and on the following day, one should worship Gaurī and Śambhu;
having performed the worship, one should sleep while fasting and chanting the praises of Śaṅkara.
Having fashioned auspicious forms of a man and a woman out of ground śāli rice flour,
one should place them in a vessel, worship them, and perform a night vigil.
Having worshipped Hara according to the prescribed rites and bathed him with clarified butter and other substances,
one should take that flower at dawn and offer it to him.
One should worship the preceptor with devotion, as well as the twice-born with sweet food;
and there, according to one's ability, one should also cause that [gift] to be given to married couples.
One should perform this in its entirety every month according to this rite;
then, at the end of Kārttika, one enters the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
I shall now proclaim their names; listen to them in order month by month.

"From here" means after Mārgaśīrṣa. However, for Mārgaśīrṣa, the two names Śambhu and Gaurī have already been stated at the very beginning, for the purpose of establishing the basis for worship and sacrifice, and for the sake of contemplation.

Thus, when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, one should worship Girīśa and likewise Pārvatī on the fourth lunar day; having performed the recitation of mantras, one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should always worship Bhava and Bhavānī in the month of Māgha,
and in Phālguna, one should worship the omnipresent Mahādeva together with Umā.
In the month of Caitra, the wise man should worship the goddess Lalitā and the god Śaṅkara;
and in Vaiśākha, he should indeed worship Sthāṇu and recite the mantra equal in number to the births of the world.
One should worship Rudra together with Rudrāṇī in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
and the beautiful-eyed Paśunātha together with Satī in Āṣāḍha.
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha together with Sunandā in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
and the Lord Bhīma together with Kālarātri in the month of Bhādrapada.
One should worship the god Śiva together with Durgā in the month of Āśvayuja;
and in the month of Kārttika, one should worship the all-pervading Lord Īśāna together with the goddess Śivā.
O observer of excellent vows, these names are prescribed for recitation, meditation, worship, and so forth;
indeed, one does not possess accomplishment without these names and forms.
One should offer flowers every month for worship;
I shall now describe them in order, for they bring immediate satisfaction.
In the first case, a blue lotus is appropriate; in its absence, indeed others. One should employ fragrant leaves and worship with devotion.
Karavīra, nimba leaves, kiṃśuka, kunda, mālikā,
pāṭala, kadamba, tagara, droṇa, and mālatī.
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, these [mantras] should be applied with devotion throughout all twelve months in their stated sequence, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the Lord."
And likewise, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be performed monthly;
for no other purifier is remembered as superior to the five products of the cow.
When the vow has been thus performed, O auspicious lady, endowed with devotion to Śiva,
at the end of the year [one should offer] a canopy, a banner, a bell, and a lamp.
One should offer a fine incense burner to Śaṅkara;
having bathed and worshipped him, one should then place a golden flower-vessel.
Then, O Hara, one should duly offer a pair of images made of rice-flour,
as well as the food offering (naivedya) and the sacrificial oblation (bali), having prepared them according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Śambhu, and then go to one's own home;
[one should represent] Mahādeva as a square and Umā as a triangle.
Having meditated, one should present that pair, together with pearls and other ornaments, to the preceptor;
one should worship the image with devotion and likewise honor twelve of the best of the twice-born.
Likewise, O Brahmin, one should feed couples according to one's capacity;
[one should offer] auspicious vessels made of gold, each weighing one karṣa.
Having caused a most beautiful image of Umāmaheśvara to be made,
one should offer sixty-four pearls and four corals.
Indeed, there should be that many rubies and copper images;
one should place all these requisites upon a pair of garments.
[75] One should give four hundred and eight jars, as well as a pair of sandals,
all together with gold, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and water.
On that day, he should provide food for the poor and the suffering without restriction; furthermore, he should worship [the deity] according to his ability until nightfall.
One should not make [the offering] deficient or excessive according to the measure of one's own wealth;
rather, one should worship with mere imagination and avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
One should apply oneself with the conviction: "This will surely bring about non-separation, bestow beauty, good fortune, and sons, and grant both wealth and food."
Thus ends the Aviyoga-vrata.
[The Saubhāgya-tṛtīyā-vrata] according to the Varāha-purāṇa.
Agastya said: Beyond this, O highly fortunate one, listen to the vow that brings about good fortune, by which prosperity arises for both women and men.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one should fast at night, remaining pure and speaking the truth.
Having worshipped Hari together with Śrī, or Rudra together with Umā,
one should worship the feet with "To the Deep One" (gambhīrāya) and the hips with "To the Fortunate One" (subhagāya).
One should worship the belly with "O God of gods," the chest with "O Blue-throated One," the head with "To the Three-eyed One," and all around with "To Rudra."
Having thus worshipped Viṣṇu together with Lakṣmī and Hara together with Gaurī with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order, the wise man [should proceed].

Then, O Great King, one should cause a fire-oblation (homa) to be performed before him with honey and clarified butter, along with sesame seeds, while reciting "O Lord of Good Fortune" (saubhāgyapataye).
Then, one should eat wheat-based food that is free of oil and unmixed with salt on the surface of the earth; this same rule is prescribed for the dark fortnight as well.
O King, on the second day of the month beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should feed milk-rice there;
thereafter, from Kārttika onwards, one should feed barley-food.
With a serene mind, one who is discerning should, according to his ability, offer either śyāmāka grain or sacrificial oblation (havis) to a worthy Brahmin recipient.
On this earth, one should give even to one who possesses little wealth, provided he is not deficient in limbs, has mastered the Vedas, conducts himself virtuously, and is endowed with good conduct.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa [the vessel] accompanied by six bowls:
one bowl for honey and ghee, and a second filled with clarified butter.
The third is filled with sesame oil, the fourth is combined with molasses;
the fifth is full of salt, and the sixth is filled with cow’s milk.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, one becomes fortunate and handsome to behold.

Thus ends the Saubhāgyavrata. [Thus concludes the section on the vows for the third lunar day within the Vrata-kāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, the Great Minister of Peace and War to the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Govindacandra.]
Now, regarding the fourth-day vows [Aṅgāraka-caturthī], they are described therein in the Matsya Purāṇa.
O Dānava, when the fourth lunar day coincides with a Tuesday,
one should perform a bath with clay, adorned with rubies.
Reciting the mantra "Agni is the head of heaven," one should stand facing north;
however, a Śūdra remains silent, mindful of the earth, and sits devoid of ritual enjoyment.
When the sun has half-set, having smeared the courtyard with cow-dung and adorned it on all sides with flower garlands and unbroken grains of rice;
Having performed worship, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with saffron;
in the absence of saffron, red sandalwood is prescribed.
Four water-pots (karaka) should be prepared, provided with various kinds of food and edibles,
and filled with red śāli rice and rubies.
Having placed those [offerings] in the four corners, one should likewise present various fruits and all such things as perfumes and garlands.
Having worshipped a tawny cow with golden horns,
silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, together with her calf, as well as a very gentle, red bull capable of bearing the yoke;
The seven grains, combined with the inferior [grains].
"The seven grains" are barley, wheat, rice, sesame, *kaṅku*, *śyāmāka*, and *cīnaka*. Likewise, [he saw] a person the size of a thumb,
made of gold, with exceedingly long arms.
Four-armed, seated upon a golden vessel filled with jaggery and mixed with clarified butter.
This gold should be given to a twice-born who knows the melodies of the Sāman, who has conquered his senses, who is a worthy recipient, and who is endowed with virtuous conduct and noble lineage.
Nor indeed to one who has a family, nor to one possessed by hypocrisy.

“O son of the Earth, of great splendor, born from the sweat of the wielder of the Pināka bow; desiring beauty, I have sought refuge in you—accept this water-offering (arghya); salutations be unto you!
Having offered the arghya with this mantra using water mixed with red sandalwood, [one should proceed].
Then one should honor the most excellent brahmin with red garlands, garments, and so forth.
With that very same mantra, one should give land accompanied by a pair of cattle,
and according to one's ability, a bed furnished with all its necessary accessories.
Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is one's own favorite at home—
that very thing should be given to a person of virtue by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and dismissed the eminent brahmin,
he should eat at night food that is not pungent or salty, mixed with ghee.
I shall now tell you of the merit that belongs to that man who, according to his ability, should perform this Aṅgāraka-aṣṭaka rite in its entirety, or even in four parts.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune in birth after birth,
he shall become a devotee of Viṣṇu or Śiva and a sovereign of the seven continents.
For seven thousand kalpas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the Aṅgāraka-caturthī. [The Vināyaka-caturthī is described] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
On the fourth day, however, O King, always abstaining from food and observing the vow,
he gives sesame-rice to a Brahmin and himself consumes sesame-water.
When the completion of the vow occurs at the end of two years,
Vināyaka, being pleased with him, grants his desired fruit.
Thus ends the Vināyakacaturthī;
[80] [the Aṅgārakacaturthī].
When the fourth lunar day coincides with the fourth lunar day and is joined with Mars,
one should observe a fast on that very day and worship Mars according to the prescribed rites.
Regarding the phrase "but the fourth," it is used in a distributive sense (vīpsā), meaning that the fourth lunar day joined with Mars is understood.
Having fasted by means of a night-meal (nakta), O Lord, for four days joined with Mars,
hear what kind of procedure is to be followed on each of those fourth days.
Having respectfully fashioned a golden image of Mars together with Vināyaka,
one should offer ten gold pieces as the primary gift, or five, or even two and a half.
With devotion, one should prepare vessels made of gold, silver, or even copper,
weighing twenty palas or fifteen palas each.
O hero, twenty karṣas, and likewise twenty half-karṣas,
as well as a silver pala, half a pala, and even a quarter-pala should be prepared according to the prescribed measure.
According to one's capacity or wealth, and with devotion, having installed the Lord of the House even in a vessel made of copper, he should wrap it completely with cloths.

[81] Adorned with various Sindhu-colored garments and red cloths—here, "the lord of the house" refers to Mars (*kuja*). "Sindhu-colored" is an adjective qualifying the garments; thus, the meaning is "with garments of Sindhu colors.
O King, one should always give this to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
"To the speaker, O mighty-armed one, to the virtuous, for the sake of welfare, O King—
thus has this meritorious lunar day, the most excellent of all lunar days, been described."
Having fasted upon it, O Bhārata, a man attains a divine form;
he becomes equal to Atri in beauty, O hero, and like Hari in splendor.
O King, having attained such a form here, one goes to the abode of Bhīma.
"Ātreya" is the Moon; "Hari" is the Sun; and "Bhīmasya" refers to Maheśvara.
This occurs through the grace of Vighnātha, Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the World.
O King, for those who recite, listen to, and especially practice it, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
Thus ends the Aṅgāraka-caturthī [and the Avighna-caturthī-vrata].
In the Varāha Purāṇa, Agastya said:
"O King, I shall describe such a vow; listen to it."
"By performing this correctly here, no obstacle shall arise.
O King of kings, this vow should be undertaken on the fourth day of the month of Phālguna; eating only at night, the breaking of the fast is prescribed with an offering of sesame seeds and rice.
That very same [offering] should be poured into the fire and that should be given to a Brāhmaṇa;
having thus performed the divine Cāturmāsya vow on the fifth day.
Having fashioned a golden elephant-faced [image], one should cause it to be given to a Brahmin,
along with five vessels of milk-rice from which the water has been removed.
Having thus performed this vow, one is liberated from all obstacles;
in ancient times, Sagara did so when an obstacle arose for his horse sacrifice.
"By performing this very same rite, he attained the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha),
just as in the past the god Rudra did while destroying Tripura. Since he performed this very act, Tripura was brought down by him."
Thus, as he was going to heaven, he observed this very same vow.
Even by other rulers desiring to conquer the earth,
or by those seeking the fruits of asceticism, the supreme pacification of obstacles is for the sake of performing sacrifice.
To the divine hero, the elephant-faced one, the pot-bellied one, the one with a single tusk, the destroyer of demons,
who arose from the impurity of the body of the Mountain’s Daughter.
To the sky-walker who holds an axe in his hand.
Having thus worshipped with hymns of praise, one should again perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the sake of destroying obstacles;
when this is done, [the obstacles] quickly go to their destruction.
Obstacles and undertakings both attain success.
Thus ends the vow for the removal of obstacles [the Kundacaturthī] in the Devīpurāṇa.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, the fourth lunar day known as Kunda should be observed with fasting, O best of gods; thereafter, sovereignty shall be attained.
One should bring all the various offerings and every necessary utensil:
kunda leaves and fruit, potherbs, salt, jaggery, and sugar.
O best of gods, pieces of sugar, cumin, coriander, and various grains should be given with devotion to young girls.
One should cause a sun-dish and likewise vessels, especially those made of clay, to be given to the Goddess, saying: "May she be pleased with me always."
By this method, O Śakra, good fortune and the continuity of one's lineage increase;
there is no doubt in this matter, for what I have spoken cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the Kundacaturthī vow [also known as Gaṇeśacaturthī] from the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
O best of men, having bathed in a river on the fourth lunar day, one should not eat;
wearing red garments and anointed with red perfumes, one should remain thus.
Then, with a red-colored mind, one should worship Gaṇādhīśa Vināyaka according to the prescribed ritual,
beginning with a bath using water infused with red sandalwood.
Having smeared [the image] with red perfume, one should worship it with red flowers;
then he offered incense mixed with ghee and sandalwood.
Having offered an oblation of turmeric, jaggery, and sugar-candy soaked in ghee,
and having thus worshipped Vināyaka for a year, he then praised him.
Ikṣvāku said:
"Having paid homage to Mahādeva, I shall praise that Vināyaka,
who was likewise praised by Skanda during his consecration in the past."
I first bow to that Vināyaka, by whom lineage, merit, fame, and the life of a celibate student are attained for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
To Mahāgaṇapati, the heroic and powerful one who increases victory—
whether he has one tusk, two tusks, or four tusks, and possesses four arms.
Three-eyed, with a trident in hand, red-eyed, and the bestower of boons;
this son of Tryambaka has spike-like ears, is fierce, and is the leader of the staff-bearers.
Reddish in color, carrying a staff, with a face like fire and fond of oblations—
he who, when unworshipped, creates obstacles for men in all their undertakings.
I bow to him, the leader of the Gaṇas, the formidable and fierce son of Umā,
intoxicated with pride, the three-eyed one, born from the mouth of Bhava.
I bow to Vināyaka, who resembles ten million suns, whose radiance is like crushed collyrium, who is eternal, perfectly immovable, and peaceful.
Homage be to him who has the form of an elephant; homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas!
Homage to him whose form is like Meru and Mandara; homage to the dweller on Kailāsa!
Obeisance to you, Virūpa, whose true form is his own nature, to you who observe the vow of celibacy;
O Vināyaka, obeisance to your mind, the God praised by your devotees.
In the past, for the sake of accomplishing the task of all the gods,
you assumed the form of an elephant and terrified all the dānavas.
Since your leadership over the sages and the deities has been revealed,
you are therefore worshipped by the foremost gods, O Vināyaka.
Having propitiated you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the omniscient one who can assume any form at will,
for the sake of my purpose, with red flowers and water mixed with red sandalwood paste.
Clad in red garments, one should worship and recite [the mantra] on the fourth lunar day,
either three times or once a day, being self-restrained and moderate in diet.
One may bring under control a king, a prince, or even a royal minister;
or one may subjugate a kingdom together with its entire realm, free from all obstacles.
O Vighnavināyaka, ensure that there be no obstacle to my ascetic practice;
you have been well-conceived by me and especially worshipped with devotion.
Whatever fruit is obtained at all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained at all sacrifices,
that same fruit one attains by praising the god Vināyaka.
For him there shall be no adversity, nor shall he suffer defeat;
no obstacle shall arise for him, and once born, he shall remember his past lives.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain a boon within six months;
within a year, he attains spiritual accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
[Thus ends the Gaṇeśa-caturthī-vrata.
These are the Caturthī-vratas. Now, the Pañcamī-vratas.
Regarding Nāgapañcamī, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O King, the fifth lunar day is beloved by the nāgas and increases their joy."
It is said that on the fifth day there is a great festival for the nāgas.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kāliya, Maṇibhadraka,
Airāvata, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kārkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
These men grant fearlessness as well as the means of life to living beings—
those who bathe the nāgas with milk here on the fifth lunar day.
They bestow upon their families the gift of life— the granting of fearlessness—
toward those seven nāgas who are constantly being burned by their mother day and night.
