[88] Those who, endowed with faith and devotion, bathe those nāgas with ablutions mixed with cow’s milk and clarified butter, they cause them to be extinguished [of suffering].
"It is certain that there shall be no fear of snakes in their family," having first provided food for the Brahmins according to their desire.

[89] Having released [the water], may all those nāgas who dwell upon the surface of the earth, those who reside below in the Heli-sad region, and those situated in the intermediate space or in heaven, be pleased.
Homage indeed to all those nāgas who are in the rivers, those who are the serpents in the lakes, and those who are in the ponds and reservoirs.
Having honored the Nāgas and the Brahmins and having dismissed them as was appropriate,
the lord of men should thereafter eat together with his servants.
First one should eat sweet food, and secondly, thereafter, according to one's desire. Having made this rule, learn from me what the fruit thereof is:
upon death, one goes to Nāgapura, being honored by hosts of apsarases.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he enjoys himself for his desired length of time;
then, returning from there, this king shall become the foremost among those who bear weapons.
He is born enriched with all kinds of jewels and abounding in vehicles;
for five births in each Dvāpara age, he becomes a king.
Free from mental and physical ailments, and accompanied by his wife and sons,
he should therefore be honored and revered with offerings of ghee, milk-rice, and agallochum.
Thus ends the Nāgapañcamī [also known as the Nāgadaṣṭoddharaṇapañcamī]. Sumantu said:
O King, a man bitten by a snake who meets his death goes downward;
having gone downward, he immediately becomes free from poison—of this there is no doubt.
Śatānīka said: "Tell me what must be done if one's father, or brother, or even daughter, mother, son, or wife has been bitten by a snake."
[91] O best of Brahmins, tell me, O tiger among the twice-born, what gift, vow, or fast is for his liberation, so that I may indeed perform it.
Sumantu said: "O King, having fasted on the fifth lunar day, which increases the prosperity of the Nāgas,
listen, O Indra among kings, descendant of Bharata, to the specific ritual procedure for each individual."
O Lord of the Earth, that fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is declared to be full of merit; it should be observed.
O Bhārata, one should know that for twelve months the recitation of the *japya* must be performed;
on the fourth lunar day, however, eating only once a day (*ekabhakta*) is prescribed, while on that same day, eating only at night (*nakta*) is also proclaimed.
O King, having fashioned an elephant made of gold, or even one made of wood, or else one made of clay, which consists of many parts;
“Consisting of much weight” means consisting of a load of gold; “made of kaladhauta” means made of silver.
[On the fifth day, one should likewise worship the five Nāgas with devotion.
O observer of good vows, [one should worship them] with *karavīra* flowers, *śatapattras*, and *jātī* blossoms.
Likewise, one should worship the supreme Nāga with abundant perfumes;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with ghee, milk-rice, and sweetmeats.
Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, and Kambala;
likewise the Naga Kārkoṭaka and the Naga Aśvatara.
One should recite the names of Ghṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kāliya, Takṣaka,
and the great serpent Piṅgala month by month.
[93] At the end of the year, there should be a breaking of the fast and a feeding of great Brahmins;
O King, this ritual for the Naga was performed by Gaurika, who was learned in the Itihasas.
Likewise, O Lord of the Earth, a reddish-brown cow (*arjunī*) should be given to the reciter;
this is the rule declared by the wise for the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇaka*), O King.
O tiger among the Kurus, by giving a Naga fashioned from a bhāra of gold, as well as a cow, to Vyāsa, you shall attain freedom from your debt to your father.
O King, O hero, your father’s grandfather indeed performed such worship of the fifth day,
having abandoned the Nāgatas.
O King, having gone to the Puṣpottara assembly hall, and likewise to the Puṣpasad assembly hall; O King, having gone to the Śunāsīra assembly hall, and likewise to the Bhāgyasad assembly hall.
Having gone to the assembly of all the gods, he went to the assembly of the Lotus-born (Brahmā).
"Śunāsīrasadaḥ" means the assembly of Indra; "bhāgyasadaḥ" means the assembly of Āditya; "kañjajaḥ" is Brahmā. Others as well who shall perform this unsurpassed vow [shall likewise go].
"The one bitten shall attain liberation; he will reach an auspicious state.
Thus ends the *Nāgadaṣṭoddharaṇapañcamī* [94].
Likewise:
O lord of men, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On both sides of the door, one should draw fierce venomous serpents with cow dung.
One should worship the gateway according to the rules with curd, dūrvā sprouts, and kuśa grass,
as well as with offerings of fragrant flowers and by gratifying the brahmins.
O hero, for those who here worship the nāgas with devotion in that place,
there shall never be any fear of serpents anywhere.
Thus ends the Sarpābhaya-pañcamī;
likewise the Ālekhyasarpa-pañcamī.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the fifth day,
a man endowed with faith who paints the Nāgas using pigments of black and other colors—
One should worship with perfumes and flowers, and with ghee, milk-rice, and guggulu;
having worshipped the best of the twice-born with milk-rice enriched with clarified butter.
At night, he himself should eat that food, restrained and free from envy;
then the serpents, Takṣaka and the others, will become pleased with him.
For seven generations of his family, there shall be no fear from serpents.
This is the Ālekhyasarpa-pañcamī, also known as the Śānti-pañcamī.
Likewise:
"And so, O joy of the Kurus, on the fifth day of the month of Āśvayuja,
having fashioned serpents out of *kuśa* grass, one should worship them together with Indrāṇī."
O lord of the people, having bathed him with ghee, water, and milk,
[he should offer] wheat soaked in milk and various kinds of foods.

O tiger among the Kurus, O King, for that person who, being pure and endowed with devotion, worships the Nāgas according to the prescribed rite in that [place], Śeṣa and the others [will grant their favor].
The Nāgas become pleased here, O Lord, and he indeed attains peace;
having reached that world of peace, he rejoices for eternal years.
Thus ends the Śāntipañcamī. [96] [The Nāgamaitrīpañcamī]
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"That fifth lunar day is auspicious, blessed, and the remover of all sins; on this day, one who entirely avoids pungent and sour foods [attains great merit]."
One should bathe the nāgas with milk; they will then become friends.
Thus ends the Nāgamaitreyapañcamī, also known as Śāntipañcamī.
In the Varāha Purāṇa, Agastya said:
"O King, I shall proclaim the Śānti-vrata; listen to it."
By the performance of which there shall always be peace for householders.
O King, beginning on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika,
one should observe for one full year the practice of eating while abstaining from water.
Having worshipped the Lord Hari at night as he rests upon Śeṣa,
one should worship his feet with "To Ananta" and likewise his waist with "To Vāsuki."
Having worshipped the belly for Takṣaka and the chest for Karkoṭaka,
one should worship the throat for Padma and the two arms for Mahāpadma.
One should first worship the face as Śaṅkhapāla and the head as Kuṭilā; having worshipped them as belonging to Viṣṇu, one should then worship each separately.
Regarding the phrase "and separately": the meaning is that one should worship the eight nāgas, beginning with Ananta, individually.
One should perform a ritual bathing of Hari with milk, dedicating it to them;
furthermore, a wise person should offer oblations of milk along with sesame seeds before him.
Thus, at the end of the year, one should provide a feast for Brahmins;
having fashioned golden serpents, one should present them to the Brahmins.
O lord of men, for him who performs this vow with devotion in this manner,
there shall be constant peace, and no fear from the nāgas shall arise.
Thus ends the Śāntipañcamī vow.
[98] Now, the vows of the sixth day (Ṣaṣṭhīvratāni).
[Kāmaṣaṣṭhī] Regarding this, in the Varāha Purāṇa,
Agastya said:
O Great King, now listen to me as I speak of the vow of desire (kāmavrata),
by which desires— even those merely conceived in the mind— shall be perfectly accomplished.
He who observes this vow for one year, eating only fruit on the sixth lunar day,
and eating only at night on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha;
On the sixth day, however, the wise king should consume a single fruit;
thereafter, he should carefully eat pure rice while maintaining silence.
O Indra among kings, having remained for that single day on the seventh [lunar day] either with Brahmins or with fruits alone, O King, one should perform the concluding rite (pārayana).
One should perform the fire-ritual, worshipping Keśava in the form of Guha according to the prescribed rule, and observe the vow for one year.
Six-faced, Kārtika, Guha, Senānī, Pāvakātmaja,
Kumāra, and Skanda— by these names Viṣṇu is thus to be worshipped.
Upon the completion of this vow, one should provide a feast for Brahmins;
one should present to a Brahmin a six-faced image made entirely of gold.
O Six-faced God, may all my desires be fulfilled;
by your grace, O Brahmin, please accept this with devotion without delay.

[99] Having given this to a Brāhmaṇa along with a pair— “with a pair” meaning accompanied by a pair of garments— and having recited this mantra, all desires whatsoever shall be fulfilled right here in this very birth.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus ends the vow of Kāma.
[Regarding Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: O King, by eating only fruit on the sixth lunar day— especially during the month of Kārtika—
one who has been deprived of his kingdom will specifically regain his own realm before long.
O Great King, the sixth lunar day always grants all desires;
it should be observed with diligence at all times by one who seeks victory.
This great lunar day, the sixth (Ṣaṣṭhī), is beloved by Kārttikeya;
for it was on this day that the high-souled one attained the command of the divine army.
Because in ancient times Skanda was endowed with glory on this sixth day, therefore one should not eat on the sixth; likewise, one may attain the state of Bhārgava.
[100] Having offered the *arghya* to Kārttikeya while standing facing south, O observer of noble vows,
one should offer curd, ghee, water, and flowers with this mantra:
O Skanda, son of the Seven Sages, Mahāsena, you of great strength, born of Rudra and Umā, six-faced one, conceived by Gaṅgā— homage be to you!
May the Commander of the Divine Army be pleased;
may he fulfill my vow by giving food and whatever else remains to the brahmin.
Afterwards, having eaten at night and using the ground as his vessel,
he [obtains] that fruit which was declared by Skanda regarding this sixth-day vow.
Therefore, O Great King, listen as I describe this in its entirety:
he who, on the sixth lunar day, shall subsist on fruit and take his meal only at night;
Whether during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, one who is self-restrained and concentrated shall attain success,
steadfastness, nourishment, sovereignty, long life, and freedom from disease.
Skanda will undoubtedly bestow both benefits for the next world and for this one;
indeed, if one is unable to fast, the observer of the vow may subsist on food taken at night.
One should not eat oil on the sixth lunar day, nor during the daytime, O joy of the Kurus;
for that man who observes the *nakta* fast on the sixth day, O best of the Bharatas, [attains great merit].
Freed from all sins, one shall go to the abode of Gāṅgeya;
here, Gāṅgeya is Kārttikeya.
There will certainly be a residence in heaven; there is no doubt about this.
Having come here at the end of time, he shall partake of the fruits as described;
he will become a king of kings, worthy of being venerated even by the gods.
Thus ends the Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī.
[Regarding Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī] Āditya said:

Having diligently observed the night-meal (nakta) according to the prescribed rules on the sixth day of the dark fortnight at the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship [the deity] as "Aṃśumān."
Having consumed cow urine according to the prescribed rule, a person should sleep at night without food;
such a man obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, during Puṣya, they indeed desire the thousand-rayed, radiant sun.
"They desire" means they wish for it;
by consuming clarified butter there, a person obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer [the ritual] named Divākara;
having drunk cow's urine at night, one attains the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Mārtaṇḍa and consume sesame seeds;
one shall obtain the meritorious fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And in the month of Caitra, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the one named Haṃsa;
by consuming white flowers, a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the deity named Sūrya on the Kṛttikā constellation;
having drunk the meritorious water of kuśa grass, with anger conquered and the senses subdued.
One shall obtain the fruit of the Vainateya sacrifice, which is like the Mahāmedha sacrifice;
this refers to the month of Vaiśākha.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped the Lord of the Day (the Sun), one should drink water from the horns of a cow.
One enjoys the entire fruit of the gift of ten million cows by worshipping the deity named Arka in the month of Āṣāḍha and consuming cow dung.
O Lord, having worshipped the one named Aryaman in the month of Śrāvaṇa and drinking milk, he goes to the world of the Sun for two hundred years.
For more than ten thousand years, he rejoices in the abode of the Sun;
on the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Bhāskara.
By consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one obtains the full fruit of wisdom;
and on the sixth lunar day of the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship the deity known as Bhaga.
Having consumed a blade of dūrvā grass even once, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Furthermore, on the sixth day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the deity named Śakra.
One who eats the fruit with cow’s urine shall obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
at the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the worship of the Sun.
One should devotedly offer them milk-rice mixed with honey and well-saturated with clarified butter, along with gold and garments according to one's means.
That man who, for one year, should thus perform this practice continuously, ought to offer a black, milch cow to the Sun.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of his who performs the Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow with devotion:
he shall be completely liberated from all sins and endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
That man rejoices in the world of the Sun for eternal years. Thus ends the Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow.
Now follow the Saptamī vows.
[Śākasaptamī]:
Regarding that, it is stated in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, and restraint of the senses."
Worship of the Sun, the fire-oblation, contentment, and the avoidance of theft.
This dharma is always established as common to all vows. Likewise:
"The man who, having undertaken the Saptamī-kalpa, is nevertheless of a dark (tāmasa) nature..."
He who abandons [the vow] out of desire or even fear should be known as fallen by the wise;
however, that man who observes the fast on the seventh day and eats only at night—
Having observed a fast on the sixth day while eating only once on the fifth,
one should offer prepared vegetables along with various kinds of hard and soft foods.
Restraining his speech, a man shall eat at night for the sake of the gods and the Brahmins;
whoever performs this vow for as long as he lives, [shall attain great merit].
His prosperity, victory, and indeed the three goals of life increase;
and when he dies, he attains heaven, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
He rejoices in the world of the Sun for many series of Manvantaras;
and having returned here at the end of time, he chastises his enemies on all sides.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall be a donor for a long time as a lord of kings;
O King, he enjoys other horses in battle against his enemies.
O tiger among kings, by subsisting on vegetables and fasting on the seventh lunar day,
Gaya obtained that sacred ford known as Paitra-gaya.
Formerly, by Kuru here, through his subsistence on vegetables alone,
that Vivasvat made Kurukṣetra a field of dharma.
The seventh, ninth, sixth, third, and likewise the fifth lunar days—
these indeed are the "slaves to desire" for men and women right here in this world.
The seventh day of the month of Māgha, likewise the ninth of Āśvayuja,
the sixth of Bhādrapada, and the third of Vaiśākha are indeed auspicious.
The fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada should be known as the meritorious Nāgapañcamī;
indeed, these are the specific auspicious lunar days (tithis) within these months.
Having prepared well-prepared vegetables along with drinks and solid foods,
and having given them to a Brahmin according to his capacity, the observer of the vow eats afterwards at night.
O descendant of Kuru, this vow should be undertaken during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
however, it is traditionally taught that the first breaking of the fast occurs after four months.
And here, worship of the Fire-god should be performed with agasti flowers;
saffron should be used as an ointment, and incense made from aparājita plants should be offered.
One should perform the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise consume that same substance.
"Of Vibhāvasu" means of the Sun.
And here, milk-rice (pāyasa) is prescribed as the food offering for the deity.
That very same vegetable should be given to the Brahmins, while one should eat it oneself;
it should be accompanied by auspicious vegetables and provided with various kinds of food and drink.
[106] O King, on the second day of breaking the fast, those flowers which indeed possess auspicious fragrances, as well as white sandalwood, were offered to the Lord.
There should also be agallochum incense, as well as an offering of jaggery cakes;
the bath here is with water infused with *kuśa* grass, and the ritual consumption is of cow dung.
In the third [month], karavīra flowers as well as red sandalwood;
and among incenses, guggulu is always dear to the God.
Rice cooked with *śāli* grains is always dear to the God as an offering;
that very same [rice], O Lord, accompanied by foods to be chewed and licked, and joined with black potherbs (*kālaśāka*), the wise man should present to the Brahmins.
The wise know that bathing with a paste of white mustard seeds is also prescribed here.
The consumption of that [consecrated food] itself is auspicious, removing all sins and bringing good fortune;
at the conclusion of the third breaking of the fast, there should be a great feast for the Brahmins.
The hearing and the recitation of this Purāṇa are commended when performed while standing before the deity as well as before Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause [the teaching] to be heard from a Brāhmaṇa reciter, and not from one born of another caste;
likewise, one should honor all those Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability and with devotion.
O King, one should present two pure garments to the reciter;
when the reciter is honored, the god Bhāskara is always pleased.
Karavīra flowers according to his desire, as well as red sandalwood;
guggulu resin according to his desire, and milk-rice always according to his desire.
For him, sweetmeats are as desired, just like a copper vessel;
for him, ghee is as desired, and a reciter is always as desired.
And the Purāṇa of Savitṛ, O descendant of Kuru, may be recited at will;
thus is this seventh full lunar day always dear to the Lord of Rays.
Having observed this Śākasaptamī vow here, a person is not joined with misfortune.

Having commenced on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should perform it every month; furthermore, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be performed on whichever seventh day of the bright fortnight occurs during the four-month period. Thus, the breaking of the fast occurs three times in one year. In this very manner, such a vow should be performed throughout the intervening years [for as long as one lives].
[Yajñasaptamī]
Vādudeva said: Next,
I shall now describe in brief the occasional sacrifices (naimittika-yajñas) to be performed on the seventh lunar day, during eclipses, and especially at the transits of the sun (saṅkrāntis).
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, having once eaten sacrificial food during the day,
and having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at twilight and prostrated before Varuṇa;
Having restrained his senses and meditated upon him, he should sleep on the ground at night; having gone to a bed of darbha grass, he should bathe in the morning and remain well-restrained.
At the beginning and likewise at the end of everything, one should worship Varuṇa as before;
for the Bahvṛca should indeed offer oblations into the fire, having duly conceived it as the Sun-fire.
I shall now describe, in brief, the rite of making fire into the sun and the libation:
having inscribed the syllable Oṃ with the Astra-mantra and sprinkled the fire with the Sāvitrī-mantra.
"With the *astra* [mantra]" means with the *astra-mantra*. "With the *Sāvitrī*" means with the *Sūrya-gāyatrī*.
Having scattered and spread out the *darbha* grass in a place and at a time as desired, one should touch the vessels in the manner of a wheel, with blades pointing eastward and northward.
Having prepared two blades of kuśa grass as a purifier (pavitra), with tips intact and measuring a span (prādeśa) in length,
one should sprinkle the vessels with it, purify them, and then liquefy the clarified butter (ājya).
Then, having lit a firebrand over a vessel situated in the northern part and performed the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*),
one should likewise perform the purification of the clarified butter (*ājyotpavana*) three times.

Having wiped the *sruva* ladle and other implements with those *darbha* blades that have been sprinkled with water, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire; there, one should worship the Sun and perform recitation (*japa*).
O tiger among kings, the oblation is offered with the hand placed on the ground, upon a support, or in the palm; it is not offered while held in mid-air.
In the intermediate space, over the *parṇika* grass and so forth, one should take the *sruva* ladle with the right hand and offer again into the purifying fire.
All the rites previously enjoined should be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
“With the heart” means with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
Having performed the libations starting from the sun, one should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should worship Varuṇa with reverence on the seventh lunar day of the month of Māgha.

One should give pieces of sugar-candy to the Brahmins according to one's ability, and one should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's means; thus the fruit born of sacrifice is obtained.
And thus, one should worship the Sun in Phālguna, the Radiant One (Aṃśumālin) in Caitra,
Dhātṛ in the month of Vaiśākha, and Indra-Ravi in Jyeṣṭha.
One should worship Bhaga in the months of Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa,
likewise Parjanya in Bhādrapada, and Tvaṣṭṛ in Āśvina and Kārttika.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Mitra, and in Pauṣa, one should worship Viṣṇu as the Sun;
by doing so day after day, one obtains the desired fruit that is said to result from a full year of worship.
One endowed with devotion and faith shall swiftly attain all that;
likewise, having fashioned a golden chariot when the year is complete.
Yoked with seven horses, adorned with various jewels,
and featuring a beautiful image of the Sun in the center fashioned from pure gold.
Having adorned it with jewels and placed it upon a golden lotus,
he set that excellent chariot in motion, with the charioteer standing at the front.
Having honored the preceptor, who knows all ritual manuals and is surrounded by twelve Brahmins who are the presiding deities of the months in their proper order, at the front of the chariot.
Having intentionally praised him like the sun, one should indeed worship him with jewels and other offerings;
having thus fully honored the brahmins who are the lords of the months, one should then present the offering.
One should present a chariot, an umbrella, a village, cows, and auspicious land to the preceptor;
and one should offer horses to the twelve lords of the months.
Thus, having offered ornaments such as gold and jewels according to one's devotion and capacity,
and having prostrated before him, one should announce that the vow is complete.
"From this point forward, there shall be no fault for me even if I fail to perform my vows.
"So be it," the lords of brahmins and great teachers replied again and again.
Having bestowed many blessings, he should say, "May [the deity] be pleased," [adding],
"O Āditya, by whatever desire you have been propitiated through these vows."
May he grant you that desire; may your vow be fulfilled—especially toward virtuous brahmins and those who are disciplined.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability to the poor and the destitute,
and having fed the Brahmins, one should thus conclude this vow.
Having performed this for seven years, the king becomes righteous;
thus indeed, O King, he shall become exceedingly dear to the Sun.
He enjoys for more than a hundred years, in happiness, a perfected mandala that is a hundred yojanas in extent, free from rivals, and without thorns.
Even one devoid of wealth, having performed everything as prescribed, should give a copper chariot with devotion at the conclusion of the vow.
The wise man enjoys a vast mandala eighty yojanas in extent;
even one who is destitute of wealth should likewise offer a chariot made of flour.
Long-lived, stainless, and happy, he enjoys [the earth] for sixty yojanas;
at the end of the kalpa, having once reached the world of the sun, he shall attain it.
Thus ends the Yajñasaptamī vow.
[Rathāṅgasaptamī] Vāsudeva said:
O upholder of my lineage, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
eating a single meal is prescribed, and on the sixth day, eating only at night is declared.
Some desire the fast of the excellent vow on the seventh day;
others here desire its fulfillment on the sixth or indeed on the seventh.
Having observed a fast on the sixth lunar day, the wise man should worship the Sun with gathered karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
O mighty-armed one, O observer of noble vows, one should worship the Lord of the gods, Śaṅkara, the Sun, the lord of the planets, with fragrant guggulu resin.
In this manner, one should worship the Sun for four months beginning with Māgha;
furthermore, for the sake of one's own purification, there is the consumption of cow dung.
One should perform a bath with cow dung here for the sake of self-purification,
and one should also feed the Brahmins of both celestial and terrestrial realms with devotion.
In the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha as well, white sandalwood is prescribed,
as are white flowers endowed with auspicious fragrance.
Likewise, black agallochum should be used as incense, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is the supreme food offering;
with that very same [offering], O great-minded one, one should feed those brahmins.
The spiritual son (putraka) should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform an ablution with that very same substance;
it is prescribed that during the months beginning with Kārttika, this should be done with Agasti flowers.
O tiger among the Yadus, the worship consists of incense that is invincible,
as well as an offering of molasses cakes and sugarcane juice, so it is remembered.
With that very [offering], one should feed those brahmins according to one's capacity;
one should also cause them to sip water with kuśa grass and perform their bath for the sake of success.
O Great-minded One, at the conclusion of the third fast, in the month of Māgha,
it is declared that the food and milk-rice (pāyasa) should be twice the amount.
Wise men should perform the worship of the God of gods according to their ability,
as well as the mounting of the chariot and the chariot procession, O observer of noble vows.
Indeed, when one possesses the means, a gift of a golden chariot should be made for the sake of attaining the vow,
as prescribed here when wealth is available.
Thus, O son, this auspicious seventh [vow], Rathāṅgā, has been described;
it is renowned as Mahāsaptamī, which brings great merit and great prosperity.
"Having fasted on this day, one obtains wealth, sons, fame, and knowledge.
Thus ends the Rathāṅgasaptamī (also known as Rathasaptamī).
Brahmā said: O Mahādeva, in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, one who has conquered his senses,
having fasted on the sixth day, [should worship] with offerings of perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the Maker of Day, one should sleep at night before him;
then, having awakened on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun with devotion.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
[offering] pieces of sweetmeat, *modakas*, as well as cakes made of sugarcane and molasses.

[115] Then, when the year is complete, on the seventh day, the wise one should cause the festival procession of the God of gods to be performed; he should carry it out according to the previously mentioned procedure.
But having performed even a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance, he who beholds with devotion that Sun, the Lord of the World, mounted upon his chariot, goes to the supreme goal.
On the third day, eating only once; on the fourth, eating only at night is prescribed;
on the fifth, eating only what is unasked for; and on the sixth, one should likewise fast.
On the seventh day, one should break the fast after seeing the God seated upon his chariot,
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite with devotion and according to one's capacity, O Three-eyed One.
Having fashioned a golden chariot resting upon a copper vessel,
one should place within the center of the chariot the newly consecrated *vyoman* (celestial orb) adorned with jewels.
One should place a ruby in the center, a pearl in the east;
then an indranīla gem in the south, and a marakata gem in the west.
O Rudra, O Destroyer of Andhaka, the wise one should place coral in the north, along with a vajra;
it may be white, yellow, black, or even red.
O Bhava, one should place these garments in all directions;
at the position of the chariot, there should be banners adorned with bells and ornaments.
Having thoroughly adorned the chariot on all sides with garlands of flowers,
and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rule, one should offer it to Bhāskara.
Or, having fed the Brahmins, one should present it to the teacher;
O Śaṅkara, whoever studies the seventh Kalpa along with its narratives [attains this].
O beloved of Pārvatī, that twice-born man should be known as the preceptor for the castes in their proper order— namely, for the Sauras, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Śaivas.
But in the absence of gold, one should prescribe a silver chariot;
in its absence, one should have a copper chariot or a celestial chariot (vyoma) constructed.
But in the absence of copper, a chariot made of flour is prescribed;
O Mahādeva, it should be placed upon a copper vessel containing gold.
One should present a pair of silk garments to a Brāhmaṇa—
specifically to the aforementioned Mahādeva, the high-souled reciter.
Adorned with the five jewels, with beautiful limbs, and clothed in white,
one should perform this according to one's own capacity, O Virūpākṣa, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
O Hara, O Rudra, this meritorious, sin-destroying Rathāṅgā Saptamī has been described to you by me; it is celebrated as truly great.
O Upholder of the Earth, bathing, giving gifts, performing fire-offerings,
and worshipping the Lord of the Planets shall result in merit equal to a hundred thousandfold.
Thus, when the seventh day of the month of Māgha has arrived, this [day] is most meritorious;
by fasting upon it with devotion, a man shall become an attendant of the Sun.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the state of a deity, a Kṣatriya may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa;
a Vaiśya attains the status of a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya.
A maiden shall obtain a husband endowed with learning and discipline;
a childless woman shall find a son and good fortune, O Lord of the Gaṇas.
O Destroyer of Tripura, beloved of Pārvatī, even a widow who fasts on this seventh day shall not encounter widowhood in future births.
Having many sons and much wealth,
she shall become beloved by her husband for as long as seven births, whether she be a woman or likewise a man.
Thus ends the Rathasaptamī.
[Regarding the Phalasaptamī] Sumantu said:
Then, O Mahāmati, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, one should first observe a fast; hear now what the procedure for that occasion shall be.
On the fourth day, he should eat only what is unasked for; on the fifth, he should take a single meal;
on the sixth, devoted to fasting, he should conquer his anger and master his senses.
Having propitiated the Sun with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
the Putraka should sleep at night on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the deity.
Meditating in his mind upon the God who destroys the suffering of all beings,
who pacifies all defects, and who annihilates all sins.
Having awakened on the seventh day, he should perform a feeding of Brahmins after having worshipped the Sun with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Indeed, they declare that the offerings for the deity there consist of fruits:
dates, coconuts, and likewise rose-apples.
Mātuluṅga fruits are prescribed here by the wise;
having fed the Brahmins with them, one should then eat them oneself.
Likewise, O observer of noble vows, listen to other [substitutes] in the absence of these as well:
one should have flour made from rice and wheat prepared, O leader of the Gaṇas.
One should cook these, made with molasses as their core, by means of heating them in ghee;
mixed with four parts of barley-gruel, one should offer them to Āditya.
Then, having performed the fire-rite, one should feed the Brahmins;
in this manner, the supreme vow is to be observed for twelve months.
Month after month, one should observe this vow with devotion: subsisting on fruit, gathering fruit, and eating fruit, while also feeding Brahmins.
Listen also, O observer of noble vows, to the procedure for the ritual bath and the consumption [of the five products]:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
O observer of noble vows, a paste made from sesame and mustard seeds, white clay,
a paste of dūrvā grass with ghee, and water used for washing a cow’s horn [are also recommended].
The exudation of the *jātī* flower is highly recommended for the act of bathing;
furthermore, when consumed, these [substances] indeed remove all sins.
The wise know that starting from the month of Bhādrapada, they follow the sequence accordingly;
thus, having reached the end of the year, one should feed the best of the twice-born.
Then, O Mahādeva, one should offer to them divine and terrestrial fruits;
and those vows should be performed with golden fruits according to one's ability.
Or else a cow with her calf, or land endowed with crops,
or a brick mansion provided with all kinds of grain.
One should give red garments, a copper vessel, and coral;
these are for one who possesses wealth, but hear from me what is for the poor man.
Having fed the twice-born with fruits made of flour mixed with sesame powder, one should then present them with silver fruits.
One should present to the preceptor a pair of garments dyed with cinnabar,
along with gold and the five precious gems, for the sake of Mahādeva.
In this manner, dear son, the annual breaking of the fast is properly completed;
thus indeed is this most meritorious seventh day, which destroys all sins.
Having fasted upon which all men go to the same world as the Sun,
being constantly honored by the gods and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The man who always worships the Sun with this [hymn] goes to the Maker of Day,
liberated from poverty, suffering, and evil deeds.
A Brāhmaṇa attains liberation; a Kṣatriya goes to heaven;
a Vaiśya attains the same world as the gods of wealth; and a Śūdra shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
A childless woman obtains a son, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate;
even a widow who is chaste shall, through devotion, worship the Sun with this [rite].
O giver of honor, a woman shall not suffer widowhood in another birth;
indeed, this Phala-saptamī should be known as equal to the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
O Ḍiṇḍi, it is remembered that this bestows all desires upon those who read and listen to it.
Thus ends the saptamī of the fruit. [The saptamī of names:
Brahmā said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the secret Nāmasaptamī,
which is indeed the most sacred of the sacred and the destroyer of great sins.
The seventh [chapter], composed by Mātreya, delivers men from existence—seven descendants, seven ancestors, and the fathers as well; of this there is no doubt.
He who performs the Nāmasaptamī cuts through diseases that are difficult to cure, conquers enemies that are hard to defeat, and attains wealth that is difficult to acquire.
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking sons obtains sons; and one seeking dharma shall attain dharma.
Protecting all the commitments (samayas), the wise one should act in this manner; O being, listen to the commitments for the sake of your welfare as I speak them.
A person devoted to the Sun should, on the seventh lunar day, perform acts of friendship toward Gaṇanāyaka in every way, and should also meditate upon Bhāskara.
On the seventh day, one should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing;
one should neither bathe with *āmalaka* fruits nor engage in any quarrel whatsoever.
[122] In the same way, a wise man should neither give nor drink impure food or liquor;
he should not harbor malice toward anyone, nor should he practice harshness.
One should not speak to a Caṇḍāla nor to a woman in her courses;
one should not touch a person of low status, nor should one look upon a corpse.
One should not snap one's fingers, nor laugh, nor sing, nor even a song;
one should not dance with excessive passion, nor play musical instruments and the like.
One should not lie down with a woman, nor should one indulge in gambling;
one should not weep with the shedding of tears, nor should one eat the five-leafed vegetable.
“Durodara” means gambling. “Pañcaśākikā” refers to the five vegetables: roots, tubers, fruits, flowers, and leaves.
One should not pull at the lice on one's head, nor should one practice speaking falsehoods.
One should avoid speaking ill of others and excessive grief.
One should not strike any living being, nor should one overeat;
one should not sleep during the day, and one should avoid hypocrisy and deceit.
[123] One should also diligently avoid wandering in the streets;
furthermore, O Destroyer of Tripura, hear now another rule regarding this matter.
The Nāmasaptamī vow should always be performed starting from the month of Caitra;
however, in the month of Caitra, the Sun-god is to be worshipped with the word "Dhāta."
In Vaiśākha, he is indeed called Aryaman; in Jyeṣṭha, he is proclaimed as Mitra;
in Āṣāḍha, he is known as Vāruṇa; and in Nabhas, he is said to be Indra.
Vivasvat is remembered [as the presiding deity] in Nabhasya, while Parjanya is traditionally assigned to Āśvayuj;
Pūṣan belongs to the month of Kārttika, and he is said [to preside] over Mārgaśīrṣa.
Bhaga is to be honored in the month of Pauṣa, while Tvaṣṭṛ is said to be worshipful in Māgha;
Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the month of Phālguna, and the Sun-god (Bhāskara) is to be saluted.
On every seventh day, the wise man should feed those who prepare the food;
having fed them according to the prescribed rite, food with ghee should be given.
A gold māṣaka as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given to the officiating priest alone;
furthermore, food with ghee and red garments should indeed be offered.
But in the absence of those who may be fed, the best of the twice-born are worthy recipients;
likewise, they should be fed with supreme faith by those endowed with it.
"Furthermore, the reciter is always a Brāhmaṇa who knows the ritual manuals (kalpa). Thus,
O Leader of the Gaṇas, this seventh [rule] has been told to you."
When heard, it removes sin and bestows the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Nāmasaptamī vow. [124]
[Jayā Saptamī] Brahmā said:
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—
Mahājayā, Nandā, Bhadrā, and Vāmā are proclaimed.
When the constellation consisting of five stars occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
then that seventh day should be known as Jayā.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited, or used for libations and the worship of gods upon that [day], all is said to be multiplied a hundredfold; so too is the worship of the Sun.
O Bhāskara, when the swan has mounted the swan, that supreme white seventh [tithi] should be observed by oneself according to this rite.
O Lord of the Earth, in ancient times, there were three breaking-fast days for that [vow];
the first breaking-fast was prescribed by the wise to occur after the first four months.
O observer of noble vows, the flowers of the *karavīra* are prescribed here, as well as red sandalwood; for incense, *guggulu* is traditionally recommended.
[125] One should indeed offer *kāsāra* mixed with white sugar as an oblation (*naivedya*) to the Sun.
*Kāsāra* is well known in the world as being prepared by frying wheat flour in molasses and ghee. *Sitāsāra* is that which contains a great abundance of sugar.
Having worshipped Mārtaṇḍa, the lord of the wise, according to this procedure—
One should honor the earthly Brahmins with various kinds of food and edibles according to the prescribed rule;
one should feed the Brahmins at the Kāsāra, for thus the breaking of the fast becomes fruitful.
One should eat in that manner oneself, being pure and observing silence;
it is proclaimed that there is a single meal on the fifth day, while a night-meal (nakta) is prescribed for the sixth.
Having observed the fast on the seventh day, the breaking of the fast should take place on the eighth;
here, one should bathe with white mustard seeds and consume milk-rice.
May Bhānu be pleased with me here; likewise, [I offer] tooth-wood and that which is born of the sun.
O Bhīma, hear now the second account of my breaking the fast as I relate it.
One should prescribe *mālatī* flowers, as well as *śrīkhaṇḍa* sandalwood,
milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the food offering (*naivedya*), and the *vijaya* incense for the Sun.
O Lord, one should feed the Brahmins and likewise eat oneself;
in this rite, one should proclaim the name of the deity, saying, "May the Sun be pleased with me."
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and use a tooth-stick made of khadira wood;
this is the procedure for the second breaking of the fast that has now been declared by me.
Now listen to me as I describe what should be done on the third breaking of the fast:
on this occasion, a wise person should worship the Sun with Agasti flowers.
In this context, the unguent is said to be sandalwood and saffron;
likewise, *silhaka* resin is prescribed as the incense that is supremely pleasing to the Sun.
Rice cooked with śāli grains, combined with milk-rice (rasāla), should be offered as a sacrificial oblation;
it should be given to the Brāhmaṇas and likewise eaten by oneself.
One should consume water infused with *kuśa* grass and use the *badarī* fruit for cleaning the teeth;
one should then recite the name of the deity: "May Vikartana be pleased with me."
At the end of the rainy season, the worship of the God of gods must be performed according to the prescribed rite,
with offerings of perfumes and flowers, as well as various theatrical performances.
Having thus honored the Lord of Gods with gifts of cows, gifts of land, and the gratification of Brahmins, he stood before the God.
One should cause the recitation of the book, which brings supreme merit and fortune, to be performed,
having diligently honored the reciter with garments, perfumes, and incense.
Standing before the deity, one should then recite the mantra:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, destroyer of all diseases and afflictions!"
O Lord of the planets, scorcher of the worlds, maker of light, dispeller of darkness!
This seventh lunar day, named Jayā, has been established for the sake of the God of gods.
O Hero, by my grace, this auspicious, merit-bestowing, and sin-removing seventh day shall be [efficacious] for him who performs it according to this rite.
O Lord, for one who has observed this Saptamī, O Hero, all his acts such as bathing and so forth shall become a hundredfold, and men shall attain great splendor.
Having obtained wealth, grain, gold, sons, long life, and strength,
O tiger among gods, one goes to the heavenly world.
Therefore, having returned from there to earth once more, the wise one shall become a king of kings.
Thus, O hero, this seventh [vow] has been described, named Jayā.
That which, when performed, heard, or remembered, bestows the world of Haṃsas— thus is the Jayā Saptamī. [The Vijayā Saptamī.]
If the seventh day of the bright fortnight should fall on a Sunday, that seventh day is named Vijayā; what is given on that day yields great fruit.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and likewise fasting—
all these on Vijayā-saptamī destroy even the most heinous sins.
On the fifth day there should be a single meal; on the sixth, they prescribe eating only at night;
on the seventh, there should be a fast; and on the eighth, the breaking of the fast occurs.
Devoted to fasting on the sixth lunar day, one should worship the Sun as mounted upon his horse,
with perfumes, flowers, and offerings, full of devotion and endowed with faith. "Devoted to fasting" means one who intends to observe the fast on the seventh day of victory (vijayā-saptamī).
Having prepared an offering on the ground before the deity,
one should sleep while reciting either the Gāyatrī or the Saura-sūkta.
Or having awakened on the seventh lunar day, O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should perform ablutions and [recite] the three-syllabled or the six-syllabled Mahāśvetā mantra.
Having worshipped the Lord of Planets and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rules,
one should feed the Brahmins with devotion and according to one's capacity, O Leader of the Gaṇas.
One should offer rice cooked with milk, cakes, and sweets filled with sugar according to one's ability,
as well as milk-rice with ghee to the Brahmins according to one's means.
Having given the sacrificial fee with devotion, one should then dismiss the Brahmins.
Thus, O God, has this meritorious Vijayasaptamī been described.
Having fasted there, a person shall go to the supreme abode of Vairocana;
red oleanders and saffron are for the unguent.
Indeed, the Vijaya incense in this [rite] brings satisfaction to the Sun;
it is meritorious, a remover of sins, and a destroyer of great transgressions.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, what is given or offered here does not perish"—
thus is known the Saptamī [Jayantī Saptamī].
Brahmā said:
O Three-eyed One, that seventh lunar day in the bright fortnight of Māgha is called Jayantī; it is meritorious, auspicious, and a destroyer of sins.
O beloved of Pārvatī, listen to the procedure by which one should observe the fast;
four ways of breaking the fast have been described by the learned.
On the fifth day, however, there is a single meal; on the sixth, a night-meal is prescribed;
on the seventh, there is fasting; and on the eighth, the breaking of the fast occurs.
O observer of noble vows, in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra,
one should offer *baka* flowers, grains, saffron, and ointments.
In this rite, the food offering consists of sweetmeat balls (modakas), and clarified butter is prescribed as the incense;
the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the supreme means of purification.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should feed the Brahmins with sweetmeats according to one's ability;
O Lord of Beings, one should indeed offer rice cooked with milk to the twice-born with devotion.
Whoever thus worships Bhāskara, who is honored by the world,
shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every such breaking of the fast.
Having performed worship on the second breaking-fast day, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
this applies to the months of Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha, O observer of good vows.
O observer of noble vows, for the purpose of worshipping the Sun here, one should offer white lotuses;
O Bhīma, white sandalwood is prescribed, and guggulu is said to be the incense.
O Lord of Gods, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, as well as in Bhādrapada, O All-pervading One, the food offering consists of molasses-cakes and the consumption of cow dung.
In the month of Āśvina as well, one should prescribe red sandalwood;
here, *mālatī* flowers are used, and the incense is said to be *vijaya*.
An offering of food filled with ghee should be presented, as well as a meal for the twice-born;
furthermore, the consumption of water infused with kuśa grass is the supreme means for purifying the body.
This third fast, known as Pāraṇa, is declared to be the destroyer of sins.
O King, for the sake of your welfare, I shall now describe the fourth *pāraṇa*, which yields the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices and is dear to the Sun-god.
O Hero, in the month of Kārttika, and likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa,
O Śiva, and in Puṣya, O tiger among gods— listen now to the flowers in their entirety.
Red oleanders, red sandalwood,
incense known as Amṛta, and milk-rice as the supreme food offering.
Likewise, the *vajra* consisting of *arjunīya* is considered the supreme *prāśana*. The "Amṛtadhūpa" is described in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* as follows: agarū, candana, mustā, silhaka, and vṛṣaṇa.
However, that which arises from the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should be prepared in equal proportions.
“Arjunīyam” means derived from the cow; “vajram” means clarified butter (ghṛta).
Herein the names of the high-souled Bhāskara have been proclaimed:
Citrabhānu, Bhānu, Āditya, and likewise Bhāskara.
"May [the deity] be pleased"— with such words at all fast-breaking ceremonies and similar occasions,
whoever performs the worship of the Fire-god according to this rule, [attains the highest reward].
On this lunar day, O Mahādeva, he attains the supreme state;
having thus observed the seventh [lunar day], O Bhīma, one shall obtain all desires.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth;
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one attains abundant auspiciousness.
O Bhīma, when a full year has passed,
worship should be performed for the Sun with offerings of perfumes and flowers, and by the satiation of Brahmins.
With various kinds of spectacles and by honoring the reciter,
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and having fully honored the Brahmins—
Having honored the reciter who is twice-born, one should utter these words:
"O Lord, in matters of dharma and always in matters of worldly affairs for me..."
May there always be victory in all undertakings concerning desire;
then one should dismiss the Brahmins and the reciter, that best of the twice-born.
Whoever performs this [rite] in this manner shall always attain victory;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of the Sun.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot produced by the power of his poetry,
he resembled the sun in brilliance and was like a bird in his splendor.
“Kavija” means gold, produced from Agni, who is the poet (kavi). “Pataga” refers to the Sun. Thus ends the Jayantī Saptamī. [The Aparājitā Saptamī follows.]
Brahmā said: O Lord of the Gaṇas, that seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is renowned as Aparājitā, which destroys great sins.

On the fourth day, one should observe eating a single meal; on the fifth, one should prescribe eating only at night; likewise, there is fasting on the sixth, and breaking the fast is prescribed on the seventh.
In this regard, four concluding offerings (pāraṇas) have been described by the wise:
karavīra flowers as well as red sandalwood.
The incense rite is performed with *guggulu* resin, and the food offering consists of molasses cakes;
this is the prescribed procedure for the months beginning with Nabhasya (Bhādrapada).
White flowers, O Bhīma, as well as white sandalwood, incense, and clarified butter are prescribed here for the Sun; the food offering is milk-rice (pāyasa).
This procedure is proclaimed for the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa;
thereafter, the flowers of Agastya and saffron are used as an ointment.
For incense, storax is prescribed, or else that produced from the *bilva* tree;
and the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of *śāli* rice and *rasālā* during the months beginning with Phālguna.
O Lord of Beings, red lotuses, mustaka, and sandalwood are prescribed as the incense for Ananta; the food offering consists of sweet cakes made with jaggery.
O Lord of Beings, one should burn sandalwood with knots, agallochum, and likewise storax, as well as musta, camphor, and sugar for three days.
Thus has this Anantadhupa been described, O best of gods. "Granthi" refers to *granthiparṇa*; "Indu" refers to camphor.
Indeed, this procedure regarding Jyeṣṭhā and the other [nakṣatras] has been thus declared by the wise.
Listen, O observer of noble vows, to the names of the god and his [sacred] drinks:
Bharga, Aṃśumān, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Tripurāntaka.
And at all the concluding meals (pāraṇas), one should proclaim, "May [the deity] be pleased.
[The offerings are] cow's urine, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), warm ghee, and milk.
But he who should perform this seventh [rite], O King, according to this procedure,
shall also always remain unconquered by his enemies in battle.
Having slain his enemies, he shall also conquer the three aims of life; of this there is no doubt.
And having attained the three aims of life, he shall reach the city of the Sun.
Having worshipped the single Pūrṇāṃśu, one should complete the Khaga [rite] according to one's ability,
with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and food, and by listening to the Purāṇas.
By means of gifts of food, by the satiation of Brāhmaṇas,
and by honoring the reciter who is always dear to the Sun-god, [one attains the goal].
O Hero, that man who always performs worship on the seventh lunar day should give an elephant adorned with ornaments to Bhāskara.
Having utterly defeated his enemies, he goes to the same world as the *haṃsas*,
by means of a vehicle born of white lotuses and adorned with the banner of the son of the Ganges.
One should become like the lord of rivers and a frequenter of rivers.
"Śuklaja" means gold; "āpageya" is also indeed gold. "Āpagādhipa" is Varuṇa.
Thus ends the seventh [chapter], the Aparājitā.
[Mahājayā Saptamī] Brahmā said:
When the sun enters its transit on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight, [that is the Mahājayā Saptamī].
Then indeed that seventh lunar day, beloved of the Sun, shall be a great victory.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these are declared by the highly effulgent Sun to be multiplied ten millionfold.
That man who bathes the Sun with ghee out of devotion to her shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and thereafter go to the abode of the Sun.
The devoted man who bathes the Sun with milk,
being liberated from all sins, attains the same world as the Sun.
Having remained there for a long time, the lotus-born one becomes a king;
this is declared to be the seventh [day] of great victory, O Destroyer of Tripura.
Having fasted with devotion upon this [day], a person shall obtain the unshakable heavenly realm;
from there he goes to the Supreme Brahman, having gone to which he does not grieve.
Thus ends the Mahājayā Saptamī.
[Regarding the Nandā Saptamī:
Brahmā said:
O Hero, that seventh day in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Nandā; it is auspicious and brings joy to all.
On the fifth day, however, a single meal is prescribed; on the sixth, a night-meal is proclaimed;
and on the seventh, the wise declare that one should observe a fast.
In this regard, the wise who desire [merit] prescribe three types of offerings here:
jasmine flowers, as well as fragrant sandalwood.
In this case, one should prescribe incense blended with camphor and agallochum;
and curd-rice mixed with sugar is the food offering dear to the Sun.
One should give that very same [food] to the Brahmins and then eat it oneself;
this is the rule for the first breaking of the fast, performed for the sake of worshipping the Sun.
O Lord, [offer] palāśa flowers, as well as yakṣacandana,
camphor, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, uśīra, and likewise silhaka.
O Bhīma, sa-granthi, vṛṣaṇa, kuṅkuma, gṛñjana,
and likewise harītakī— this is called the Yakṣāṅka.
Incense is prescribed as awakening, and the food offering consists of candied sweets and other delicacies;
likewise, black aloe-wood, sihla, vālaka, and vṛṣaṇa.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas with sandalwood, tagara, mustā, and prabodha, mixed with sugar and various sweetmeats.
Having obtained a nimba leaf, one should then eat while restraining one's speech;
this is proclaimed as the rule for the second breaking of the fast.
One should bring pure blue lotuses, incense of guggulu,
and an offering of milk-rice for the pleasure of the Sun.
O Hero, for the sake of purification, one should apply sandalwood paste and consume clarified butter; this supreme rite has been declared by you even for the third [day].
Listen to the names of the God which always purify men:
"May Viṣṇu, Bhaga, and Dhātṛ be pleased"—thus one should utter these words.
The man who always performs the Nandā rite according to this procedure shall attain all his desires in this world and obtain liberation.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth; a seeker of knowledge shall obtain fame and knowledge, and likewise, a seeker of fame shall obtain fame.
Having thus obtained all his desires, he rejoices for eternal years;
then, having gone to the abode of the Sun, he rejoices in the Nandana and Nandana-vardhana groves.
Thus, O twice-born one, this mother of Nanda, known as Nandā, has been described by me;
having fasted upon her and likewise heard [her story], one indeed rejoices as if having attained the Sun himself.
Thus ends the Nandā-saptamī.
[Regarding the Bhadrā-saptamī],
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the Pramathas, when the constellation of the Sun occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, then that [day] attains auspiciousness.
“The constellation of Savitṛ” is Hasta. Likewise:
“On the fourth day, one should prescribe a single meal; on the fifth, a night-meal.”
On the sixth [day], "unasked" (ayācita) is prescribed; after that, it is a fast (upavāsa).
O Lord of Gods, O Hero, the wise have declared that the ceremonial bathing (snapana) there should be performed with ghee,
as well as with milk and sugarcane juice.
Having snapped his fingers before the Lord of Gods, one should anoint him with sandalwood paste;
one should offer guggulu to him and then perform a fire-oblation (homa) in front of him.
It is made from wheat flour, stainless and resembling the moon;
it is golden, accompanied by jaggery, and adorned with red flowers.
Where its horn is the Īśāna [face], there one should indeed place a pearl;
where its tip is, there one should place a ruby or a red gem.
A wise person should place an emerald in the southwest, a ruby in the northwest,
or a lotus in the north, according to his capacity.
On the seventh lunar day, a wise man should not touch heretics, those who follow improper occupations, those who act like cats, or outcastes; he should also avoid sleeping during the day.
Whoever performs the seventh-day rite there according to this procedure,
for him all auspicious sacrifices always proceed successfully.
"He who gives *bhadra* on that [day], his son shall be *bhadra*.
Diṇḍi said:
"What is this that is called *bhadra*, and how does one obtain an ornament from it?"
"What is the fruit of giving that, and by what rite is it bestowed?
Brahmā said:
"The sky is called 'Bhadra'; it is a beautiful emblem of the gods."
One should prepare a beautiful, four-cornered [cake] made of rice flour,
mixed with cow's ghee and combined with candied sugar.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, [one should worship] especially with the powder of the four kinds of fruits, with grapes,
and with coconuts that possess auspicious fragrances.
The wise one should place a central sapphire for Bhadra according to his own capacity,
as well as topaz, emerald, and ruby.
And one should gradually place incomparable rubies in the corners;
O Lord, it should be auspicious if it measures one *prastha*, or even half a *prastha*.
Having performed this rite, one should place it before the deity;
or else, one should give it to the reciter, or otherwise eat it oneself.
Whoever performs this rite and bestows auspiciousness shall indeed attain blessings and go to the abode of the Lord of Rays.
Then, mounted upon a celestial vehicle, he would go to the world of Brahmā without a doubt;
in splendor he would resemble the sun, and likewise in radiance he would be equal to the son of Atri.
Equal in splendor to the Lord of Rays (the Sun) and in brilliance to Śaṅkara, he shall therefore come again to the earth and become its protector; of this there is no doubt.
"Through the grace of Gopati, one attains a dwelling honored by all lords of the earth.
Thus, O hero, has this seventh [vow] named Bhadrā been described.
O Hero, O Lord of the Gaṇas, by fasting upon which a man may attain the world of Brahmā—those who hear it here, those who recite it, and those who perform it; |||
Having attained auspiciousness, they all go to that eternal Brahman.
Thus ends the Bhadrasaptamī vow [also known as Trigatisaptamī].
Brahmā said: "O son of Vyāsa,
that man here who, during the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
repeatedly recites with devotion the name of the God, 'Helī'— "
Having performed one hundred and eight offerings to the deity, one who is pure should recite this;
likewise when bathing, at the time of departure, upon rising, when stumbling, or when wounded.
One should not speak with heretics, outcasts, or those who dwell at the very fringe of society;
likewise, one should worship the sun endowed with faith.
And one who is intent upon that should recite this while fixing the Sun in the mind:
"O Haṃsa, O Haṃsa, salutations to you; be the refuge for those who have no refuge."
"O Sun, be the savior of those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra!
Having thus propitiated him and observed a fast with a restrained mind, [he remained there].
On the following day, having eaten cow-dung only once during the forenoon itself,
and having bathed and performed worship, one should again proclaim the name "Haṃsa."
One should likewise pour three streams of water upon the feet of the deity during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha, and perform worship in the same manner during Jyeṣṭha.
O Kṛṣṇa, a man indeed attains the highest state in the world of mortals;
and having departed from this life, O Kṛṣṇa, he goes to the auspicious, divine abode of the swans.
[143] By the grace of the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), one indeed becomes equal to Indra;
this occurs in the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and the auspicious Bhādrapada.
In the same manner, having likewise fasted and performed worship according to this rite during the month of Āśvayuja, one should then proclaim: "O Mārtaṇḍa!"
Purified by the consumption of cow urine, one shall go to the city of Gaṇādhipa,
having propitiated the immutable-souled Lord of the worlds.
At the time of death, one should remember the Sun according to the sacred scriptures;
as for the consumption of milk, this is the rule proclaimed by me.
O Kṛṣṇa, one should duly perform [the rites] for four months beginning with Kārttika; by that very same procedure, one should proclaim [the worship] of the Sun.
He goes to the world of light, the realm of the Sun, remembering the Maker of Light at the time of death;
every month, he should give gifts to the twice-born according to his desire.
When the four-month period has arrived, one should perform the recitation of a book,
or a narrative concerning the Sun here, or even his songs of praise.
[144] The hearing of the Dharma is always desired by one who has the Dharma as his banner;
for "Dharmadhvaja" is the Sun. Therefore, having honored the reciter, the rite should be performed with faith.
O best of the twice-born, by means of this cooked offering and the recitation,
the desired Śrāddha for the Sun-god is indeed performed according to the divine injunctions.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, by constantly reciting the praises of the gods, a man shall always attain the threefold supreme destination known as the three worlds.
It has been told to you that by the first gift of a cow, which is the breaking of one's fast,
a human being thereby attains lordship as well as enjoyments.
By the second [fast], a man shall likewise obtain enjoyments from the Lord of the Clan;
by the third breaking of the fast, he shall likewise attain the world of the Sun.
Thus has been fully explained,
O tiger among gods, this supreme procedure for attaining the [desired] state of existence, as taught in the vow of the seventh lunar day.
But that woman who, endowed with faith and likewise with devotion, performs this seventh pilgrimage to the three sites, attains the threefold goal.
This meritorious triple-course, which removes evil, has been proclaimed;
it is praised for the propitiation of the Sun and always brings forth strength.
Likewise, she is always meritorious in her actions and the bestower of the preeminent among the three goals of life (*trivarga*).
"Gotrāri" refers to Indra; "trivargajyeṣṭhadā" means the giver of *dharma*. Thus concludes the *Trigatisaptamī-vrata*.
[Pāpanāśinī Saptamī] Brahmā said:
When the asterism Karo occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, [that is the Pāpanāśinī Saptamī].
Then this seventh day of great merit, which destroys all sins, belongs to her.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of Gods, Citrabhānu, the teacher of the world, in that [place], one is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
And he who observes the fast on that day with a disciplined mind,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever gift is given with the sun in view,
or whatever oblation is performed there, all that shall become inexhaustible.
Having recited even a single verse from the Ṛgveda with a mind full of faith,
one certainly obtains the fruit that comes from the entirety of the Ṛgveda.
The *sāman* yields the fruit of the *Sāmaveda*, the *yajus* yields the fruit of the *Yajurveda*,
and the *atharvan* yields the entire fruit of the *Atharvaveda*.
O Kṛṣṇa, because the Sun (Bhāskara) destroys every single sin here by means of his rays on this seventh lunar day, it is therefore called Pāpanāśinī (the destroyer of sins).
Having worshipped the Sun in this [tīrtha], they go to the city of Saumanasa,
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot produced from gold.

“Saumanasa-pura” refers to the world of the gods. “Karbura” means gold. O Kṛṣṇa, you are like the sun in brilliance, like the immortals in splendor, equal to Atri in beauty, and always like Hari in valor.
There he rejoices for a very long time together with hosts of gods;
returning again to earth, O Kṛṣṇa, he shall indeed become a sovereign lord of the earth.
Thus ends the Pāpanāśinī Saptamī.
[147] [Mārtaṇḍa-saptamī]
Brahmā said:
O sinless Kṛṣṇa, I shall now describe to you another [vow], the Mārtaṇḍasaptamī;
having fasted on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa.
Having duly worshipped that Mārtaṇḍa while muttering "Mārtaṇḍa,
Mārtaṇḍa," one should worship Kutapa with devotion, endowed with supreme faith.
“Kutapa” refers to the sun. With a concentrated mind, intent upon him, and reciting the name “Mārtaṇḍa,” one should worship with flowers, incense, offerings, and so forth, as well as through fasting.
O you whose banner is Garuda, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
while sleeping or upon waking, or if one stumbles, one should utter the name "Mārtaṇḍa."
One should avoid conversation with heretics who persist in improper actions;
likewise, [one should avoid] cow urine, cow dung, curd, or even milk.
One should consume that which has arisen from the *godehata* for the sake of self-purification;
on the second day, having bathed again and likewise worshipped that Sun, one should do the same.
Having worshipped it with that very name and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin,
he should then eat [food] prepared from the products of a cow's body.
[148] In this very manner, having fasted diligently throughout all the months,
a wise man should, according to his capacity, give daily provisions for cows every month.
Furthermore, when the year has concluded, having given a daily portion of fodder to another cow according to one's ability,
hear what fruit one enjoys thereafter.
Whatever fruit a man enjoys by giving five cows with golden horns and a bull as the sixth to the twice-born every month; [that same fruit he obtains by this other means].
By fasting according to this vow, one fully attains all that [is promised];
and one reaches that world where Mārtaṇḍa dwells.
“Kṛṣṇa is equal to Śāṇḍileya in splendor; there is no doubt in this matter.
“Equal to Śāṇḍileya” means equal to fire.
Thus ends the Mārtaṇḍasaptamī.
[The Saptamī of Infinite Fruit] Brahmā said:
O Acyuta, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada—
Having bowed his head to the Sun, one should worship the one who has seven steeds as his vehicle.
[149] O Hero, by means of offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth, and by the gratification of the *kutapas*—
the term "*kutapas*" here refers to Brahmins—
one who is self-restrained should avoid conversation with heretics and the like.
Having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin, he should eat at night while restraining his speech,
whether standing, walking, or sitting comfortably, even during moments such as hunger or stumbling.
Reciting the name of Āditya and likewise pronouncing it,
according to this very procedure, for twelve months in succession.
Having observed the fast until its completion, and having fully worshipped the Teacher of the World on the day of breaking the fast,
one attains nourishment by pleasing Him here through the merit of listening to His teachings.
Thus, whatever man or woman, being pure, should perform the worship of the Sun, having attained heaven, enjoys infinite fruit.
Thus ends the Saptamī of Infinite Fruit. [The Saptamī of the Unimpaired.
Brahmā said:
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, one who is pure should worship the Lord of Gods, whose vehicle is the horse, with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
O Lord, having obtained here abundant and inexhaustible merit immediately following his dharma,
he has come to that auspicious, divine world of the Lord of Birds in the next life.

The meaning of "immediately after the [recitation of the] Dharma" is as follows: "the lord of birds" here refers to the Sun. Without engaging in conversation with heretics and the like, self-restrained, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin, he should eat at night while remaining silent.
Every year, one should employ the *avyaṅga* [thread] for the God of gods.

One should understand that the *avyaṅga* is made from beautiful cotton thread of a single color, shaped like the sloughed skin of a snake, hollow inside, and measuring one hundred and twenty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—this is the best; measuring one hundred and twenty finger-breadths is the middling; and measuring one hundred and eight finger-breadths is the short. This has been explained in detail in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* of the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
On the seventh [lunar day], there is here the most auspicious and secret [rite] for the Lord.
Just as they know there are other purifiers among the various Ṛg-verses, so it is here indeed.
Likewise, O Lord, in this month, a man who is free from physical defects is proclaimed among the gods born of the *Ṛgveda*—
he who, with devotion, installs [the image] of Bhāskara, O Acyuta.

Having performed the feeding of Brahmins according to the rules with devotion, ensuring they are free from physical defects, accompanied by the sounding of bells and musical instruments and the abundant chanting of the Veda;
Mounted upon a divine vehicle, he comes to the world with ease;
by this very method, indeed, for twelve months in succession.
Having observed the fast until its completion, and having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin on the day of breaking the fast—
whosoever, being pure, should thus perform the propitiation of the Sun.
He shall go to the supreme world of the divine Vanamālin.
Thus ends the Avyaṅgasaptamī [and the Tritayapradānasaptamī].
Viṣṇu said:
Birth in a noble family, as well as health and wealth, are difficult to obtain in this world. O Lord of the Universe, tell me that by which this triad is attained.
Brahmā said:
He who, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the conjunction with the asterism Hastā, [worships] the origin of the world...
Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rite while observing a fast,
with flowers, incense, food, and various other offerings;
This is one vow, which involves the worship and giving of gifts corresponding to each cow taken,
and one should also bestow gifts upon the most excellent of the twice-born.
Understand, O steadfast one, that which is about to be remembered.
The *vajra* [yoga] has rice and barley as its supreme [food], gold, barley-meal, water, hailstones, food and drink, milk, and food rich in molasses and treacle.
Indrāṇī has milk as her food.
In that manner, one should give clothing in due order.
Having worshipped the Teacher of the World on that lunar day with products of the cow (*gavya*) and barley (*yavya*), as enjoined by the ritual rules—

wherein "barley" refers to the month [of Vaiśākha] and "vajra" refers to clarified butter (*ghṛta*)— [one should offer] a liquid substance rich in molasses and treacle, prepared from sugarcane juice boiled with water.
Eat grains for the sake of purification;
learn now of those things to be consumed here.
Cow’s urine, water, ghee, raw vegetables, dūrvā grass, curd, rice, barley, sesame seeds,
and lotuses heated by the rays of the sun; [153] water and lotuses likewise.
And milk should be added here in the course of each month.
He obtains birth in a preeminent family, filled with wealth and grain, adorned with lotuses, and where all suffering has been destroyed; and he possesses unimpaired sense faculties.
One becomes free from disease, wise, and happy.
“Padmāvṛte” means surrounded by lotuses.
Thus ends the seventh [tithi] of the offering of the triad. [This is the Nikṣubhārkasaptamī.]
Brahmā said:
"That woman who is devoted to the Sun will certainly become a man;
or, even while remaining a woman, she shall have an excellent husband—listen now to how this comes to be."
O Hero, the Nikṣubhārkavrata always increases the pleasure of the Sun; it brings about non-separation and accomplishes the goals of dharma, desire, and wealth.
On the seventh or the sixth lunar day, or on the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), or on a Sunday,
one who observes a fast should perform a fire sacrifice with clarified butter.
[154] Having fashioned an auspicious image of the Sun-god Nikṣubha made of gold, or else of silver or wood, one should bathe it with clarified butter and other substances.
The phrase "attains the Supreme Protector" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Nikṣubhā" is the wife of the Sun; [he is] the Sun accompanied by her. "With oblation" means with cow's ghee.
Having adorned [the image] with perfumes and garlands, and with pairs of beautiful garments, and with all kinds of foods—both solid and soft—as well as celestial chariots, banners, and chowries.
O King, one should feed those devoted to the Sun as well as the officiating priests;
and with devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee, saying, "May the Sun be pleased with me."
Having placed it in a copper or bronze vessel and covered it with a white cloth,
one should prepare the image in the center of the sanctuary.
Having placed that vessel upon his head, adorned with a canopy and an umbrella,
and likewise with banners, umbrellas, and other ornaments, he should proceed to the abode of the Sun.
[155] One should announce this vow to Nikṣubhārkadineśa;
one should place the vessel, adorned with flowers, upon his seat.
Having circumambulated the Sun and prostrated before him, one should seek his favor. Having completed this meritorious vow, hear what fruit one shall obtain.
In great vehicles resembling the suns, as vast as mountains,
he shall indeed rejoice at will in the world of the Sun together with the Sauras.
For thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of years,
at the end of that time, the highly fortunate one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, by virtue of that specific merit, endowed with all desires,
he reaches the world of Brahmā and attains supreme bliss.
Falling from the world of Brahmā, the illustrious one, honored by the virtuous and saluted by gods and asuras, attains the status of Prajāpati.
Having enjoyed pleasures here for a long time, he is glorified in the world of Soma;
and from the world of Soma, having reached the world of Indra once more, he becomes equal to Indra.
Having reached the world of the Gandharvas from the world of Indra, he rejoices;
he shall dwell happily with the Nāgas and the lord of the Gandharva kings.
Adorned with the wondrous power of great jewels,
even having reached the world of the yakṣas, he rejoices according to his desire.
Fallen from the world of the yakṣas, he sports upon the summit of Mount Meru;
having successively visited the abodes of the world-protectors, he rejoices.
Throughout the entire circle of the earth, reaching to the very edge of the world and the non-world,
