wherever he may be, he always obtains all that happiness in its entirety.
Having attained dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as sovereignty, he rejoices;
from Āditya, when he is well-pleased, yoga is obtained—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Nikṣubhārka-vrata.
Sumantu said: [The Nikṣubhārka-catuṣṭaya-saptamī].
But she who, observing the vow with constancy on the sixth and seventh lunar days,
does not eat for one year out of a desire to conquer the great serpents;

At the end of the rainy season, having fashioned an image renowned as Nikṣubhārka and having performed the ritual procedures such as bathing and so forth, one obtains the qualities previously described.
Having gone to the beautiful city of Ādityapura, which is adorned with vehicles made of Jāmbūnada gold and provided with four gates, one obtains the entire fruit [of one's merit].
Having enjoyed all desired pleasures in all the worlds, beginning with that of the Sun,
she shall gradually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
That woman who thus observes the fast on the entire seventh lunar day shall go to the supreme abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
At the end of the rainy season, having fashioned an auspicious image made of rice-flour,
one should worship it with yellow unguents, garlands, and yellow garments.
Having performed everything previously described, one should offer it to Bhāskara;
furthermore, by means of great terrestrial vehicles possessing the luster of gold amidst the darkness.
For a thousand million years he is honored in the world of the Sun;
having enjoyed all desired pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and others, he dwells there.
Having come in due course into this world, she finds a husband according to her desire—
one of noble birth, endowed with beauty, and proficient in all the scriptures.
On the seventh [lunar day], she who remains without food and is restrained in the three ways should,
at the end of the year, offer an elephant made of flour.
Having fashioned a silver lotus with a pericarp made of gold,
one should devoutly place it upon that [base] and perform the remaining rites as previously described.
Even the evil committed through desire, including even the killing of a fetus—that all is destroyed by the gift of an elephant; there is no doubt in this matter.
By means of the Mahāpadma celestial chariot, the person goes to the same world [as the deity];
for more than a hundred crores of years, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
O lord of men, she enjoys pleasures in the worlds beginning with that of the Sun;
then, returning gradually to this world, she finds a husband according to her desire.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of wealth and grain,
great in enthusiasm, great in heroism, great in being, and great in strength.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha,
she who is firm in her vow remains for one year fasting and deprived of all enjoyments.
At the end of the year, having fed an excellent brahmin, one should present a sun-god fashioned from all types of fragrant substances and enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls.
He was a wise reciter, learned in the Itihāsas, accompanied by his wife,
and adorned with magnificent celestial vehicles and divine fragrances.
He shall sport for more than a hundred yugas and be honored in the world of the Sun;
in splendor he resembles the sun, and in brilliance he is like Hari.
Having enjoyed all pleasures at will in the world of Bhānu,
she returns in due course to this world and finds a king as her husband.
O King, he who thus performs this meritorious vow called Nikṣubhārka, which removes the fear of sin, attains the supreme goal.
O mighty-armed hero, endowed with supreme faith for one year,
at the end of the year you should feed the reciter together with his wife.
Having honored the couple who recite the Mahābhārata,
one should likewise worship them with perfumes, garlands, garments, and ornaments.
Having placed it in a copper vessel adorned with full vajras,
one should offer a golden sun and moon to those two according to one's ability.
Nikṣubhā is to be known as the Brāhmaṇī, and Arka is proclaimed as the Vācaka;
therefore, one should worship them both with faith, like the Lord of the Sun.
Thus ends the vow of the four Nikṣubhārka days.
[Regarding the Ubhayasaptamī:
Sumantu said:
Come now, I shall fully explain to you the unsurpassed vow of the Sun,
which bestows the highest joy regarding dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
with his senses subdued and speaking the truth, bathes with wheat and milk products.
One should diligently observe a fast on the seventh lunar day of both fortnights;
O observer of good vows, one should worship the Sun and Śāṇḍilya at the three junctions of the day.
He should always sleep on the ground and remain devoid of all enjoyments;
then, when the month is complete, on the seventh day, O subduer of enemies, [he should offer] with ghee and other substances.
Having performed his bath and the great worship with the Sūrya-mantra, O Bhārata,
he should offer as an oblation one *prastha* of cooked rice prepared with milk.
Having fed eight Brahmins who are devotees of the Sun, O Bhārata,
one should also give a tawny cow to the Sun-god, O great king.
I shall describe the fruit of the merit for one who thus performs this incomparable Sūryavrata, which is endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
With celestial chariots resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
crowded with hosts of apsaras, and endowed with great splendor;
Amidst the sounds of singing and dancing graced by hosts of gandharvas,
being fanned with yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras, he proceeded.
Endowed with wealth and sovereignty, he goes from the thousand-rayed sun to the supreme abode where the radiant Sun resides.
For as many hairs as there are on that person, for that many thousands of yugas shall he be honored in the heavenly world within the family born from him.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage,
and having attained the yoga of knowledge, he shall go to the abode of the Sun itself.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming oil-cakes mixed with ghee while having his senses subdued;
And there should be a fast on the seventh day of both fortnights;
O lord of men, one should perform the consecration with ghee for the Sun on the seventh day.
And one should give a young cow, dark blue in color, to the Lord of Day;
having gone to the beautiful city of Āditya, one enjoys pleasures as desired.

O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Phālguna— subsisting on śyāmāka grain, milk, and nīvāra rice, with anger conquered and senses subdued— [attains great merit].
On the sixth or even the seventh day, one should be devoted to fasting;
on the eighth day, however, there is a great ceremonial bath with the five products of the cow, ghee, and other substances.
Having bathed [the image] with the barks of milk-exuding trees, one should worship it;
then, one should offer a cow to the one garlanded with rays (the Sun), as previously described.
Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun, he rejoices for eternal years—
he who, when the month of Caitra has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night.
O King, one who has restrained his senses, while eating rice mixed with milk,
should offer a young Vaiṣṇavī Pāṭalā flower to the Sun.
By means of vehicles made of topaz and adorned with various swans and other birds,
one shall go to the delightful abode of the Sun, which is difficult for those of undisciplined soul to attain.
O Indra among kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Vaiśākha,
consuming curd-rice while having conquered anger and subdued his senses;
Sleeping in a cow-pen, sleeping on the ground at night, wearing but a single garment,
and he should observe all the common rules of discipline as they have been prescribed.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform a bath with ghee and other substances;
O King, one should give a white, young cow, adorned for the Sun.
With great, adorned vehicles white as conch shells, jasmine, or the moon,
and yoked with white Garuḍas, he shall go to the abode of the Sun.
Surrounded by women of surpassing beauty,
he enjoys for an inexhaustible time lotuses fragrant as blue water-lilies.
O mighty-armed hero, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Jyeṣṭha,
consuming milk-rice together with ghee and honey—
He should remain in the *vīrāsana* posture during the night and follow the thousand-rayed sun.
"Vīrāsana" refers to remaining seated without sitting down. He should always act for the benefit of cows and avoid harming them.

On the seventh lunar day of both fortnights, one should perform the ritual procedures beginning with the bath. The word "of both" refers to the two fortnights. And one should give a smoke-colored cow, adorned, to the Sun.
In peerless Great Vehicles that resemble blue lotuses and are adorned with great lions, he rejoices for inexhaustible time.
He who, being self-restrained, observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āṣāḍha,
should eat cow's milk mixed with ṣaṣṭika rice only once [a day].
O great king, one should give a cow of auspicious appearance to the Sun,
and perform the general ritual procedure that was previously described by me to you.
In vehicles resembling pure crystal and drawn by peacocks,
endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, he shall roam in the sky like the sun.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, he who delights in the welfare of all beings should observe the practice of eating only at night, subsisting on milk-rice made with ṣaṣṭika rice.
One should give a yellow-colored cow to the high-souled Bhāskara;
one should perform everything else in common that was previously mentioned, as you have considered it.
Traveling by means of various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles drawn by swans and cranes,
the illustrious one goes to the City of the Sun and attains the aforementioned fruit.
O Hero, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Bhādrapada,
having taken refuge at the foot of a tree, should offer the remains of the oblation into the fire.
Compassionate toward all beings, he should sleep at night in a sheltered place;
O Hero, he should give a young cow to the high-souled Bhāskara.
With celestial palaces that resemble the moon in appearance, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli, furnished with ruddy geese, and granting all desires;
Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun, he, who is worshipped by both gods and asuras,
rejoices in great vehicles until the dissolution of all beings.
The illustrious one who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āśvayuja,
consuming only ghee, having conquered anger and subdued his senses;
One should give a cow, radiant as a lotus petal, endowed with divine ornaments, young, and yielding milk, to the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
With celestial chariots that resemble clear pearls, are beautifully adorned with blue lotuses, are accompanied by *jīvañjīvaka* birds, and fulfill all desires; [165]
O King, resembling the sun in brilliance, he shall go to the world of the sun;
resembling the moon in beauty, he shall resemble the sun in splendor.
O Indra among kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika,
subsisting on milk-rice, speaking the truth, and having his senses subdued;
One should give a cow to Divākara that possesses a radiance equal to fire and the sun;
and by performing the previously mentioned rite, a man shall become equal to the Sun.
In great vehicles resembling mountains and like the crests of the fire of time,
with the majestic bearing of great lions, he rejoices happily like the sun.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming barley-meal mixed with milk while his senses are restrained;
Likewise, O tiger among the Kurus, one should present a black cow adorned with various ornaments to the Sun, and one should also perform the prescribed ritual.
Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun in vehicles resembling white lotuses and yoked with white horses, he is endowed with supreme splendor.
Non-violence, truthful speech, non-stealing, forbearance, and uprightness;
performing the fire-sacrifice at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
O descendant of Kuru, by fasting on both fortnights on the seventh lunar day,
one who performs this supreme vow while relying upon these qualities [attains these results].
The seventh [verse] proclaims both; it removes the fear of all sins, pacifies all diseases, and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Observing such rules as these, one should always practice the solar vow;
he shall go to the vast abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
Thus ends the Ubhayasaptamī vow.
[Regarding Putrasaptamī] Āditya said:
He who, having fasted on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
worships me with devotion— to him I shall become a son.
And thus, O best of gods, on both seventh lunar days, month after month,
whoever should worship me with devotion and respect, offering one [lamp] each time.
I grant him a son born from my own body,
as well as wealth, fame, progeny, and supreme health.
[167] But he who, O Brahmin, in the month of Māgha during the bright fortnight, having conquered his senses and being self-controlled,
does not speak with heretics or those fallen from their village duties;
Having fasted according to the rules on the sixth lunar day and having worshipped me with devotion using white garlands and unguents, the wise man should sleep on the ground at night.
Having risen early on the seventh day, O Brahmin, and performed the rites such as bathing,
one should worship me and then perform the *vīra-homa*.
Having gratified Hari, the lotus-eyed one, with devotion through oblations of curd-rice,
milk, and milk-porridge, the twice-born likewise [offered].
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of that very dark fortnight,
one should worship with fragrant red lotuses and other red flowers.
O Lord of the Gods, a man who always worships me in this manner with devotion according to the prescribed rite obtains the fruit of both [the rites], including a son.
“Vīrahoma” is the fire-oblation (agnihoma). “Hari” here refers to the sun. “Of him” means of Māgha.
Thus ends the Putrasaptamī. [168]
[Sarvāptisaptamīvrata] Brahmā said:
Listen now to the Sarvāpti-saptamī in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Avoiding conversation with heretics and the like, he remained devoted to the Sun.
With self-restraint and one-pointed mind, one should worship the Sun-god;
the breaking of the fast is prescribed at the end of six months, beginning with Māgha and ending with Śuci.
"Śucyantaka" means the end of the month of Āṣāḍha. Mārtaṇḍa is proclaimed as the first name, the second is Arka,
the third is Citrabhānu, and after that is Vibhāvasu.
*Bhaga* is to be known as the fifth, and *haṃsa* is proclaimed as the sixth.
During the first six months, sesame seeds are used for bathing and consuming.
In the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed;
it is highly commended for both bathing and consumption, as it destroys all evil.
Having performed the worship of the deity every month according to the prescribed rule,
one who possesses faith should partake of the offering and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his own capacity.

And one should perform the breaking of the fast, the propitiation of the deity, and worship with devotion, according to one's ability and according to the rules, out of devotion to Ravi, the Lord of Heaven.
One should indeed eat at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances,
on the sixth day of the dark fortnight while observing the vow, or else on the seventh day.
Having dwelt here, O knower of dharma, one who is intent on pleasing the swans attains all desires, whatever he wishes for in his heart.
Therefore, this seventh [stage] is renowned in the worlds as "the attainment of all" (sarvāpti);
for it is that which has been undertaken by those devoted to Dharma, having been made their object of desire.
"Resorted to day by day, she fulfills all desires.
Thus is the Sarvāpti-saptamī (also known as Kāmadā-saptamī).
The Grandfather said: O Supporter of the Earth, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
a man or a woman, having fasted, should worship that Dispeller of Darkness.
Chanting the name of Sūrya with devotion, filled with spiritual feeling, and having conquered his senses,
he should proclaim the praise of Sūrya alone while rising and while lying down.
Then, when another day arrives— the eighth— being self-restrained, one should bathe, duly worship the Sun, and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Having performed the rite of offering oblations of clarified butter into the fire dedicated to Ravi,
and having prostrated before the Lord of the World, one should utter these words:
In former times, having propitiated the goddess Sāvitrī, he indeed obtained his desire;
may that Lord of Gods, Vibhāvasu, grant all my desires.
Having worshipped him, Diti obtained all her desires exactly as she wished;
may that Lord of Heaven, being pleased with me, grant all my desires.
Having worshipped that Sun, the lord of gods regained his kingdom after it had been lost; may he grant my desires.
Having thus worshipped and especially completed the ritual offering here,
O serpent-bannered one, one should eat the sacrificial food (haviṣya) properly while remaining self-restrained.
Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣᭋha—
being most intent upon this, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) shall be accomplished through these four months.
Then, for four months, one should worship the Sun with *karavīra* flowers;
one should burn black agallochum as incense and consume water produced from a cow's horn.
One should also offer food offerings and sweetmeat balls to the Brahmins.
Now, listen to another [account] regarding the rites that are to be performed starting from the month of Āṣāḍha.
Jāti flowers are praised; guggulu is said to be the incense;
one should eat water from a kutapa vessel, and likewise milk-rice as the food offering.
One should consume that very [substance] oneself and perform the remaining rites as before.
"Kutapodaka" means water infused with *kuśa* grass.
In the months beginning with Kārttika, cow's urine serves for the purification of the body.
Mahāṅga incense is prescribed, as well as worship with red lotuses;
and indeed, *kāsāra* should be offered as the food-oblation (*naivedya*) to Bhāskara.
And every month, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be given to a Brahmin;
furthermore, at the conclusion of each fast, one should perform a propitiatory rite for the Sun according to one's desire.
According to one's ability and as is appropriate, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
it is held that the Seven-Horsed One (the Sun) is pleased when worshipped with sincere devotion alone.
At the conclusion of the fast, having been worshipped according to one's ability and installed, the Sun,
being propitiated, shall grant all desired objects unimpededly.
This meritorious seventh day, which removes sins and grants all desires,
bestows upon one whatever longed-for objects one wishes for, O Garuḍa-bannered Lord.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth shall obtain wealth;
one overcome by disease shall obtain health; and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
By fasting on this day, one may obtain reunion after being away from home;
one attains all desires and rejoices even when dwelling among cattle.
Returning again to the earth, O Kṛṣṇa, that man becomes like a rain-cloud upon the surface of the ground; there is no doubt of this through the grace of the Lord of the Cowherds.
The *mahāṅgadhūpa* (great-limbed incense) is described as stated in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*. It is as follows:
camphor, sandalwood, flowers, *aguru*, *tagara*, *gṛñjana*, sugar, *kṛṣṇa*, *mahāṅga*, and likewise *sihlaka*.
"This great-bodied incense is remembered as always dear to the God.
Thus, "gone to heaven" means having gone to the celestial realm.
This concludes the Kāmada-saptamī-vrata.
[Siddhārthakādi-saptamī]:
Saptāśvatilaka said:
"O Vainateya, learn from me the ritual procedure for the vow of Saptamī."
For this is the supreme secret, the ultimate means of propitiating the Sun.
The first [offering] should be made with white mustard seeds, the second with *vārka* pods,
the third with black pepper, and the fourth with *nimba* leaves on the seventh lunar day.
The fifth [day] should be joined with six, and the sixth is the seventh of the fruit;
the seventh is without impulsion, O Hero, and is thus proclaimed as the Seventh [Saptamī].
Thus, these seven sets of seven [days] should be performed by one desiring prosperity;
accordingly, I shall now describe their performance in due order.
The seventh day of the bright fortnight should be observed either in the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa;
for one who is afflicted by illness, there shall be no violation of the rules caused by a fortnight or a month.
One should perform the cleaning of the teeth when half a watch remains [of the night];
"when half a watch remains" means during the remaining half-watch of the preceding day.
I shall now describe those desire-yielding trees that are found there on the seventh [level].
Through *madhūka* there shall be the attainment of a son; through *arjuna*—where "arjuna" means *kakubha*—the descendant of Bhṛgu becomes firm.
And through *badarī* and *bṛhatī*, one is quickly liberated from diseases.
There will be sovereignty under the *nimba* tree, an accumulation of wealth under the *khadira*,
the destruction of enemies under the *kadamba*, and the gain of riches under the *atimuktaka*.
One attains respect everywhere by giving what grows from the *āṭarūṣaka* plant;
indeed, one attains preeminence among kinsmen when the *aśvattha* tree bestows its fame.
By resorting to the śirīṣa tree, one attains vast prosperity;
for one who cultivates the priyaṅgu plant, supreme good fortune shall arise.
The accomplishment of one's desired aims shall be constant through the regular use of the *plakṣa* tree;
however, one should not consume a tooth-stick that is split or possesses a wound.
One should eat a morsel the size of a span, avoiding what is wet or dry, crooked, or devoid of skin; one should avoid food that is either too long or too short.
Facing either north or east, seated comfortably and restrained in speech,
one should then form the desired object in the heart and consecrate it with the mantra.
With this mantra, the wise man should use the tooth-stick:
"O Lord of the Forest, I recognize you as the giver of boons and the fulfiller of desires."
"O tooth-stick, grant me constant success; homage be to you!
Having recited this three times, one should then consume the tooth-cleansing stick.
Afterwards, having washed that wood, one should cast it away in a clean place;
for success is attained when it falls upwards or remains facing [the practitioner].
If it falls otherwise than this, one should bring it back and discard it again;
if it should fall with its face turned away, the tooth-cleansing stick must be used three times over.
One should recognize this as a failure; that seventh [night] must not be accepted.
On that night, the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should sleep while attending to auspicious practices.
Wearing an unwashed garment, pure and endowed with proper conduct,
O bird, he should rise early in the morning once that night has passed.
The wise man should wash his face, clean his teeth,
and, having become pure and seated, bow his head to the sun.
Having performed the recitation as desired, one should offer oblations into the fire;
then, at the time of afternoon, having bathed with water from a horn.
Having sipped water according to the prescribed rule, remaining silent, dressed in white garments, and pure,
he should worship the god Divākara with devotion according to the ritual injunctions.
[176] One should sleep before the deity, intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Hereafter, I shall declare by which [practices] one may point to whatever fruit [is attained].
Having duly completed all rites, such as recitation and fire-offerings, on the seventh lunar day, a man of firm vows who has seen [these things] in a dream [should proceed].
Having established oneself upon the ground for sleep, one should meditate upon the God of gods;
if, in this dream, a person should see the rising sun.
All his prosperities— such as the banner of Śakra, the lordly elephant,
the bull, the elephant calf, the cow calf, and food and drink— are [attained].
The attainment of a water-pot, a spotless mirror, or a jar brings a festival of happiness;
the flow of blood is a sprinkling that brings about supreme sovereignty.
Climbing seven trees shall swiftly bring about sovereignty;
milking a buffalo, a lioness, or a cow within one's own hand [brings similar results].
Their binding results in the attainment of sovereignty, but touching their navel leads to misfortune;
having pounced upon them, one may devour even a lion, a cow, or serpents.
O bird,
that man who eats milk-rice (pāyasa) shines like one who has offered his own limb as an oblation into the fire or who has drunk liquor.
If it is in a vessel or a lotus leaf, his sovereignty shall be supreme;
whether in gambling or in battle, victory indeed brings happiness.
Or there may be the cracking of limbs or the piercing of the head upon the ground;
"cracking of limbs" refers to the sound of the joints of the body. Also, [the falling] of white garlands, garments, horses, cattle, and birds.
They always praise gain as well as the smearing with excrement;
there shall be safety when traveling by horse-carriage, and the arrival of subjects when traveling by chariot.
May those with various heads and arms place the Goddess Śrī in their hands;
may approaching the forbidden be meritorious, and the study of the Vedas be supreme.
Whatever gods, twice-born men, heroes, teachers, elders,
and ascetics say to men in a dream, they know that to be indeed the truth.
O Lord of Birds, their sight is auspicious and their blessing is a boon;
a king would rather undergo the severing of his own head than lose such wealth.
Upon weeping, there is the attainment of food; upon being bound in fetters, the acquisition of a kingdom;
and indeed, [the sight of] a mountain, a horse, a lion, a bull, and an elephant.
He who, exerting his prowess, ascends to it attains great sovereignty;
swallowing the planets and stars, he may even cause the earth to revolve.
Uprooting even mountains, the king becomes sovereign upon the earth;
O Lord of Birds, there is the emergence of bodies and the coiling of entrails.
A vehicle is the cause of sovereignty and happiness for those traveling upon the oceans and rivers;
having crossed over rivers or even the ocean, one reaches the further shore.
O Hero, for one who accomplishes this, there shall be a gain as complete as a lotus;
even for one who crosses over a mountain, there will be wealth as well as victory.
O bird, if one sees raw meat, excrement, or various kinds of fruit,
or if one sees [the dreamer] eating worms, there will be a swift arrival of wealth.
The acquisition and even the sight of women who are ill-favored,
as well as union with auspicious things, health, and wealth— [these are the results].
Whatever sovereignty or attainment of a kingdom is described in a dream, there shall be no doubt that it will come to pass; by seeing those various signs, there is no uncertainty.
Having seen an auspicious dream, one should not go back to bed;
and in the morning, O Lord of Birds, one should recount the dream exactly as it was seen.
The wise man [should offer gifts] to the Bhojakas, Brahmins, friends, and the deities;
thereafter, at the time of midday, having bathed with a restrained mind.
Having duly worshipped that auspicious god Divākara according to the rules, he,
having properly performed his recitation, remained silent, and then offered oblations into the fire.
Having emerged from the temple, he should then feed the Brahmins;
likewise, red garments and fragrant perfumes [should be offered].
Fragrant garlands, sacrificial food,
and even a milch cow should be given to the reciter,
as well as whatever else may be dear to him.
There would be no gain for the reciters.
Then those brahmins who possess distinguished wisdom,
who are indeed the deities of the mantras and have offered oblations into the fire, and who are likewise devoted to the study of the Sāmans, deserve [the honor].
Or those who know the Yajus and are conversant with the rules of the Ṛcs.
Having thus performed [this] seven times for each of the seven [deities], how could a man who is endowed with devotion, full of faith, and free from malice, not obtain the fruit?
Whatever fruit may result from ten horse-sacrifices performed,
a human being attains that same fruit by performing the Saptasaptī sacrifice.
O Hero, there is nothing difficult to attain that cannot be obtained through these seven;
nor is there any disease in this world that is not pacified by them.
Those terrible leprosy diseases which are difficult to cure in this world are devoured like serpents by Garuḍa.
Having thus performed seven [cycles] of the seventh [day] according to the rules, through specific vows and observances, a man of virtuous character,
endowed with the fruits of learning and wealth, shall be possessed of happiness and merit.
Following that, he goes to the eternal world of the one with sharp rays (the sun).
Hereafter I shall explain the desired offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth,
by which specific gift that particular fruit is obtained.
Worship with *mālatī* flowers brings about divine presence;
with *karavīra* flowers, one attains health as well as incomparable sovereignty.
With the flowers of Mallikā, the practitioner becomes possessed of enjoyments;
with white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), there is good fortune, and with [other flowers], there is eternal wealth.
By means of *gandhakubjaka* flowers, one attains supreme sovereignty;
by means of the scents of lotuses and water-lilies, one shall also obtain stainless fame.
By means of various kinds of *mukurakas*, one is quickly liberated from disease.
*Mukurakas* refers to mirrors.
For one who constantly worships the Sun, food becomes inexhaustible.
Worship with mandāra flowers destroys all forms of leprosy;
likewise, by worship with bilva flowers, one attains great prosperity.
By worshipping with *arka* flowers, the Lord, the granter of boons, becomes ever-present as *Arka*;
by worshipping with a garland of *bakula* flowers, he grants a beautiful daughter.
The Sun-god, when worshipped with *kiṃśuka* flowers, does not cause affliction;
with *agastya* flowers, he bestows success and favorability.
One who is always honored with lotuses should give a beautiful woman;
by worshipping with a garland of forest flowers, one shall forever be free from agitation.
The man who worships the two-rayed deity with Aśoka flowers never again falls into delusion.
The Sun, when worshipped with hibiscus flowers, is propitiated without effort;
the Lord of Gods is pleased by devotion—what need is there for anything else?
The Sun-god is not to be worshipped with *kaṇṭakārikā* flowers, nor with those produced from the *unmattaka*,
nor with flowers born of the *āmra* tree.
The flower of the *āmrātaka* tree appears like a discarded offering (*nirmālya*);
because it is not fresh on the outside, one should therefore avoid it.
One who desires prosperity should not give what is unknown, nor what is withered, nor what is defiled,
nor indeed what is stale.
He who releases the deity out of a desire for flowers at that very moment shall obtain fragrant flowers as his sustenance, and no others.
Having committed the murder of a Brahmin here, a greedy and deluded meat-seller reaches the Mahāraurava hell and is cooked there for eternal years.
Behold, I shall proclaim to you the supreme procedure for offering incense,
and the fruit that arises from the offering of such incense to the God of gods.
The Sun always makes his presence known through the incense of sandalwood;
indeed, he bestows whatever a person desires by his very presence.
In the same way, one should grant excellent desired boons by means of agallochum incense;
and a person seeking health should always burn guggulu.
The Sun is always pleased by the offering of *piṇḍāṅga* incense;
*piṇḍāṅga* is *sihlaka*.
He bestows health and prosperity, and there shall be supreme good fortune.
A man always obtains good fortune by means of the incense of *kundaka*;
"kundaka" is the resinous exudation of the *mallaka* tree.
By means of the incense of *śrīvāsaka*, his trade shall become fruitful.
By burning resin (*rasa*) and indeed *sarjarasa*, there shall be the acquisition of wealth.
"Śrīvāsa" is *sarala*; "rasa" is *vola*. And by burning *devadāru*, there occurs incomparable and inexhaustible gain.
Anointing with saffron shall grant all desires;
having become happy in this world, the donor attains heaven.
By the gift of sandalwood, the Sun-god grants everything;
even one seized by hundreds of diseases quickly attains health.
By means of fragrant scents, a man attains supreme good fortune;
by means of musk and sandalwood, he shall obtain incomparable sovereignty.
Having worshipped the deity according to the rules with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
a person should thereafter prepare an offering of food (naivedya) according to his capacity.
Among flowers, the jasmine is preeminent; among incenses, the kunda is best;
among perfumes, saffron is supreme; and among ointments, sandalwood is the finest.
Ghee is best for the offering of lamps, and sweetmeats (modaka) for the food offering;
having thus worshipped according to the rules and performed circumambulation, one should proceed.
Having bowed his head to the god Bhāskara, the dispeller of darkness,
he ascends a variegated vehicle and goes to the same world as the Sun.
“Kārbura” means golden.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, one should perform the recitation (japa) as desired,
and one should offer oblations into the fire according to the ritual prescribed by rule.
Previously, seven [fasts] were always to be performed one by one for each of the seven [days].
That which is performed after drinking a handful (prasṛti) of water is the Udakasaptamī.
O Hero, that which is always known as Udakasaptamī is the giver of happiness; it is also called Varāṭikasaptamī.
Whatever other Saptamī has been mentioned, after that I shall describe the auspicious one.
Whatever food a man may obtain for three cowries,
he should eat that which was acquired for this price.
"Whether it be inedible or edible, no deliberation should be made in this matter.
Thus ends the Saptamī of Siddhārthaka and others, the Udakasaptamī, and the Varāṭikāsaptamī.
[The Seventh Day of Cow-Dung, etc.
Sumantu said: He who, subsisting on cow-dung, should cast it away for twelve seventh days of the bright fortnight.
O Indra among kings, one may subsist on barley gruel or even eat only withered leaves.
Subsisting on milk, or eating only once a day, or again subsisting on alms-food,
or even subsisting on water, one should worship the Sun.
With various offerings of flowers— lotuses, fragrant lilies, and water-lilies—
and with diverse kinds of perfumes, incenses, guggulu, and sandalwood.
Having honored them with kṛsarā, milk-rice, various kinds of food, and diverse ornaments, O best of men, a person [should further honor them] with gold, food, and other gifts.
O hero, that fruit which one obtains through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees is obtained here solely on the seventh lunar day of the sun.
Mounted upon a supreme celestial chariot (vimāna), he is honored in the world of the Sun;
thereafter, upon the exhaustion of his merit, the king is born into a great family.
Thus, with devotion and a concentrated mind, worshipping Vivasvat every month according to the prescribed rite,
one should recite these names with devotion.
In the month of Madhu, he is Viṣṇu; in Mādhava, he attains his purpose. In the bright fortnight of the month [of Vaiśākha], he is Vivasvat, and in the month of Śuci, he is Divākara.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, Parjanya is to be praised; likewise, Varuṇa in Nabhasya;
and Mitrā, the Maker of Day, in the month of Āśvayuja.
Mārtaṇḍa, possessing a golden luster, is to be known in Kārttika;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, Kuja is proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins.
Pūṣan is indeed to be worshipped with diligence in the month of Pauṣa;
Bhaga is to be known [as the deity] in Māgha, and Tvaṣṭṛ likewise in Phālguna.
In this manner, one should recite the names in sequence for the pleasure of the Sun;
and on the seventh day, being well-composed, one should perform the rite of incense and worship.
The man who performs [this] with devotion attains the supreme goal;
in splendor he resembles the sun, and in radiance he is like an immortal god.
All this has been told to you, which destroys the sins of one who listens;
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion.
O Hero, one should not give to an evildoer, nor even to one who has not performed austerities;
one should not give to an ungrateful person, nor to an atheist, nor to one of cruel deeds.
Thus ends the Gomayādi-saptamī.
[187] [The Sarṣapa-saptamī]
Brahmā said:
Having worshipped the God according to the rules with flowers, incense, and so forth,
one should thereafter offer an oblation of food (naivedya) according to one's ability.
Among flowers, the *jāti* is supreme; among incenses, the *vijaya* is foremost;
among perfumes, saffron is best; and among ointments, red sandalwood is preeminent.
For the offering of a lamp, clarified butter is best; for the food offering, sweetmeat (modaka) is supreme. By giving these, the Lord of Gods indeed becomes present.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite and performed circumambulation,
he bowed his head to the god, the god of gods, the Sun.
Then, seated comfortably and facing the sun, he should look [at it];
having thus prepared the white mustard seeds, he should hold them in his hand together with water.
Having placed that desired object in his heart according to his wish,
a man should drink while satisfying the Brahmin, touching it with his teeth only once.
O one of good vows, having taken two on the second and seventh days,
exactly three are to be drunk on the third and seventh days.
On the fourth day, one should drink four; on the fifth, exactly five;
and on the sixth, one should drink six of them—such is the Vedic revelation.
On the seventh day, a person should drink seven [mouthfuls] combined with water;
this mantra is to be understood as the one for consecration from the very beginning.
O Siddhārthaka, you are indeed always heard of everywhere in the world;
likewise, may the Sun make me also successful in my goals.
Then, having touched the sacrificial oblation, one should perform the silent recitation as desired,
and one should also offer oblations into the fire according to the rite prescribed by rule.
In this manner, these seven subsequent seventh-day rites should always be performed,
beginning with water and ending with the five products of the cow on the seventh day.
One [offering] is accompanied by water, two are joined with ghee,
the third is together with honey, and the fourth is likewise with curd.
A twice-born man should drink five [grains] mixed with milk, six combined with cow dung,
and seven with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), using white mustard seeds.
Whoever performs the Saptamī of Mustard Seeds according to this rite shall always have many sons, great wealth, and his goals accomplished.
In this world, a man who is a Brahmin goes to the fire.
Thus ends the Sarṣapa-saptamī.
[The Seventh-Seven Chapter] Sumantu said:
Those which were previously spoken by Āditya himself to the bird (Garuḍa)...
The seven Saptamīs of the mighty-armed Aruṇa are highly honored.
The first is with *arka* capsules, the second likewise with black pepper;
the third is with nimba leaves, and the fourth is with the seven fruits (*phalasaptamī*).
The fifth is Anodanā, the sixth is Vijayā-saptamī, and the seventh is to be known as Kāmikī; learn from me their ritual procedure.
One should undertake the Saptamī vow during the bright fortnight, on a Sunday, when the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and under a lunar mansion bearing a masculine name.
In all circumstances, he should be a celibate student, endowed with purity, having his senses subdued,
devoted to the worship of the Sun, self-controlled, and likewise intent upon recitation and burnt offerings.
On the seventh [lunar day], the self-controlled man should regularly observe the practice of eating only one meal;
on the sixth, he should not engage in sexual intercourse and should avoid honey and meat.
One should lead one [line] with *arka* capsules, another likewise with black peppers (*marica*),
another with neem leaves (*nimbapatra*), and the one called "Fruit" (*phalākhyā*) marked by fruits.
Without rice and without food, fasting according to the prescribed rule,
one should observe the Vijaya-saptamī by subsisting on air alone for a day and a night.
[190] Having thus performed these seven times each month, the wise one should perform the rite according to the rules; thereafter, he should perform that which fulfills his desires.
Having written their names individually upon separate slips of paper,
one should place all those papers into a new jar.
Therefore, whether he be a fool or even a wise man, whoever does not know that purpose should extract [the essence] alone; he should do that without hesitation.
O scorcher of foes, that which is performed every month according to that very same rule,
up until the seventh [month], should be understood here as the *kāmikī* (desire-yielding) vow.
"Thus, O King, these seven seventh-day observances were proclaimed by Vivasvat himself; the man who performs them with devotion goes to the abode of the Sun."
With *arkasaṃpuṭaka* one obtains pure wealth extending for seven generations;
with black pepper, there will indeed always be union with beloved sons for one who desires them.
All diseases are pacified by nimba leaves, of this there is no doubt;
likewise by its fruits, and by abundant sons, grandsons, and even daughters' sons.
Likewise, from the absence of boiled rice come grain,
gold, silver, as well as fame, wealth, health, and even progeny.

Having observed the Vijayā fast, a king always conquers his enemies; likewise, those who have observed it according to the prescribed rules shall accomplish their desired objects that grant all wishes.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain inexhaustible wealth;
one desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one seeking a kingdom shall attain a kingdom.
O delighter of your lineage, this Kāmadā [Saptamī] grants the desires residing in the heart of any man or woman who observes the Saptamī vow as prescribed.
One who performs this with a self-restrained mind indeed attains the supreme goal;
however, if a breach of the vow should occur through delusion, negligence, or greed, [one must perform atonement].
Then one should not eat for three nights, or else have one's hair shaved;
having performed this expiation, one becomes a practitioner of the vow once again.

Having worshipped the Sun on the seventh lunar day with garlands, incense, and other offerings, a person who has reached the seven [stages] and is endowed with the seven [virtues] attains exactly those seven.
Having fed the twice-born with devotion, one shall attain imperishable heaven;
so too for him who bestows gold upon the foremost of Brahmins on the seventh lunar day.
He attains that inexhaustible state and goes to the world of the Sun.
[Thus ends the Saptasaptamī-kalpa: the Arkasaṃpuṭa-saptamī.]
Sumantu said:
Thus has the seventh kalpa been described to you in brief;
now listen with full attention as I speak of it again in detail.
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one should worship Bhāskara with devotion using flowers, perfumes, ointments, and other offerings.
O mighty-armed one, one should incense the God with arka flowers and fragrant guggulu resin;
one should incense the Sun-god with white sandalwood.
Having worshipped the Sun during the day with an offering of jaggery-rice and three types of fruits, one should sleep at night in front of him.
The wise man should mutter the supreme mantra on the ground and must not succumb to sleep,
while meditating upon the Great-Souled One, the Sun, the God of Gods.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform all [rites]— recitation, fire-oblation, and worship— always using the six-syllable mantra, with each act preceded by a hundred recitations.
Having first performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred thousand times,
one should thereafter perform all other rites, such as further recitations, with an undisturbed mind.
"O Hero, for the sake of one's own welfare and for the pleasure of the Sun, this is the Sāvitrī mantra:
'Oṃ, may we know Bhāskara; may we meditate upon the thousand-rayed one; may that Sūrya inspire us.
This recitation was proclaimed by Bhānu himself on the seventh lunar day."
By reciting this even once, a human being becomes purified; there is no doubt about this.
Then, having bathed at dawn on the seventh lunar day with a restrained mind, one should proceed.
O King, one should worship the Sun with devotion according to the previously mentioned procedure;
and with faith and devotion, O King, one should also feed the Brahmins.
One should always honor those worthy of a meal with divine enjoyments and various kinds of food and edibles according to the prescribed rules; one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
He should feed those who are devoted to the Sun; he should not feed anyone other than those devoted to the Sun.
A Brahmin who observes the seventh [vow] should be fed at the hour of Ghaṭī.
O King, those who are known in the Saura Tantras and those who have been spoken of by Divākara—
these twice-born ones are to be fed by Āditya in brief.
Thus they have been described, O best of the Kuru lineage; now hear from me concerning those who are unworthy of honor:
he who has another's wife as his mistress, and he who suffers from the disease of leprosy.
He who is devoted to another deity, as well as one who indicates the lunar mansions,
he who is intent on slandering others, and likewise a temple-priest;
For these have been declared by the Lord himself as unfit to be fed among Brahmins;
yet they may indeed practice the triple Vedic knowledge within the assembly of Brahmins.
O King, when she was thus addressed by the Sun-god himself,
"Ghaṭā," that twice-born man who possesses that jar (ghaṭā) is called "Ghaṭī."
O hero, for the multitudes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
and Śūdras who listen according to the rules, the recitation of a book performed with devotion is meritorious.
"O tiger among the Kurus, that very *samasyā* of the composition of the *Itihāsa* was told by Bhānu himself, who travels through the sky."
O tiger among kings, he who would be the author of that [work] is considered the composer of the compendium; that brahmin is indeed the instructor of the Sun.
O Bhārata, those Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas which exist were composed by Vyāsa as a means of livelihood through victory, and likewise as a means of livelihood through solving poetic riddles.
"These [names] were spoken here by the Sun-god himself as 'Victory' (jaya).
Whoever causes these to be recited for the Brahmins upon whom he depends,"
O King, he who subsists by [reciting] the *Jaya* and likewise the *Vācaka* should be honored with effort and devotion for the pleasure of the Sun-god.
He who knows the Saura scriptures, such as the Āruṇeya and others, as well as the Saptāśvatilaka,
is a true Brahmin and a knower of the Saura Tantra.
O King, he who constantly worships the Sun shall go to that supreme abode which the wise behold.
But the patron, O King, is always like the divine Sun;
he is declared by Bhāskara to be one who should be diligently fed.
O descendant of Kuru, that Brahmin who censures the enjoyer of offerings and does not likewise honor him should be known as one devoted to other deities.
O King, if a barber who is shaven-headed, deformed, pale-complexioned, and bearing conch and lotus marks should enter the house of any man;
O Indra among kings, from the house of that man who performs service for a Brāhmaṇa, the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the Sun depart.
Likewise, in the temples of the deities, there is the worship of the gods,
as well as the supreme consumption of the food offering (naivedya) under their authority.
He should be known as a *devalaka*, a Brāhmaṇa who is the lowest of Brāhmaṇas;
there is no entitlement for such men to worship the gods on behalf of others.
O tiger among the Bharatas, servants [should serve] especially in all temples, with the exception of the temple of Śiva, even when it concerns the office of a sovereign.
O King, O ruler of men, there are only two twice-born who are truly dear to the Sun:
the reciter (vācaka) and the priest (bhojaka); these two alone have attained the highest state.
Having gone to his house himself, he should touch the Brahmin’s feet with both hands out of devotion and say: "O Lord, please show me your favor."
"O hero, eat a meal in my house for the pleasure of Bhāskara,
so that the god Divākara may be satisfied when you are satisfied."
And the Brahmins, O high-minded one, should say to him when the opportunity arises:
"O Lord, for the sake of my own welfare or yours, I shall do so."
Having thus addressed [the deity], O descendant of Kuru, one should then go to one's own home;
likewise, on the following day, one should worship the god Divākara with devotion.
Then, O King, having offered oblations into the fire, one should likewise feed the Brahmins with rice of the *śāli* variety,
mung beans, and fragrant ghee.
With cakes filled with jaggery, as well as milk, curd, and jaggery—
by these, the Sun attains satisfaction for nine or seven [days].
For years, O best of the Bharatas— of this there is no doubt—
one must avoid kulattha beans, lentils, sesame seeds, and adhakī grains.
One who desires prosperity for oneself should not offer śigru, nor likewise atyartham, nor even rājamāṣa, when the sun is present.
One should certainly not offer to the Sun anything that is foul-smelling, pungent, or excessively sour, nor rice grains that are mixed with other things.
O King, having thus fed the twice-born, he should cause [the recipient] to eat from the vessel of Arka,
while bowing his head to the deity accompanied by water.
[197] Having departed from the city, O King, and having gone toward the northeast direction,
he [saw] the supreme sun in a pure place that was neither too high nor too low.
O mighty-armed one, having seen that he was born and having worshipped him,
Khakholka [beheld] that branch of his which extended toward the northeast and reached up to heaven.
Having taken two very fine, fresh leaves from a branch that are not yet detached from the sprout,
which are closely joined yet distinct, one should return home.
Having bathed and worshipped the Sun with *arkapuṣpa* flowers while facing the sky, and having fed the Brahmins, he should say: "May the Sun be pleased with me."
Having consumed the *arkapuṭa* with the mantra, O Hero, one should then eat while remaining silent before the deity, without touching the vessel with the teeth.
Oṃ, O Arka-sampuṭa, may it be well with you; may there always be great good fortune for you.
Grant me also good fortune, and by your consumption, become a bestower of wealth!
O King, O high-minded one, the wise man, facing eastward and standing with water, should recite this mantra while remembering the Sun. O Ruler, he should do so accompanied by water.
O King, he who eats after having first tasted [the offering] attains the supreme goal;
by this rule, the Saptamī vow should always be performed with devotion.
O mighty-armed one, for as long as a year, this is always for the pleasure of the Sun;
and whatever man should observe this seventh day for the sake of pleasing Bhāskara.
His wealth shall remain unimpaired and stable for seven generations;
having attained this perfection, Kauthumi, the singer of the Sāmans, came [to this state] in ancient times.
O Great-minded One, by reciting this for one month, one is liberated from skin diseases;
[the sages who attained this were] Bṛhadvalka, Janaka, Yājñavalkya, and Kṛṣṇaja.
“Kṛṣṇajaḥ” refers to Sāmba.
For by means of this [vow], having propitiated the Sun, these [people] attained equality with the Sun.
Herein lies the most auspicious, meritorious seventh lunar day (Saptamī), which destroys all sins.
O King, for those who read, listen, and especially perform it,
this [rite] should always be carried out according to the rules for the sake of their welfare, O Ruler of Men.
"O mighty-armed one, the Arkapriyā destroys great sins.
Thus ends the Arkasaṃpuṭasaptamī. [The Nimbasaptamī]
Sumantu said:
O hero, listen as I speak of the third and the seventh [vows],
which, when observed with neem leaves, are remembered as destroyers of sin and removers of disease.
[199] Likewise, there is another method of worship by which one worships Ravi—
the God of gods, who holds a mace in his hand and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Now I shall declare the procedure for worship; learn from me the extraction of the mantra, which is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the destroyer of all diseases.

*Oṃ khakholkāya namaḥ*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). *Oṃ viṭi viṭi*, for the head (*śiraḥ*). *Oṃ jvāline*, for the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *Oṃ sahasraraśmaye phaṭ*, for the armor (*kavaca*). *Oṃ sarvatejo’dhipataye phaṭ*, for the weapon (*astra*). *Oṃ sahasrakiraṇojjvalāya phaṭ*, for the upper-binding (*ūrdhvabandha*). *Oṃ pṛthivyai bhūtabhāvinyai ca namaḥ*, for the earth-binding (*bhūtabandha*). *Oṃ jvalanaprajvalanāya phaṭ*, for the fire-formation (*agniprakāra*). *Oṃ ādityāya vidmahe viśvabhāvāya dhīmahi tan naḥ sūryaḥ pracodayāt*. This is the *gāyatrī* for the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*). *Oṃ dharmātmane namaḥ*, to the east. *Oṃ yamāya namaḥ*, to the south. *Oṃ daṇḍanāyakāya namaḥ*, to the west. *Oṃ romanthāya namaḥ*, to the north. *Oṃ śyāmapiṅgalāya namaḥ*, in the northeast (*aiśānī*). *Oṃ dīkṣitāya namaḥ*, in the southeast (*āgneyī*). *Oṃ vajrapāṇaye namaḥ*, in the southwest (*nairṛtī*). *Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ namaḥ*, in the northwest (*vāyavī*). *Oṃ candrāya nakṣatrādhipataye namaḥ*, to the east. *Oṃ aṅgārakāya kṣitisutāya namaḥ*, in the southeast. *Oṃ budhāya somasutāya namaḥ*, to the south. *Oṃ namo vāgīśvarāya sarvavidyādhipataye namaḥ*, in the southwest. *Oṃ śukrāya maharkṣāya bhṛgusutāya namaḥ*, to the west. *Oṃ śanaiścarāya ravisutāya namaḥ*, in the northwest. *Oṃ anūrave namaḥ*, to the east. *Oṃ pramathanāya namaḥ*, to the north. *Oṃ budhāya namaḥ*, to the west. *Oṃ yamāya namaḥ*, to the south. *Oṃ bhagavan aparimitapūṣamālin sakalajagatpate saptāśvavāhana caturbhuja paramasiddhida visphuliṅga namo ehy ehi imam arghaṃ mama śirasi gataṃ gṛhāṇa tejorūpa anantajvalana ṭha ṭha*. This is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*). *Oṃ namo bhagavate ādityāya sahasrakiraṇāya gaccha sukhaṃ punar āgamanāya*. This is the dismissal mantra (*visarjanamantra*).
Listen; I shall explain the entire procedure for image worship in its proper sequence, as well as the rules for initiations, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O King, O best of the Bharatas, the preceptor, having sprinkled the ground before the god with water purified by mantras according to the prescribed rule, [proceeded].
Being well-composed, the knower of mantras should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of purification;
likewise, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra upon the heart and other limbs of the body.
He should perform the *tarjanī-mudrā* and the purification of the directions,
as well as the purification of the netherworld (*pātāla*) and the enclosure of fire.
One should perform the purification of the space while recollecting the weapon-mantra;
likewise, [the guardians] Yama, Soma, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Īśāna, and Agni.
This lotus is proclaimed to extend to the directions of Rudra (East), Nairṛti (Southwest), and Vāyu (Northwest).
One should lick the eight-petaled lotus, together with its pericarp, in the direction of the Sun (South).
Then, having performed the invocation, one should invoke the Sun as Sudrā;
there one should establish Khakholka, who is beautiful and the creator of the worlds.
One should establish and also bathe the one whose body is mantra with mantras;
a person should place the heart [mantra] of the deity in the southeastern direction.
Having placed the head in the northeast, one should install Śiva in the southwest;
with a mind fixed in one-pointed concentration, one should place the lotus in the east.
One should place Soma in the northeast, Lohita in the east,
the armor in the northwest, and the weapon in the west.
In the southeast is the son of Soma (Mercury), in the south is Bṛhaspati (Jupiter),
in the southwest is the preceptor of the Dānavas (Venus), and in the west is Śanaiścara (Saturn).
Likewise, he should place Vahni in the northwest and Ketu in the north;
these, born from the splendor of the gods, are located in the second enclosure.
One should establish the twelve Ādityas, the descendants of Kaśyapa who possess great strength:
Bhaga, Sūrya, Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa.
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Vivasvat of great strength,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Indra, and Viṣṇu is said to be the twelfth.

Salutations to Indra in the east, to Yama in the south, to Varuṇa in the west, to Kubera in the north, to Īśvara in the northeast, to Agni in the southeast, to Nirṛti in the southwest, and to Vāyu in the northwest. Also, Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Romantha, and Vināyaka.
Likewise, the goddess Mahāśvetā and Queen Suvarcalā,
as well as two others who were renowned, Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala.
These should be placed in front of the sun by one who knows:
Siddhi, Buddhi, the goddess Smṛti, and likewise Utpalamālinī.
And they should be established on the right side, honored by the world through mantra:
Prajñā, Tantrī, Kṣudhā, Nidrā, Hārītā, and Tuṣṭi.
One who desires prosperity should always place [the deities] to the west of Vivasvat:
Siddhi, Bhūmi, Tuṣṭi, and Paurṇamāsī, belonging to Vibhāvasu.
Likewise, she should be established on the northern side; these are the divine powers (devaśaktis).
One should offer a lamp, food, ornaments, clothing, and flowers according to the mantra.
These should always be offered according to this rite for the prosperity of the Sun-god together with his retinue, by whoever constantly worships Bhāskara.
Having attained supreme desires, he shall thereafter become like the sun;
O King, whoever worships the Sun-god according to this rite [shall achieve this].
Through the grace of the Sun, he shall go to the supreme, imperishable abode;
by this rite, having worshipped the Lord Bhāskara, one attains the Blessed Hari.
O King, by worshipping the Sun with this ritual on the sixth lunar day while remaining composed, one obtains sons as well as invincibility against enemies.
O King, having conquered anger and subdued the senses, one should then eat nimba leaves on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
Having eaten thus, O King, one should sleep on the ground before the deity;
on the eighth day, O best of kings, one should worship the Sun once again.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give them a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
One should eat sweet food, free from any sense of weariness, while remaining silent;
thus should this Nimbasaptamī be observed for the duration of a year.
By performing even the seventh [observance], one is liberated from all diseases;
being freed from all diseases, one goes to the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Nimba-saptamī.
[204] [The Phala-saptamī]
Sumantu said: Then, O lord of the earth, in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada,
having observed a fast, one should worship the Sun at twilight according to the prescribed rites.
One should worship the Sun there according to the Māheśvara rite;
then, having bathed again on the eighth day, one should worship the Maker of Day.
One should give fruits to the Brahmins, saying, "May Mārtaṇḍa be pleased," [offering] dates,
coconuts, and citrons.
Having fed the Brahmins, he should thereafter subsist on fruit alone;
O best of the Bharatas, having first respectfully consumed a single very small fruit with the mantra, he should indeed consume nothing else at all.
"O descendant of Kuru, one should likewise subsist on fruit alone on the eighth day;
thus should the Phala-saptamī be observed for the duration of a year."
And that which has been performed, O mighty-armed one, which bestows sons and grandsons—
may all my desires be fulfilled in every respect.
Having spoken thus, O King, one should eat the previously mentioned fruits;
by doing so for the duration of a kalpa, O best of the Kurus, one shall attain all desires.
Thus ends the locative case used for the fruit (*phala-saptamī*).
[The locative case used for that which is not food (*anodana-saptamī*)]:
Sumantu said:
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having fasted properly,
one should worship the Sun with devotion using flowers, incense, and ointments.
The procedure by which one should worship the deity is now being told to you;
O King, it is the same procedure by which Vaiśravaṇa always worships him.

*Oṃ prajvalane namaḥ* | *Oṃ agniprakāraḥ* | *Oṃ namaḥ śeṣaṃ samitprakāraḥ* | *Oṃ sahasrakiraṇojjvalāya svāhā* | *Oṃ yaṃ vaḥ* | *Oṃ pṛthivyai sarvauṣadhirūpiṇyai svāhā* | *Pṛthivyantaṃ namaḥ*. This is the mantra for the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making the deity manifest). In one’s own self and in the body of the deity: *Oṃ dharmātmane namaḥ*, in the east. *Oṃ daṇḍakāya namaḥ*, in the south. *Oṃ romanthāya namaḥ*, in the west. *Oṃ satatojjvalarūpāya namaḥ*, in the north. *Oṃ śyāmapiṅgalalohitāya namaḥ*, in the northeast (*aiśānī*). *Nīlalohitāya namaḥ*, in the southeast (*āgneyī*). *Śanaiścarāya namaḥ*, in the southwest (*nairṛtī*). *Vajrapāṇaye namaḥ*, in the northwest (*vāyavī*). *Oṃ namo haradehāya mahābalaparākramāya sarvatejo’dhipataye svāhā*, in the north. *Oṃ śaktidharāya namaḥ*, the first doorkeeper in the east. *Oṃ haradehāya yajñarūpadharāya namaḥ*, the second doorkeeper; this is the mantra in the south. *Oṃ haritāya namaḥ*, in the west. *Oṃ aśvamukhāya namaḥ*, in the north. Thus, the four doorkeepers are established. *Oṃ kundendukṣāraprabhāya svāhā*, the first horse. *Oṃ raktākṣaraktavarṇadīptāya namaḥ*, the second horse. *Oṃ kṣīravarṇatejasvine namaḥ*, the third horse. *Oṃ bhinnāñjanavarṇāya namaḥ*, the fourth horse. *Oṃ tīvratejase namaḥ*, the fifth horse. *Oṃ vyomavarṇāya pradīptamāline namaḥ*, the sixth horse. *Oṃ sarvavarṇāya sarvādhipataye namaḥ*, the seventh horse. *Oṃ namo agaśakaṭāya kavacine kaśyapaputrāya prajāpataye namaḥ*. *Oṃ anantadevāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ asādhāraṇavikramatejase namaḥ*. This is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*). *Oṃ bhāskara devādhideva gaccha gaccha yathāsukhaṃ svabhavanaṃ punar āgamanāya*. This is the dismissal mantra (*visarjanamantra*). With the Gāyatrī mantra, one should perform the offering of welcome, water for the hands (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and a seat (*āsana*), followed by the presentation of perfumes, flowers, incense, jewels, fire-oblations (*homa*), and other offerings.
The mudrā of the bud-like lotus, the niṣkarā, and another called nāgā, as well as the vyomamudrā and the ugrā— these others are thus remembered.

Oṃ tejase namaḥ—this is the crest-lock (śikhā). Ādityāya tejo’dhipataye namaḥ—this is the armor (kavacam). Ādityāya sahasraraśmaye namaḥ—this is the weapon (astram). Oṃ tejo’dhipataye namaḥ—this is the face (mukham). Oṃ meavṛṣaṇāya namaḥ—this is the private parts (guhyam). Oṃ sahasrakiraṇāya namaḥ—this is the feet (pādau). Oṃ dīptadīptādhipataye namaḥ—this is the back (pṛṣṭham).

At the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, let there be salutation to the Supreme Self;
having worshipped with these mantras, which are illuminated by the word "namaskāra" at their conclusion.

One should offer a vessel of sesame seeds and gold to a Brāhmaṇa;

One should present a vessel of ghee together with gold and a water-pot, [saying]:
"May the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, the Sun-god, be pleased here."

then, in the thirteenth month, one should give thirteen cows.
One who is free from envy should give even a single milch cow, adorned with clothing and ornaments and richly decorated with gold, to one who is destitute of wealth.

Completely liberated from all evil, he is honored in the world of the sun;
here in this world, infinite lifespan, health, and sovereignty are born.
The Kalyāṇasaptamī always removes all sins, is worshipped by all the deities, and eternally pacifies all that is evil.
Thus ends the Kalyāṇasaptamī.
[The Viśokasaptamī] Pulastya said:
O bull among sages, I shall likewise describe the Viśoka-saptamī,
by fasting upon which a man never experiences grief here in this world.
Having bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
and having first cleaned his teeth, he should take his meal of kṛśara.
Having observed the vow of fasting, he should remain celibate during the night;
then, having risen at dawn, he should perform his ablutions and recitations, being pure.
Having fashioned a golden lotus, one should worship it with the thought,
"This is the Sun," using *karavīra* flowers and a pair of red garments.
Just as the world is always free from sorrow because of you, O Āditya,
so may I be free from sorrow, and may devotion to you be mine in every birth.
Having thus performed worship on the sixth day, one should honor the twice-born according to one's ability;
then, having slept and consumed cow urine, one should rise and perform the daily obligatory rites.
Having diligently honored the brahmin with a vessel of jaggery,
he should present that pair of garments and the lotus to the brahmin.
Having eaten food without oil or salt on the seventh lunar day while observing silence,
one who desires prosperity should thereafter listen to the Purāṇas.
By this procedure, one should perform everything for both fortnights until the seventh day of the bright half of the month of Māgha.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus;
one should also give a bed with its furnishings and a tawny, milk-yielding cow.
He who, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, performs the Viśokasaptamī according to this rite, shall go to the supreme goal.
For as long as there may be a full hundred million thousand births,
he— freed from disease and misfortune— does not encounter sorrow.
Whatever desire one may long for, that one obtains in abundance;
but he who makes himself free from desire attains the Supreme Brahman.
Thus ends the Viśokasaptamī.
[213] [The Phalasaptamī]
I shall also proclaim another [observance] called Phala-saptamī,
by fasting upon which a man becomes liberated from sins and partakes of heaven.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the fifth lunar day, one who is firm in his vows,
having fasted on the sixth, should have a golden lotus fashioned.
The knower of ritual action, having fashioned an image of gold the size of a single fruit, should give it along with sugar to a Brāhmaṇa who has a family.
At the hour of twilight, one should give [the gift] with the thought, "May Bhānu be pleased with me";
and having honored the Brahmins with devotion, one should partake of a meal of milk on the seventh lunar day.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should practice the renunciation of fruits until the seventh day of the dark fortnight arrives;
having fasted on that day, one should perform the ritual according to this very sequence.
In the same manner, one should give a golden fruit marked with gold,
following this very procedure on both the seventh lunar days for an entire year.
Having observed the fast, one should give [the offerings] in sequence and recite the mantras of the Sun:
Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śakra, Hari, and Śiva.
"May the glorious Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Varuṇa be pleased"—
thus one should recite each name individually on the seventh lunar day of every month.
One should practice the abandonment of [unwholesome] fruits while performing a single counter-measure;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments.
One should give a jar of sugar accompanied by a golden lotus and fruit,
so that the desires of those devoted to you, O Sun, may always be abundant.
Likewise, may there be for me the attainment of infinite fruit in birth after birth,
whoever shall perform this Phala-saptamī which bestows infinite fruit.
With his soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun;
whatever [sin] he has committed, such as the drinking of liquor and so forth, whether here or in the hereafter.
All that perishes for one who performs the Phala-saptamī;
by constantly performing this Saptamī, one becomes free from disease.
One shall deliver twenty-one persons— both those who have been and those yet to be.
Thus ends the Phala-saptamī [also known as the Śara-rāsa-saptamī].
Sumantu said:
I shall now describe the Śarkarāsaptamī, which likewise destroys all impurities,
so that longevity, health, and sovereignty may arise in infinite measure.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, one who is firm in his vows,
having bathed in the morning with white sesame seeds, should wear white garlands and white unguents.
Having drawn a lotus with its pericarp upon the sacrificial ground using saffron,
one should offer perfume and incense to it with the mantra "Namaḥ savitre."
And he should place a water-pot together with a vessel of sugar,
having adorned it with white garments, white garlands, and white unguents.
One should worship [the deity] joined with gold while reciting this mantra:
"Since you make the universe known, you are recited as the 'Proclaimer of the Vedas' (vedavādī)."
Since you are indeed the nectar of immortality for everyone, therefore grant me peace;
then, having drunk the five products of the cow, one should sleep on the ground at its side.
He remains recollecting the Saura-sūkta and listening to the Purāṇas;
then, when the day and night have passed, on the eighth day, he performs his daily obligatory rites.
One should present all of that to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice mixed with sugar and clarified butter.
He himself, remaining silent, should eat [the food] without oil or salt;
by this procedure, he should perform everything month after month.
[216] For a year, one should provide a bed accompanied by a jar of sugar,
as well as a single milch cow equipped with all necessary utensils.
And one who is capable should give a house equipped with all furnishings;
indeed, he should purchase it for a thousand gold coins and give it as such.
Alternatively, ten gold coins, or five, or even according to one's ability, should be given; as before, the recitation of auspicious blessings (svastivācana) should be performed.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one incurs faults.
For from the mouth of the Sun as he drinks nectar, drops of nectar fall.
Those known as rice, mung beans, and sugarcane gathered upon the earth;
and from this sugarcane, which was of the nature of nectar, the essence of sugar was extracted.
Therefore, sugar is desired by the Sun and is meritorious for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
the Śarkarā-saptamī in the month of Jyeṣṭha bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
It pacifies all suffering and increases one's sons and grandsons;
he who performs this with supreme devotion goes to the Supreme Brahman.
[217] One shall dwell in heaven for one kalpa and thereafter go to the supreme goal. Thus ends the Śarkarāsaptamī.
[The Kamalasaptamī]
Sumantu said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the Kamala-saptamī,
by the mere recitation of which the Sun-god is pleased in this world.
Having bathed on the Vasantāmalasaptamī day with white mustard seeds,
and having placed a golden lotus in a vessel of sesame seeds;
Having clothed it in a pair of garments, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers, saying:
"Homage to the one who holds a lotus in his hand; homage to you, the sustainer of the universe."
"O Divākara, homage to you; O Prajñākara, let there be homage to you!
Then, at the time of evening, [he should go] equipped with a water-pot.
Having honored the Brahmin with garments, garlands, and ornaments, one should give him [the gift];
if one has the means, one should give a tawny cow (kapilā), having adorned it according to the prescribed rite.
After a day and night have passed, one should subsequently feed the twice-born on the eighth lunar day;
then, according to one's ability, one should eat food devoid of meat and oil.
By this procedure, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight month after month,
one should perform everything with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus;
and to a Brahmin, one should give a cow that is well-endowed with gold and yields milk.
One should provide food, seats, lamps, and desired articles of utility;
whoever performs the Kamala-saptamī vow according to this rule [shall attain the fruit].
He attains infinite prosperity and rejoices in the world of the Sun;
then, day after day, he goes separately to each of the seven worlds.
[219] Surrounded by apsarases, he then goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the Kamalasaptamī; [followed by] the Mandārasaptamī.
Now I shall fully describe another meritorious [observance], which destroys all sins,
grants all desires, and is known by the name Mandārasaptamī.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
a wise man who eats only at night should use a tooth-stick and then fast on the sixth day.
Having fully honored the brahmins, one should consume the mandāra flower at night;
then, having risen at dawn and performed his bath, he should again [honour] the twice-born.
Having fashioned eight mandāra flowers, one should feed [the guests] according to one's ability;
likewise, one should fashion a very beautiful golden figure with a lotus in its hand.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus out of black sesame seeds in a copper vessel,
one should place a golden mandāra flower to the east, dedicated to Bhāskara.
Likewise, with the word "namaskāra," one should offer to the Sun on a petal in the southeast;
similarly, to Arka in the south, and likewise to Aryaman in the southwest.
One should worship [the deity] in the west for Vedadhāman, in the northwest for Caṇḍabhānu, and in the north for Pūṣan; after that, [one worships] for Ānanda.
The householder, restrained in speech and facing the east, should eat [the food] without oil or salt;
indeed, by this very rule, he should perform everything month after month.
One should perform this for as long as a year, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
at the conclusion of these vows, having placed [the image] upon a lotus, one should proceed as follows.
One who desires prosperity should give [offerings] together with cows to Vibhavata;
homage to Mandāranātha and to the one whose abode is the Mandāra tree!
O Ravi, deliver me from this ocean of suffering and saṃsāra;
whoever performs the Mandāra-saptamī according to this rite [shall do so].
A mortal who dwells [in this] becomes exceedingly happy and rejoices in heaven for an eon;
[this is] a lamp for the terrifying darkness of the veil of the flood of sins.
By performing this Mandāra-saptamī, which bestows the fruit of one's desired aims, one shall not wander in saṃsāra and shall then obtain all enjoyments.
Whoever recites or even hears this is also liberated from sins.
Thus ends the Mandāra-saptamī [the Auspicious Seventh].
Sumantu said: Now I shall also describe another auspicious Śubhasaptamī,
by fasting on which a person is liberated from disease, suffering, and grief.
Having performed his ablutions and recitations in the auspicious month of Āśvayuja, being pure,
he should then cause the Brahmins to recite [the prayers] and begin the Śubhasaptamī rite.
One should devoutly fumigate the Kapilā cow with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, [saying]:
"I bow to her who was born from the Sun, the abode of all worlds."
I shall bring you, who possess an auspicious body, for the sake of all accomplishments;
having adorned you, together with a prastha of sesame seeds and joined with a copper vessel.
Likewise, a golden bull, draped with garments and garlands,
together with various kinds of fruits and edible foods combined with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
At the time of twilight, one should offer [the oblation] with the words, "May Aryaman be pleased";
then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should sleep on the ground without any sense of envy.
Then, when morning has dawned, one should worship the twice-born with devotion;
according to this rite, a man should always give [offerings] month after month.
At the end of the year, one should give two garments, a golden bull, and likewise a cow made of gold, along with a bed provided with sugarcane stalks and molasses.
Provided with a pillow for rest, accompanied by a vessel and a seat,
along with a prastha of sesame seeds in a copper plate and likewise a golden bull.

having descended at the beginning of the Kalpa, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
For the sake of destroying a thousand killings of Brahmins and a hundred killings of embryos,
this meritorious and auspicious Saptamī is recited.
Whoever should recite this, or hear it for even a moment, or even see it shining by chance—
