[The Ārogyasaptamī is described] in the Varāhapurāṇa.
Furthermore, O Great King, I shall describe another vow known as Ārogya,
which is supremely meritorious and destroys all sins.
Having fasted on the seventh day of that very month of Māgha,
one should worship the god Bhāskara, the eternal form of Viṣṇu.
The Lord Ravi, the sovereign of all, is to be worshipped with this mantra: "O Āditya, Bhāskara, Rave, Bhānu, Sūrya, Divākara!"
Having taken food on the sixth day, one should observe a fast on the seventh;
one should eat on the eighth day—this indeed is the rule and the sequence.
Whoever worships the Sun according to this rite for a full year,
for that person health, wealth, and grain arise in this very birth.
And in the hereafter, an auspicious state which, having gone there, one does not return.
Thus concludes the Ārogya-saptamī vow.
[The Putra-saptamī]
O Lord of the Gods, that vow for obtaining a son consists of fasting on the seventh day during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Having made the formal resolve on the sixth day, one should worship the Sun on the seventh day—
the God who has arrived accompanied by the deities and surrounded by the Mothers.
Then, at the clear dawn, being self-restrained, he should worship Govinda according to the rules and the previously prescribed ritual with eight oblations.
In front of him, one should perform a fire-oblation with black sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
one should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give them sacrificial fees according to one's ability.
Then one should first eat a single *bilva* fruit oneself;
afterwards, one may eat as desired food rich in fats and endowed with the six tastes.
A man who observes the fast according to this very procedure every month on the eighth day of the dark fortnight will obtain a son, even if he is currently childless; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Putrasaptamī.
Thus concludes the section on Saptamī vows within the Vrata-kāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.
Now, regarding the Aṣṭamī vows [the Durgā-aṣṭamī vow],
it is stated therein in the Devīpurāṇa:
Brahmā said:
I shall proclaim the vow of the Goddess, which accomplishes all desires.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should subsist on air alone.
Having bathed and wearing wet clothes, with anger subdued and mind composed,
one should bathe the Goddess with water and then bathe her again with milk.
Then one should cause guggulu incense and turuṣka to be offered;
"turuṣka" is sahlaka.
Then, after the bath with scented water, one should bathe [the deity] again with water.

One should give maidens and twice-born men according to one's ability, and to them one should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),

by that [birth], he attains that supreme yoga which brings about the attainment of Śiva.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, having anointed oneself with [the substance] taken from the tip of a cow’s horn,
one should bathe while it exhilarates one's own body.

having bathed with *āmalaka* fruits, being pure and avoiding social contact, one should worship the Goddess with *yūthikā* flowers and bathe her with milk.
With agarwood for incense and offerings, and lamps fed with sesame oil,
he should feed those maidens and twice-born men who abide in virtuous conduct.
One should not look upon heretics nor those excluded from the sacred scriptures;
according to one's ability, a sacrificial fee should be given, and an auspicious benediction should be pronounced.
That breaking of the fast is for oneself, and one obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice;
thereafter, one should bathe the Goddess with curd and water.
Having applied yellow pigment (rocanā) to the head, one should burn incense for the child;
likewise, one should worship [the child] with lotus petals and white sugar mixed with the nails.
One should devotedly offer as an oblation rohita fish, meat from the śalyaka porcupine,
and preparations of wheat cooked in ghee.
O Lord of the Earth, having fed the maidens and the twice-born,
one should give sacrificial fees according to one's ability and then have oneself fed.
A human being obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
such a person becomes healthy, happy, and blessed in this very world.
Having recited the names of Durgā, one is glorified in her world;
O Bhārgava, one should bathe with earth purchased for a price during the month of Kārttika.
Having bathed the Goddess with scented water, worship her and anoint her with uśīra;
incense made of the five flavors should be offered, and lamps should be lit with sesame oil.

The food offering consists of barley-gruel and clarified butter; one’s own meal is provided for the maidens and the Brahmins, followed by the recitation of auspicious benedictions and the giving of sacrificial fees, with the prayer: "May Śiva be pleased."
By this method, O child, one obtains the fruit of the gift of knowledge;
as a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, he shall at the end attain the state of Śiva.
Likewise, O Bhārgava, having bathed on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with mountain clay, one should then bathe the Goddess with water from sacred fords.
One should perform the anointing with bālaka, kuṣṭha, jāti, and gajājñaya;
one should offer black agallochum as incense and kindle lamps with clarified butter.
Curds with rice should be offered as the food-oblation, and the virgins should be fed with that very same meal;
sacrificial fees should be given according to one's means, and that constitutes the breaking of the fast for oneself.
May Umā be pleased with my speech; one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In this very world, he becomes wealthy and an enjoyer of pleasures, and at the end of the body, he reaches the abode of Brahmā.
On the eighth day of the month of Pauṣa, having bathed with the tips of dūrvā grass and wearing white garments,
one who has conquered anger should bathe the Goddess with camphor water.
The wise one should anoint [the image] with saffron, or with musk and sandalwood;
he should burn incense and worship her with *kuraṇṭaka* flowers.
An offering of kṛśara and jaggery should be made, and maidens should indeed be fed by him;
he himself should break his fast with that, and according to his ability, he should satisfy the twice-born with offerings.
May the goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is ever pleased, be gracious to me;
by performing this rite for the lord of planets, one shall obtain the fruit of the gift of land.
O Bhārgava, having bathed with the mud from the horns of cows during the month of Māgha, one becomes fortunate, endowed with wealth, and shall attain auspiciousness in the hereafter.
Having bathed the Goddess with water, as well as with milk and ghee,
one should bathe her again with waters and anoint her with saffron.

One should offer incense made of *devadāru* wood and worship with *kunda* flowers; one should present an offering of food filled with ghee, and likewise honor maidens and Brahmins with that same [offering].
He should feed himself with that [offering], and let there be a sacrificial fee; "May Jayā be pleased!"—O Śukra, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices here; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Phālguna, having bathed with mustard seeds, one should bathe the Goddess with water infused with māṣa beans,
as well as with sugarcane juice and again with that same water.
In the application of *rocanā*, worship is performed together with *śataparṇikā*;
the lamp is with ghee, while the incense consists of sandalwood, *nakha*, and sugar.

In the offering of food, one should provide *aśokavartī* lamps; likewise, when feeding young girls, one should partake of that meal oneself, give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and have the words of benediction (*svasti*) recited.
May Vijayā always grant me happiness and may my desires be fulfilled;
by this ritual, O Śukra, one obtains a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Endowed with faith, one obtains [the fruit] from which this world consists of the Goddess;
on the eighth day of Caitra, one should bathe at the site of the Mothers with earth and water.
Having bathed the Goddess with the waters of sacred fords, one should smear her with a fragrant unguent;
then one should worship her with incense, turuṣka, and uśīra, accompanied by lights.
The food offering should consist of rice cooked with milk and sugar, even when offered to young girls;
that same food should be eaten by oneself, and one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
Having worshipped the Vidyās and Kanyās for the fulfillment of all desires and for my own happiness,
one shall obtain the fruit of the gift of gold.
[231] Indeed, on the eighth lunar days of the month of Vaiśākha, one should bathe oneself and the deities with mango fruits and water infused with māṃsī and vālaka.
Anointing with camphor and fruit-essence, incense, and the five fragrant substances should be offered; and the worship of the Goddess should be performed with *ketakī* and *campaka* flowers.
An offering of sugar and milk, a meal for virgins and Brahmins, and his own breaking of the fast;
with that, he should give a sacrificial fee according to his capacity.
One should cause Aparājitā and Bhavānī to be recited under the name Śivā;
she shall be pleased with me at all times and shall grant my desired object.
O Bhārgava, by this one also obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords;
at the end, one goes to the world of the Sun and always becomes equal to Him.
On the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the wise man,
having renounced all attachments, should bathe with sesame seeds and water infused with rose-apple (jambu) fruit for the sake of the Goddess.
One should bathe and anoint [the deity] with that fragrant nakula;
thereafter, the best of those who worship the planets should honor him with vijaya flowers.
“Vijaya” refers to the *kakubha* tree.
As an offering (*naivedya*), roasted barley flour (*saktu*) should be given, and sugar should be offered even to young girls.
A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given according to one’s means, and one should cause the *carvikā* verse to be recited.
On the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one obtains the equal fruit of the Śukra-sacrifice and the Sautrāmaṇi; likewise, one should bathe [the deity] with the Lord of Night (the Moon).
Then, having bathed the goddess Varadā with water from jars and with water,
and having anointed her with camphor, sandalwood, and the liquid of *rocanā*, [he should proceed].
Incense made of sandalwood, camphor, valerian, and white *sihlaka*;
foods filled with sugar; and auspicious drinks.
One should cause food to be given to maidens and Brahmins, as well as for oneself;
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and recite the mantra "mahiṣaghnī."
A garland of lamps made with ghee alone bestows all desires;
one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, the gift of land, and all sacred fords.
O Śukra, this excellent vow, the great Durgā-vrata, is a code of conduct [established] by me, by Rudra, and by Viṣṇu, desiring the welfare of the world.
In former times, this was performed by Bhānu in the battle for the destruction of the planets,
as well as by the gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, kinnaras, and humans.

O tiger among planets, this was indeed performed by the Apsarases and women for the increase of good fortune; and whoever should perform it according to the prescribed rite, [shall likewise attain success].
By hearing this, a mortal obtains all the pleasures desired by the senses;
he gains his wishes, and even a barren woman gives birth to a son.
Thus ends the Durgāṣṭamī vow [the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī];
Brahmā said:
Whether in Āśvina, or Māgha, or Caitra, or even Śrāvaṇa,
the vow of Hari should be performed starting from the dark fortnight and ending with the light fortnight.

"From the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇāt*) means from the dark half. "The limit of the bright [fortnight] of Hari" (*śuklāvadhiṃ hareḥ*) refers to the bright fortnight; and this is to be performed within the months themselves, starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day of the bright fortnight, in the manner that will be described.
One should perform the rite on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina by eating only one meal a day, [worshipping] the Goddess in the form of Maṅgalā, or else as Carughātinī.
One should worship according to the distinction of men with perfumes, garlands, and offerings;
O child, one should feed young maidens and those men who are devotees of the Goddess.
The ninth day should be observed at night; one should pass the tenth day without eating;
one should fast on the eleventh day—this is the rule that should be followed.

“Again, the same rule applies”: the meaning is that just as the four days beginning with the eighth day of the dark fortnight were spent with one-meal, night-meal, food obtained by begging, and fasting, so too should another four days be spent.
O Brahmin, one should fast according to the prescribed rite until the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
every day, however, there should be giving, fire-offerings, recitation, worship, and the feeding of virgins.
One who has conquered anger, as well as one devoted to the Goddess,
should perform the ninefold animal sacrifice (paśupāta) consisting of buffaloes, goats, rams, and so forth.
It should be performed for the sake of spirits and vetālas, and never out of a desire for one's own self.
“The maiden should be adorned”—this is the remainder [of the instruction].
Then there is the viewing of actors and dancers, as well as processions and the night vigil (prajāgara).
One should give gifts according to one's ability to all beings,
even to those who take refuge in the form of Mahābhairava and wear garlands of bones.
O best of gods, she should be especially honored with garments, ornaments, and other such things; this must be done for the sake of attaining all desired objects.
By this method, O Śukra, one obtains the desired fruit:
Maṅgalā, Bhairavī, Durgā, Vāhāhī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
Umā, Haimavatī, Kanyā, Kapālī, Kaiṭabhasvanī, Kālī, Brāhmī, Maheśī, Kaumārī, and Madhusūdanī.
One should indeed mutter these names: Vārāhī and Vāsavi;
one should worship and feed the maiden according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
Clothing and ornaments, as well as bracelets and waist-bands,
should be given according to one's own ability by those devotees who are established in happiness for the sake of the Goddess.
Alternatively, for nine nights, or seven, five, or three;

these options regarding the nine-night period and so forth imply that the feeding of the girls and others must be performed after making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) every day— this being with respect to this particular view—
[performed] by those who have eaten once a day, or at night, or as alms, or even while fasting.
O Śukra, a man should observe the vow until the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
on that day, he should worship Maṅgalā in a mandala prepared according to the rules.
O Śukra, who possesses all the perfections of saṃsāra, who bestows all branches of knowledge,
and who grants all desires— one shall obtain all desires.
O child, it bestows wealth upon one who desires wealth, grants a kingdom to one who desires a kingdom,
bestows health and sons, and destroys all sins.
This should be performed by all castes—by men, women, children, and eunuchs alike;
for such a person there shall be no mental anxieties, no physical ailments, and no fear of enemies.
In battles, even a single person alone shall always achieve great victory;
all undertakings will succeed through hearing [this], of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the eighth-day vow (*aṣṭamīvratam*).
[The Puṣpāṣṭamī] is described in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the auspicious and greatly meritorious fruit of the monthly worship;
having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
One should bathe [the image] with ghee and milk, worship it with *karavīra* flowers,
and having duly performed the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), likewise provide a meal for the Brahmins.
Having had the *pavitraka* fashioned with thread spun by a maiden,
and having adorned it with variegated flowers, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood;
Having observed a fast on the seventh day and fed Brahmins on the eighth,
he who dedicates [the rite] with devotion shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, he will indeed become a king on the surface of the earth; of this there is no doubt—on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having bathed me with devotion using either milk or ghee,
O Goddess, one should perform worship according to the prescribed rite using Apāmārga.
Having mounted a swan-vehicle, he shall go to my world in the heavens;
so too for one who worships with *arka* flowers on the eighth day of the month of Āśvayuja.
One should bathe [the image] with the fragrance of curd and anoint it with saffron;
then, mounted upon a vehicle made of red chalk (gairika), which is auspicious and adorned with garlands of banners, one should proceed.
Accompanied by excellent peacocks, he goes to my abode—
that man who, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, [performs this rite].
One should bathe [the image] with honey and milk and worship it with *jātī* flowers;
then, having mounted a golden vehicle adorned with a network of tinkling bells, one proceeds.
[237] O Goddess, that man who, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, performs the rite with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), goes to my city, beloved by the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having bathed [the deity], one should worship with devotion and honor him with *baka* flowers;
a man who has observed a fast on the seventh day should perform the rites according to the rules on the eighth day.
"Having transcended the three worlds, he shall go wherever I am—
any man who, on the eighth day of the month of Pauṣa, worships me with devotion."
Having bathed the Unmattaka with flowers and ghee,
he ascends a divine celestial chariot known by the name Puṣpaka.
Having reached my abode, he rejoices for eternal years—
he who worships with bilva leaves on the eighth day of the month of Māgha.
Having bathed me with devotion using sugarcane juice,
[he gave me] a vehicle equal to the sun in brilliance and equal to the moon in beauty.
That man who, with scented water, [performs the rite] in the month of Phālguna, ascends and rejoices eternally in my world; of this there is no doubt.
He who worships with *droṇa* flowers shall obtain half the throne of Indra;
likewise, O Goddess, the man who [worships] in the month of Caitra with water and flowers.
Having bathed [the deity], O beautiful one, one should worship with devotion using arka flowers;
thus one obtains the great fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
Furthermore, whatever man, on the eighth day of the month of Vaiśākha,
bathes [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with water scented with camphor and agallochum;
One who worships with white mandāra flowers shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
likewise, he who bathes me with curd on the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha [shall obtain the same].
He who worships with lotus flowers on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, using excellent waters from various sacred fords, shall go to the supreme goal.
Having bathed him, one should worship him with devotion using *dhuttūraka* flowers;
thus he is honored by Gandharvas, Uragas, and birds, as well as by the immortals in heaven.
And she sports with me for as long as there are fourteen Indras;
O Goddess, he who should thus observe the eighth-day vow for a year [attains this].
There is no returning for him again; I speak this truth:
[whether he worships] Nīlakaṇṭha, Śiva, Śambhu, Bhīma, or Maheśvara.
O Goddess, [I bow to] Mahādeva, who is without eyes, the fierce Tryambaka,
and the Lord Śiva, who is worshipped in all the worlds.
One should recite these names of mine during these remaining months.
Thus ends the Puṣpāṣṭamī vow.
[The Dūrvāṣṭamī] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: Viṣṇu said:
O Brahmin, that man who, having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, worships Śaṅkara with devotion and endowed with faith;
O Sage, he who worships Gaṇeśa together with dūrvā grass goes to the supreme abode where the three-eyed God resides.
Having worshipped Maheśāna with all kinds of divine fruits, perfumes, flowers, and unguents, and having honored him with dūrvā grass, one is liberated from all sins.
In a pure place, upon freshly grown dūrvā grass, the best of Brahmins should install the liṅga and then worship it with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One should worship Śaṅkara with devotion using dates, coconuts, and citron fruits, and likewise honor the twice-born according to the rules with dūrvā grass.
O best of the twice-born, a man endowed with faith should offer the *arghya* to the Three-eyed One with curd and unbroken rice,
having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and *śamī* wood.
He indeed would have been born only once, yet he is worshipped by all the gods;
O Dūrvā grass, you are born of nectar and are worshipped by all the gods.
"O son of the Moon, having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods with dūrvā grass, Durvāsas burned away all that evil deed which I had committed."
One who observes the excellent vow should give coconuts and other fruits to the Brahmins;
having consumed curd and worshipped the Three-eyed Lord, he should return home.
O King, Dūrvā grass is known as Gaurī, while Śaṅkara is indeed the fruits.
O Brahmin, whatever man worships Śaṅkara on this lunar day, [attains great merit].
He shall go to a beautiful home honored by divine gandharvas;
having observed a fast on the seventh day, he should worship Śiva on the eighth.
By the very same procedure previously described, he attains all his desires;
the seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge, and the seeker of a son obtains a son.
One who desires wealth shall always obtain it, and one who desires a wife shall find her;
indeed, whatever a person may desire in his mind, that he shall attain.
The person who thus worships Bhūteśa with dūrvā grass and fruits is liberated from the multitude of sins of seven births; there is no doubt about this.
Having observed a fast on the seventh day, one should worship Śiva on the eighth day,
O best of Brahmins, with dūrvā grass, curd, unbroken grains, and auspicious fruits.
Then, O twice-born one, he should honor the Brahmins with various kinds of fruits;
he should eat food that is not cooked by fire, as well as curd and fruit.
O Brahmin, he should eat food that is free from pungent substances and salt, mixed with honey;
he should offer fruits to the Brahmins and himself subsist on fruit.
Having bowed his head to the *dūrvā* grass and to Śiva, he attains auspiciousness;
thus, with devotion, he performs the worship of Mahādeva.
O Brahmin, he attains membership in the assembly of the gods and is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
thus is the meritorious eighth lunar day known as Dūrvā, which removes all sins.
This applies especially to women of all four castes.
Thus ends the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow.
[Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī]
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, please tell me in due order how the entire ritual procedure for the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī is performed, and what must be done."
Īśvara said: Now, when the winter season has arrived, specifically in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having observed the *nakta* fast and become pure, one should consume cow's urine at night.
"Āhāra" means eating; however, one should not eat solid food there.
By that [eating] at night—whether by consuming or by partaking—it is designated as "nakta."
Having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion, one should sleep on the ground at night;
the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice shall be eightfold.
A person should mutter the name of Śaṅkara in the evening, at night, and likewise during the day;
in the month of Pauṣa, having consumed cow's ghee and observed the practice of eating only at night.
One who, purified and intent on offering hymns of praise, worships Śambhu with devotion, obtains the merit of eight Vājapeya sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Māgha, one should prescribe the practice known as Māheśvara, consisting of consuming only milk;
having worshipped Maheśvara, one should sleep at night without food.
By the recitation of the name of Maheśa, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices;
in the month of Phālguna, one should glorify Mahādeva on the dark lunar day.
Having consumed sesame seeds and remaining without food, one should recite [the mantra] at night with a concentrated mind,
while chanting the name of the God and likewise remembering Śaṅkara.
The fruit of reciting this name as previously mentioned is eightfold that of the Rājasūya sacrifice; it is called "Mahādeva" therein.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship the highly meritorious Sthāṇu and consume honey;
having partaken [of it] according to the rule at night, one should sleep during the night without food.
By chanting the great mantra of Sthāṇu, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices;
one should worship the god Śiva with water from kuśa grass during the month of Vaiśākha.
Having recited that auspicious mantra, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink the water from the horns of cows while reciting the mantra named Paśupati.
O Brahmin, by chanting [this] to Paśupati, one obtains the merit of ten million cows;
furthermore, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should proclaim the name "Ugra."
There, one should cause [the practitioner] to consume cow-dung that yields the fruit of eight Sautrāmaṇī sacrifices;
for whoever recites this mantra, which bestows all accomplishments.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the rite called Śarva is proclaimed, which brings about the destruction of all sins;
one who is well-purified by meditation should consume arka at night while reciting the mantra.
For more than a full hundred million years, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
one should recite the mantra of the three-eyed god on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada.
One should consume a bilva leaf and obtain the fruit of a year-long initiation;
there, with a single-pointed mind and well-purified, one should meditate upon Tryambaka.
And in the month of Āśvayuja, O Hero, one should consume rice-water;
by remembering the god named Aiśa, one obtains eight lotuses.
Having consumed curd in the month of Kārttika,
one who is well-purified should remember Rudra at night— he who is the destroyer of all sins.
One obtains the eightfold fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
there is no ritual action devoid of mantra, and that which is devoid of mantra does not succeed.
For without mantra, O Goddess, even with effort it would be in vain;
therefore, with every exertion, one should utter the mantra in this way.
O Goddess, when the vow is completed at the end of the year, there is great fruit;
indeed, by the grace of this very [vow], one attains the state free from all affliction.
O Śambhu, O Lord of the Gods, during the auspicious seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, one should offer this vow [to you] through your grace.
"O Lord, this most highly honored vow has indeed been completed in its entirety. Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, [she said: "O Śaṅkara, be present here!"
"By your grace, O Lord of Gods, I shall recite [the mantra] according to my ability;
at the end of the year, an offering of libations with bulbs, roots, and fruits is prescribed."
And having invited Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva and firm in their vows according to my ability,
please show me your favor with supreme devotion.
"I shall perform the meritorious *tarpaṇa* (satisfaction) of the vow as enjoined by Śiva.
*Tarpaṇa* means "filling" [or fulfillment].
Having thus worshipped, one should afterwards offer various kinds of foods, both solid and soft.
And a black cow with white markings, beautiful in form and yielding abundant milk,
should be given— her horns tipped with gold, her hooves silvered, and adorned with ornaments of bells.
O beautiful goddess, for the sake of spiritual welfare, a cow should be given to the preceptor, adorned with garments and flowers, wearing a garland of blossoms, and auspicious in appearance.
One should know the teacher to be Śiva, and Śiva to be in the form of the teacher;
for there is no difference between the two, namely the teacher and Śiva.
For this reason, O Goddess, the Guru is Sadāśiva, who is always to be worshipped;
he is the one who delivers mortals from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen are equal to that gift which is given to the guru, which Sadāśiva himself always accepts.
Therefore, with every effort, the Guru should always be worshipped.
Thus has been told to you the entire supreme ritual for the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī.
The man who performs this rite for a year according to this rule,
being endowed with the fulfillment of all desires, goes to the supreme state.
Thus ends the vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Having diligently observed the night-meal (nakta) according to the prescribed rule on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the god Śaṅkara.
Having drunk cow urine according to one's capacity, one should sleep at night without food;
the fruit of this shall be eightfold that of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, having worshipped Maheśvara by the name Śambhu in the month of Pauṣa,
and consuming clarified butter on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains the merit of eight Rājasūya sacrifices.
O Brahmin, one should worship Maheśvara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha;
by drinking cow’s milk at night, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
And having worshipped Mahādeva in the month of Phālguna, one should consume sesame seeds;
the fruit of this shall be eightfold that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And in the month of Caitra, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Sthāṇu;
having consumed roasted barley grains, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By worshipping the one named Śiva in the month of Vaiśākha and drinking water from kuśa grass at night,
one obtains ten times the fruit of the Puruṣamedha sacrifice.
Having worshipped Paśupati in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink water from the horns of cows;
one shall thereby obtain that fruit which results from the gift of ten million cows.
Having worshipped the one named Ugra in the month of Āṣāḍha and having consumed cow-dung,
one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred years.
Thus, having worshipped the Sun in the month of Śrāvaṇa, a person should consume [the fast-food] at night;
such a human obtains the fruit of a sacrifice involving a hundred cows.
One should worship Tryambaka on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada;
having consumed a bilva leaf, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the month of Āśvayuja, it is prescribed that one should consume rice-water;
by chanting the name of the Lord, one shall obtain the fruit of a lotus.
On the eighth day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the deity named Īśāna;
by drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) once, one obtains the fruit of the five great sacrifices.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva,
offering milk-rice mixed with honey and well-drenched in clarified butter.
According to one's capacity, one should devotedly present gold and garments to them;
likewise, black water-pots filled with sesame seeds and accompanied by various kinds of food and edibles.
In this rite, twelve [cows] should be given, accompanied by umbrellas and pairs of sandals;
one should offer to Rudra a black, milch cow.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of that man who, with devotion, performs the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow continuously for an entire year.
Completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers, he shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva; having attained the celestial realm, he does not return here again.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow according to another method,
as found in the Matsyapurāṇa.
Sūrya said: Now I shall describe the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, which destroys all sins,
so that peace and liberation may especially come to men.
One should worship Śaṅkara in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Śambhu in Pauṣa; one should worship the god Maheśvara in Māgha, and Mahādeva in Phālguna.
A person should likewise worship Sthāṇu in Caitra and Śiva in Viśākha;
similarly, one should worship Paśupati in Jyeṣṭha and Ugra in Āṣāḍha.
One should worship Śarva in the month of Śrāvaṇa, then Tryambaka in Nabhasya,
Hara in the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise Īśāna in Kārttika.
On all Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī days, one who has fasted should, with devotion to Śiva, worship the twice-born according to one's ability with cows, land, gold, and garments.
Cow’s urine with ghee and milk, sesame seeds, barley-water and kuśa-grass water,
cow-horn water, cow-dung, arka-leaves, bilva-leaves, and curd.
Having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship Śaṅkara at night;
likewise, [one should worship] the Aśvattha, the Vaṭa, the Udumbara, and the Plakṣa trees.
The great seers know the Palāśa and the Jambū tree as the sixth;
[these are assigned] respectively to two months each, beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
One should eat each tooth-stick from these trees;
when finished, one should offer curd-rice, a canopy, a banner, and chowries.
One should give a bell to the deity, as well as a black cow, two black garments,
water-pots for the twice-born, and [a vessel] endowed with five jewels.
One who is unable [to give much] should, however, give black cows, garments, and various fruits; or, according to his capacity, he may give even a single cow.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one incurs fault.
By fasting on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in this manner, [one attains merit] for three hundred times seven kalpas.
A man honored by the gods is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī.
[Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī]
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*,
Viṣṇu said:
"When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, that which is the eighth day of the dark fortnight— "
And she is the remover of sin, meritorious, and the increaser of Śiva’s bliss.
O Three-eyed One, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods performed on that day shall indeed bring satisfaction to all.
O Sage, a Śrāddha performed especially on that day, as well as a Homa, brings merit according to the rules;
therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the Śrāddha on that occasion.
The wise know that eating only once a day on the fifth lunar day and eating only at night on the sixth constitute the subtle [observance];
however, there is fasting on the seventh, and on the eighth one should worship Śiva.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha rite;
having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, one should eat that which has been offered to the ancestors.
But he who performs a *śrāddha* ceremony here after worshipping the Three-eyed One,
for him his ancestors shall remain satisfied for fifteen years.
In this manner, one should perform this vow for oneself alone with devotion;
one should worship the supreme deity, the destroyer of Tripura, by means of [his] names.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Śambhu; likewise, others [should worship] Śaṅkara.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Śiva, and likewise Śarva in Mārgaśīrṣa.
Likewise, Īśāna is proclaimed for the month of Pauṣa; Ugra is proclaimed for Māgha;
the one named Rudra for Phālguna; and Bhīma is proclaimed for Caitra.
O twice-born one, one should worship Nīlakaṇṭha in Vaiśākha, the supreme Bhava in Jyeṣṭha,
Mahādeva in Āṣāḍha, and Tryambaka in Śrāvaṇa.
Learn from me these names of the months, which are the [substances for] the first-feeding rites:
cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water from a lotus-stalk.
O Brahmin, for the purification of the body, one should consume cow bezoar, the five products of the cow, earth from the Mandāra tree, as well as sesame seeds and barley.
O Brahmin, I speak of these flowers for the pleasure of the God of gods:
the karavīra, the jātī, the prāleya, and the kadambaka.
O Brahmin, likewise [the fruits of] unmattaka, bilva, śamī leaves, and baka,
as well as the flower of mālatī and that of mukuraka.
Kuśa grass and flowers, as well as the agasti flower,
silhaka, vijaya incense, buffalo ghee, and guggulu resin.
O best of Brahmins, he who thus worships the god Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura,
goes alone to the supreme state.
He who should honor the Brahmins, and especially the reciter,
as well as the devotees of Mahādeva— those twice-born ones who follow the Pāśupata path— with true devotion.
Thus, he who performs the śrāddha on the eighth lunar day and during the aṣṭakā festivals,
having worshipped Śiva, the Lord of the Gods, together with wise brahmins—
O tiger among sages, his ancestors remain satisfied for fifteen divine years, seven, seven, and seven [years].
And having thus observed it with devotion on the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī thereafter,
whatever desire a person may long for, that very thing he shall obtain.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain riches;
a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one desiring a daughter shall obtain an excellent daughter.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow.
O best of the twice-born, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Three-eyed Lord.
The man who worships the Lord of Gods shall go to the world of Īśa.
Likewise, during the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and the following one,
he should worship for those four months with clusters of blue lotuses and kadamba flowers.
One should worship Śambhu, the destroyer of Tripura, the three-eyed one, and the slayer of Andhaka,
with a cluster of *gandha* flowers and with *guggulu*.
O Brahmin, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the fruit that has the form of a deity (*devarūpa*), which purifies the body.
"The form of a deity" means the fruit of a deity.
One should repeatedly invoke the name of the deity, saying "Śaṅkara."
O Brahmin, in the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise in Kārttika, O twice-born one,
as well as in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and in the month of Pauṣa, [one should worship] Hara.
One should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rites with devotion using unmatta flowers;
one should worship Hari, the Lord of gods, with incense of camphor and agaru.
One should cause [the deity] named Virūpākṣa to consume barley according to the prescribed rite;
the excellent incense is sihlaka, and the supreme food offering is milk-rice (pāyasa).
In the month of Māgha or indeed in the month of Phālguna, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
one should worship the Three-eyed Lord with devotion using lotuses during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha.
One should worship Śambhu, Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, according to the rules,
with great incense and with incense duly prepared.
One should worship with food offerings and sugar-coated sweets while reciting the name "Īśa.
Whoever thus worships Maheśvara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight [of the month of Kārttika], [attains the highest goal].
[254] O best of Brahmins, he goes alone, one by one, to the supreme state;
O foremost of the twice-born, hear now that which is desired by the God of gods.
The incense is *unmattadhūpa*, while black agalloch (*kṛṣṇāgaru*) is always the [primary] incense;
among all fragrances, sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*) is supreme, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is always the food offering (*naivedya*).
The performer of worship is a Pāśupata who has renounced all enjoyments;
the reciter, who knows the ritual procedures, is the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having thus performed the worship according to all the prescribed rules,
at the end of the year, one should perform a great worship and the meritorious recitation of the book.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who indeed causes [this] to be made with devotion:
he attains Goloka, resplendent like Śukra.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow. [The Dampatyaṣṭamī:
O best of Brahmins, O sage, in the month of Kārttika, a man desiring a son—
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, O twice-born one, one should worship according to the prescribed rite.
Having fashioned the omnipresent Lord together with Umā out of darbha grass,
[one should worship Him] with offerings of perfumes and flowers, as well as with garments and ornaments.
O best of the twice-born, [he should take] straight darbha grasses, resembling blue beryl, complete with their roots but devoid of flowers, along with their tips and without their shoots.
O best of Brahmins, having taken [the materials], one should fashion the god Nīlakaṇṭha, the lord of Umā, as well as that goddess Umā, Satī, according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship with perfumes, garlands, and various kinds of fruits and edibles,
as well as with diverse spectacles and musical instruments played with the mouth, O observer of noble vows.
O best of Brahmins, he who thus performs the Umāmāheśvara vow with devotion,
even if he is alone, goes to the supreme state.
By four such fast-breaking meals, one *kha* is thus proclaimed by the wise;
the first fast-breaking meal, however, occurs after three months beginning with Kārttika.
O Sage, in the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Pauṣa,
[one should worship] with the flowers of the Unmattaka and with incenses as previously described.
One should worship with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and various kinds of edible offerings,
as well as with diverse spectacles and musical instruments played with the mouth, O observer of good vows.
Whoever performs this with devotion should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rite;
one should smear him with white sandalwood paste.
One should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter as an offering, and milk-rice (pāyasa) as the supreme food-offering;
one should perform the ritual bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and partake of it as well.
[256] O best of the twice-born, the goddess whose name is indeed Mahādevī is recited as Gaurī; this is so in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and likewise Caitra.
One should worship the Lord with *mālatī* flowers and with *mudgara* flowers;
the name of the God is indeed Virūpākṣa, and the name of the Goddess is Umā.
One should worship the Lord, the All-pervading One, according to the rules with agallochum incense;
likewise, one should devoutly and according to the rules smear him with saffron.
One should offer boiled rice with curd as an oblation to the Trident-bearer;
likewise, one should consume water infused with *kuśa* grass for the purification of one's own body.
Likewise, O Sage, one should recite the Dharma during the months of Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha,
using karavīra flowers as well as red lotuses.
O Brahmin, Śiva and she whose name is Śivā were indeed proclaimed by them through the smoke of the *prājāpatya* fire and with *rasālā* and *modaka* sweets.
For the bath and the ritual consumption, clarified butter and black sesame seeds are recommended by the wise;
agarwood and storax are prescribed as incense, and this is known as the Prājāpatya rite.
During the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the supreme deity, the destroyer of Tripura, according to the prescribed rites with clusters of jasmine flowers.
O Sage, one should worship the Lord of Gods according to the rules with the fourfold mixture,
with incense blended with agarwood, and with kṛśara, cakes, and milk-rice.
Whoever worships the god Hara with these four offerings at the conclusion of the fasts, shall obtain the fourfold aims of life if they so desire; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, one who does not desire obtains the fourth fruit;
"the fourth" is liberation.
A person who desires obtains their desired object according to their wish.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one seeking wealth shall obtain abundant riches;
and one seeking knowledge shall surely obtain vast knowledge from Śaṅkara.
Having thus performed this single vow, O Brahmin, one should gratify Hari at the end of the year with various spectacles and with offerings to the Brāhmaṇas.
A wise man should feed a Brahmin couple, who are experts in the ritual manual and the reciter, for the pleasure of Śaṅkara.
O Sage, one should conceive of Śambhu as the speaker and his wife Lalitā;
having gratified this divine couple with various kinds of food and edibles, one should worship them.
O best of the twice-born, one should give garments dyed with safflower to those two after having honored the best of the twice-born with various kinds of fragrant flowers.
Furthermore, O Sage, one should give as a sacrificial fee two golden images:
Mahādeva to the reciter and Lalitā to his wife.
Whoever thus worships Śambhu with devotion, endowed with faith,
shall ascend a divine, supreme celestial vehicle born of light.
Resplendent with brilliance like Śukra and possessing a luster resembling Hari,
he shall go to the supreme, immovable abode of the wielder of the trident.
"Therefore, having come here, one shall become a king on earth, a lord of sovereigns.
Thus ends the *Dampaty-aṣṭamī-vrata* (also known as *Kālāṣṭamī*).
In the Vāmana Purāṇa,
Pulastya said:
"And likewise, that auspicious Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī which falls in the month of Nabhasya..."
That eighth day of the dark fortnight which is conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras is considered Kālāṣṭamī.
In that [city], on the Ekaliṅga [tithi], Śaṅkara sleeps;
"Ekaliṅgas" are those well-known [shrines] facing west, devoid of [images of] the Bull and Gaṇapati.
It is traditionally taught that when he is present there in the spring, worship performed there is inexhaustible.
The wise man should bathe according to the rules with cow urine and water;
having bathed, he should worship the Three-eyed Lord with *kuṭaja* flowers.
Incense is made from the resin of the *kesara* tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) consists of honey and clarified butter.
*Kesara* refers to the *bakula* tree.
Having uttered, "May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me," one should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The best of the twice-born, having fasted and subdued his senses, should likewise offer the sacrificial food (naivedya) along with gold to a Brahmin in the month of Āśvayuja.
On the ninth day, one should perform a bath with cow dung and worship with lotuses.
Since it is stated, "In the same way, during the month of Āśvayuja, one should observe a fast," it should be understood that the fast was also observed in the preceding month.
One should fumigate with the resin of the *sarja* tree, and offer honey and sweetmeats as the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform an ablution on the ninth day, saying:
"May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me; let the sacrificial fee be made with sesame seeds."
In the month of Kārttika, one should perform a bath with milk or worship with karavīra flowers;
one should offer incense made from the resin of the śrīvāsa tree and an offering of honeyed milk-porridge (madhupāyasa).
An offering of food and silver should be given as a gift to the elder brother;
"elder brother" here refers to the Brāhmaṇa. [The mantra] "May the Lord Sthāṇu be pleased" should be recited immediately thereafter. "Śrīvāsa" is the Sarala tree.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform an ablution on the ninth;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ritual bath is prescribed there, and the worship is known as that of Rudra.
Incense is made from the resin of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree; the food offering consists of honey and milk-rice (pāyasa);
the food offering also includes red śāli rice; and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed.
The wise should say: "Homage be to you! May Śarva be pleased! "Arcā" means worship. "Rudrajā" means born from the *śamī* flower. "Śrīvṛkṣa" is the *bilva*.
In the month of Pauṣa, there should be bathing with clarified butter (*havis*) and worship by means of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*).
Incense made from the resin of the *madhūka* tree and an offering of honey-cakes (*madhuśaṣkulī*), accompanied by a gift of pearls,
are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the gratification of the Teacher of the World.
One should utter the words, "Salutation to you, O Lord of Gods, O Three-eyed One.
With "oblation" (haviṣā) means with clarified butter (ghṛtena).
In the month of Māgha, there should be a bath with water infused with *kuśa* grass, or worship with musk (*mṛgamada*).
The incense should be the resin of the kadamba tree; the food offering (naivedya) should be rice mixed with sesame seeds.
One should present as a food offering milk and safflower, along with gold.
One should utter: "May Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, be pleased with me.
Thus is one [vow] prescribed, with the breaking of the fast occurring after six months.
At the conclusion of the breaking of the fast, one should perform the ritual bathing of the Three-eyed Lord in due order;
having anointed the deity with gorocanā, sandalwood, and saffron, one should worship him.
Be pleased; I am wretched, O Lord, and I bow eternally to you, whose crest-jewel is the moon.
Then, O best of the twice-born, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, a fast is prescribed to be observed by one who is restrained in his vows.
On the second day, one should then perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should worship with kunda flowers and offer incense made of sandalwood.
One should offer as an oblation cooked rice with jaggery and ghee in a copper vessel,
and likewise provide sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) along with the oblation to the twice-born.
One should offer a pair of garments while pronouncing the name of Rudra;
and in the month of Caitra, one should perform a bath with Udumbara fruits and worship with Mandāra flowers.
The wise one should burn guggulu incense known as mahiṣa, anointed with ghee;
likewise, he should offer clarified butter mixed with water as a pleasing oblation.
One should present the sacrificial fee, the food offering, and the deer skin;
at the beginning and also at the end, one should utter this by name.
Endowed with faith, one should perform the propitiation of the Lord of the Gods;
in the month of Vaiśākha, a bath with fragrant flowers and water is prescribed.

O Lord, the worship of Śaṅkara has been described as a vow consisting of eating only at night and so forth; the incense is that called *sūryākhya*, the flower is likewise, and the food offering is ghee with fruit.
“Sūryākhyapuṣpa” means the flower of the *arka* plant. The name of the Lord, “Kālaghna,” should be recited by the wise man. He should present water-pots together with food offerings to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should devoutly give a pair of sandals and an umbrella as an offering, [saying]:
"Homage to you, O destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, the vanquisher of Puṣpadanta!"
One should recite this with devotion for the pleasure of the Lord of the World;
bathing in the month of Āṣāḍha and worship with *śrīphala* fruits are always prescribed.
For incense, one should use *dhūttūraka* flowers as well as *sihlaka*;
the food offering consists of cakes with fruit, and likewise, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be accompanied by ghee.
Then one should utter this: "Salutations to you, O destroyer of the pride of the Daityas.
Having performed a bath with musk in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Hari.
One should offer incense made from śrīvṛkṣa leaves together with fruit, as well as agallochum;
one should present an offering of food (naivedya) consisting of curd filled with ghee along with sweet rice balls (modaka).
One should give curd-rice with sesame, black parched grains with fried cakes,
and as a sacrificial fee, a bull and an auspicious tawny cow.
One should give gold and red garments to a Brahmin;
for the wise have proclaimed the name of Śambhu as "Gaṅgādhara."
With these six subsequent months, he shall perform the supreme breaking of the fast;
thus, having fully worshipped the one whose banner is the bull for a complete year.
A man devoted to Maheśvara attains imperishable worlds;
this meritorious vow has been described as auspicious and the bringer of all security.
"O divine sage, that which was spoken by Candra himself is so and not otherwise.
Thus ends the Kālāṣṭamī-vrata (also known as the Kālī-vrata).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa, the Goddess said:
"Excellent! You are a devotee, O knower of dharma; [you have performed] my vow of Kālarātri."
Listen; I shall tell you how the duty toward them must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the wise man, having conquered his senses,
being truthful in speech, firm in mind and self, should remain established in his observances.
[264] Having first constructed a pavilion on a level and auspicious portion of the ground—
square, even, white, and adorned with banners and flags—
Having marked out the sacrificial pit with a cord to the measure of one cubit,
one should then gather the excellent materials, as well as *darbha* grass and sesame seeds.
One should duly prepare twenty-seven auspicious fuel-sticks of Palāśa and Pippala wood, shaped like a bow.
And also water-pitchers (*gargarī*), jars, and the auspicious vessels of Hari;
"gargarī" refers to a large bowl (*maṇḍalī*);
as well as baskets, sun-leaf fans, and auspicious woven articles.
One should offer the food oblation, flowers, water for the arghya, excellent ritual substances,
and indeed all of this, as well as a beautiful fan.
One should bring fragrant flowers, such as jasmine and blue lotuses, as well as many other pure items, including kusha grass and the like.
And various products of the cow, incenses beginning with guggulu,
the consecrated water, the seats, the sacrificial porridge, and the sruva ladle.
Having thus prepared the four requisites along with those born of noble families,
he should appoint the preceptors for the purpose of the consecration (adhivāsa) on my behalf.
Those who are pure, free from anger, worshippers of the gods and Brahmins,
worthy ones born of noble families, and endowed with truthfulness, purity, and ritual action;
O child, having stayed for seven nights with these four such teachers who abide by their vows, she should be honored daily with meals eaten at night.
Then, having undertaken the observance (niyama), one should likewise cause the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed by Brahmins born of Śaṅkara in that pit which is shaped like a bow.
Listen, if one desires upward progression and the bestowing power of prosperity, one should certainly not perform the fire-oblation oneself in the absence of such [an officiant].
In their absence, he should have other Brahmins perform the worship of the ground with offerings as in the fire-oblation;
and having ascertained that she is certainly free from physical defects and born of a noble family, he should likewise [proceed].
“Born of Śaṅkara” means those born of the lineage of Śaṅkara, such as Sāmba, Gaṇādhipa, and others.
Having first worshipped these— Sāmba, Gaṇādhipa, the Mothers, Bhūpāla, and Vṛṣabhadhvaja— one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
For the sake of success in all rites, one should worship Hara, the Lord of Gods, in his causal form along with the Mothers, and in his essential form together with the Mothers.

“Bhūpāla” is Kṣetrapāla; “Āgneya” is Kārtikeya. When the sun has risen, one should offer twenty-seven fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood; likewise, when the sun has set, one should offer fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood.

The words "twenty" and "seven" are to be supplied [to the following]. At midnight, with devotion, one should perform the supreme fire-oblation (*homa*) using black sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), continuing for as long as one hundred and eight [repetitions].
By means of this mantra, which destroys all [obstacles] right there,
which grants boons, is well-perfected, and effects nourishment and peace;

Oṃ hrīṃ! Homage to the one clothed in black, who is borne by hundreds of thousands of millions of lions, O you of great strength, unconquered Pratyāṅgirā, you who attend to all armies, destroyer of spells, you who madden all beings, subduer of all spirits: destroy, destroy all faults; cut off, cut off all obstacles; rend, rend asunder all the wicked; devour, devour, O you with flaming tongue and terrifying mouth! Tear apart, tear apart all limbs; tear apart, tear apart the fetters! Pratyāṅgirā, homage be to you! Svāhā!
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should offer the sacrificial bali and the caru-oblation in all directions,
using rice mixed with sesame and combined with milk as prescribed.
One should perform this for seven days, and on the seventh day, in the directions;
there are fifty-five Vāruṇa [mantras], which are more numerous than those bound within the lineage.

Regarding the phrase "with what was previously stated for one whose kingdom is weak," the word "vāruṇī" from the subsequent passage is to be supplied here. "Pura" refers to *guggulu* (bdellium). "From persistence" means from that which is fixed daily.
Furthermore, praise should be offered by many born of the same lineage in the courtyard;
or else, having stayed there, one should remain at night indeed for the sake of worship.
O child, listen, O Lord, to that which must always be performed according to the rules as the worship of Agni by Brahmins born of the sacrifice of Dharma, for the purpose of praise.
For seven days, and likewise for another seven days, one should wash the face of the Goddess with sandalwood and agallochum, with supreme devotion.
A drawing should be made for the purpose of washing the face;
furthermore, a clay image should be established and worshipped at all times.
Having washed [the guest] with water purified by mantras and having removed his soiled garments,
one should diligently perform the worship, honoring him with honey and the madhuparka offering.
Then, having again applied the nectar, one should prepare the face and the body;
and having prepared the foods, one should employ them according to the ritual rule.
For my sake, one should prepare auspicious nectar consisting of cow’s milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, honey,
and sugar-candy.
Having prepared various kinds of foods together with rice in due order,
one should then offer condiments, drinks, and once again incense.
Then, having performed another circumambulation and prostrating like a staff,
they should quickly praise [the deities] with their own hymn composed for the time of dharma.
Then, having duly honored the Brahmins there with devotion,
one who is mindful of dharma should clothe them in garments made of gold, distributed in equal portions.
Furthermore, one should cause singing, dancing, and especially the governance of the kingdom to be performed with great effort before the Goddess in this manner.
"O child, I always accept all this out of devotion;
it is my entire property, and I do not touch anything that is hidden."
For the sake of my pleasure, one who is pure, having bathed, with senses subdued, self-controlled, and endowed with patience, should swiftly practice devotion through my mantra.
One should not allow impurity to remain on the body, since that is said to be evil;
by it one would not become virtuous, nor would there be liberation for those two.
Having thus completed [the rite], he should then go home slowly;
having gone there, the pure Brahmin, filled with joy, should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should first feed eight young maidens and eight of the best of the twice-born according to the prescribed rite, dedicating it to me and the Mothers.
And one should feed eight twice-born men who are established in their vows and devoted to the dharma of Śiva,
dedicating the offering to the god Śaṅkara, as well as Umā and Vināyaka.
Having satisfied them with devotion, one should especially gratify the officiating priest;
thereafter, having prostrated again and again, one should ask for forgiveness.
This has been described as a general rule; it may be expanded according to one's capacity.
Therein, out of compassion, one should feed the poor and the wretched.
That which is given to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, that which is given to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin),
that which is given to those who are treasuries of austerity, and likewise that which is given out of compassion;
All that gift is indeed inexhaustible due to its purity and proper performance;
it has certainly been offered to the Lord, for this is the truth, without a doubt.
"Whether they be worthy or unworthy, let all be fed together at my festival;
whether they be women or others, let everyone indeed be satisfied with the highest expectation."
Then, together with his kinsmen and with supreme joy, he,
being self-restrained, should eat the remnants of the sacrifice after the fire has been offered.
One should always perform the Kaumudī festival at the improper time during the dark fortnight;
one should begin it on the eighth day of the month of Āśvayuja, within the scope of the lunar festival.
Or else, by dwelling on a single night or by eating but one meal a day,
having abandoned the mass of evil, he shall go to the supreme goal.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or those of Śūdra birth,
whoever shall observe this vow will likewise attain freedom from suffering.
And by performing thus according to the rule, one shall possess sons and wealth;
terrible calamities do not stain him, nor is he oppressed by enemies.
This renowned vow of Kālī must be performed with diligence by those born into her lineage who desire peace, nourishment, and forbearance, as well as those who seek knowledge.
Honored by thousands of lions and by asuras,
he shall go to heaven in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, according to his conduct.
"O child, you ought to perform this vow— which I have always declared to be the destroyer of sins— with supreme devotion and without weariness."
Whoever shall establish a relationship with those born of the lowest castes and so forth,
performing it with one of inferior varna, shall by this act become a perpetrator of sin.
Thus ends the Kālī-vrata. [The Somavratam:
Now I shall fully describe another supreme vow that brings about the highest welfare.
Learn duly this meritorious illustration:
on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight falling on a Monday, one should worship Soma according to the prescribed rite,
with abundant food and a moon-disc, [offering it] to the one whose crest is marked by the moon.
One should meditate on Hara in the right half and the all-pervading Hari in the left half;
having established the liṅga with offerings such as ghee and products of sugarcane, as previously described.

One should smear the right half with sandalwood mixed with moon-essence (camphor), and the left half with saffron and agallochum; the water for the guest-offering (arghya) should be prepared in the same manner.
One should likewise worship the portion of Hara with gold together with a vajra;
and the portion of Hari especially with a pearl and a sapphire.
Afterwards, having encircled it with auspicious flowers, one should fashion a flower mandala;
then one should again perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with twenty-five lamps.
With both mental disposition and ritual procedure, again and again,
one should present the food offering (naivedya) consisting of auspicious, prepared foods and clarified butter.
Having honored the Brahmins who observe the vow as well as the Fire-god,
and having fed married couples, he should present gifts according to his ability.
O observer of noble vows, having worshipped the ancestors on the eighth day according to this rite,
listen now to what must be performed at the end of that year.
Having worshipped two pairs of white and yellow [cloths] according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should likewise offer a canopy, as well as banners and small bells.
Whether during the movement of incense or when the lamp-trees are beautiful,
having thus separated [the offerings] as before, one should perform the meal-offering.
For he who shall thus perform this five-year cycle of abdication will, without doubt,
having attained both worlds, go to the state that is free from all ailment.
[271] Without doubt, therefore, one who lives should practice according to the rule;
one should perceive that Hari himself is manifest right here in human form.
Calamities do not touch him, nor indeed does he become miserable;
he is never afflicted by fever, dysentery, or other such ailments.

“Both wings” means having reached both sides. “Abundant food” means food rich in clarified butter (*ājya*). “With *ghṛta* and so forth” means with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). “Joined with the moon” means joined with camphor. “Solid” refers to *uśīra*. “With the thunderbolt” means joined with diamond (*vajra*). “By both” refers to the Goddess and the God. “By the mental disposition” means by one meditating on Hari and Hara. “According to the rite” refers to the rite of *nīrājana*. “The parents” are those two very ones. “The movement of incense” refers to the vessel for burning incense. Thus ends the *Somavrata*. [Now follows the *Śaṅkarārkavrata*.]
Then, by means of this path, having attained that very auspicious eighth [day], one should practice according to the previously mentioned rule during the conjunction with the Sun.
However, the wise man should worship the Sun residing in the right eye;
he should join it with a ruby and gold—listen now to this application.
[272] And below the forehead of Netra, one should apply saffron and red sandalwood in a circular shape; then, one should worship Hara in the center as before.
In the absence of rubies, one should employ gold everywhere;
for its root-mantra is always the supreme seed-syllable of Rudra.
The [deity] is adorned with red garlands and garments; the food offering (naivedya) is white and drenched in ghee.
The remaining detailed ritual procedure is to be performed according to the previously established rules.
However, having fasted here on the seventh lunar day, one with restrained senses should again worship Śaṅkara and the Sun, and then consume cow's ghee to break the fast.
This should be performed according to the previously mentioned rule during the ritual of the five-year cycle;
by doing so, one shall enjoy pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and other deities before proceeding to the supreme state.
Having crossed over this, one becomes powerful, generous, and dear to one's own kin;
in this world, such a person is not afflicted and shall possess wealth and sons.
Thus ends the Śaṅkarārka-vrata.
Thus end the Aṣṭamī-vratas.
Now, regarding the ninth-day vows (*navamī-vrata*), specifically the *Śaurya-vrata*, it is described therein in the *Varāha-purāṇa*.
Agastya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed vow of valor,
by which even a coward instantly attains great heroism.
In the month of Āśvayuja, that pure ninth day (Navamī) should indeed be observed as a fast;
having made a formal vow on the seventh, one should remain without solid food on the eighth.
On the ninth day, O King, one should first respectfully partake of flour;
then, with devotion, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and worship the Goddess herself.
Having thus fasted according to the prescribed rite for as long as a year, [one worships] the goddess Durgā, the highly fortunate one, the great illusion, and the one of great splendor.
At the conclusion of the vow, the wise man should feed young maidens according to his capacity,
having adorned them with gold, garments, and other gifts according to his means.
Afterwards, one should ask for her forgiveness, saying, "May the Goddess be pleased with me.
When this is done, one who has lost his kingdom will regain it; of this there is no doubt.
The ignorant obtains knowledge, and the timid finds valor;
such is the vow of valor.
[The Ubhayanavamī Vrata] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa. Sumantu said:
The man who diligently observes the fast on the ninth day for one year,
having enjoyed pleasures in this world, shall go to heaven in the next.
When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, he who should observe the practice of eating only at night—
having conquered his senses, speaking the truth, and being free from desire and anger.
One should diligently observe the fast on the ninth day of both fortnights;
one should worship the Noble Lady three times a day with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and other gifts.
Having performed the fire-ritual according to the rules, one should prepare a bed upon the ground;
at the end of the month, one should perform a ceremonial bath for the Blessed Lady with ghee and other substances.
Having performed meditation and a great worship, one should offer it to Caṇḍikā;
one should present as an oblation a prastha of rice cooked in milk.
One should feed eight young maidens as well as Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas; "Vaiṣṇavas" refers to those devoted to the Blessed One (Bhagavatī).
Having fashioned an image of the Goddess out of flour, one should worship her under the name Āryā.
O Brahmin, having performed the ritual bath with perfumes, flowers, and guggulu resin for the four-armed goddess who holds a trident, one should likewise consume sesame seeds.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who should thus worship the Noble One:
seated upon a supreme celestial palace that resembles ten million suns, he shall dwell there.
One shall go to the delightful city of Durgā, where Caṇḍikā herself dwells and sports with gods and Gandharvas until the dissolution of all beings.
Together with twenty-one blades of kuśa grass, one enjoys desired pleasures in heaven;
then, returning again to this earth, O hero, one becomes a king upon the ground.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, one should observe the practice of eating only at night,
consuming kṛśara mixed with ghee while keeping the senses fully restrained.
Devoted to fasting on both the eighth days of the two fortnights,
one should worship Tryambikā with devotion, having fashioned [an image] from wheat flour.
O Hero, one should worship Durgā, who has eight arms and is known by the name Tryambikā,
with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and all things that are red.
One should offer black aloe as incense and offer buffalo meat;
for the ritual bath, white mustard seeds are prescribed, and for the consumption [of the remnants], barley is traditionally taught.
The man who thus worships Tryambikā during the month of Māgha ascends a divine celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
When the month of Phālguna has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming a meal of barley while keeping women at a great distance;
Having observed a fast on the eighth day of both fortnights, O King,
one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite by the name Gaurī, indeed, O King.
O Hero, having fashioned a beautiful image made of copper with thirty-two and a half arms,
one should worship it with yellow flowers mixed with sandalwood and agallochum.
Curd-rice is the food offering, while this excellent frankincense is the incense;
for the bath and the ritual consumption, grain is used, and cow’s urine serves for the purification of the body.
And on the ninth day, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the Great Goddess with ghee and other substances;
one should devoutly feed a young maiden and Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity.
O best of kings, he who thus worships the goddess Durgā with devotion goes to the supreme abode where that Caṇḍikā resides.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming rice flour mixed with milk produced from *śāli* rice;
Having fashioned [an image] of sandalwood, one should worship the Blessed Lady with devotion using perfumes,
flowers, and offerings, [visualizing her] as having twenty-five arms.
One should indeed offer incense made of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood, along with agallochum and camphor, to the Blessed Lady known by the name Jvālāmukhī.
O King, one should devotedly offer an animal-headed oblation according to the prescribed rite;
O lord of men, during the bath, one should offer water with *kuśa* grass and grain for consumption.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess of the gods and fed the Kumārī, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability; thereafter, remaining restrained in speech, one should eat oneself.
O Lord of the Earth, having ascended that most excellent celestial chariot, which is joined with clusters of rubies and features a golden jeweled altar, he dwells in the world of Viṣṇu.
O King of kings, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one intent on fasting should worship Caṇḍikā with devotion.
O Lord, having thus established her by name as "Bhagavatī," she is composed of speech,
possessing eight arms, radiant white in form, with a face resembling the full moon.
O King, one should worship the mallets according to the prescribed rite with garlands,
and with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and the Vijaya incense.
O King, one should offer as an oblation balls of molasses and incense made of guggulu;
having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter feed young maidens.
The water used for washing the cow's tail is intended for both bathing and drinking;
he resembles a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and is like the Pole Star in his brilliance.
O best of kings, he who observes the vow of eating only at night during the month of Jyeṣṭha is honored in the world of the gods, having ascended a most excellent celestial chariot.
Eating rice mixed with water along with milk,
and being intent on fasting, one should worship Umā with devotion on the ninth day.
The Brahmin woman, known by the name Śvetarūpā,
with eyes like lotus petals, worshipped him with devotion using various kinds of lotuses.
One should worship with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and incense along with agallochum,
as well as with various foods beginning with the *aśokavarti* offering.
Or one may worship a maiden or likewise Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity;
purified by consuming cow’s milk, one should then eat while remaining silent.
Having fed the women according to his ability, and especially the maidens,
he became like the sun in splendor and born of fire in brilliance.
O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āṣāḍha is honored in the world of Brahmā, having ascended a most excellent celestial chariot.
O lord of men, while partaking of sweets, snacks, and milk-rice,
one should be devoted to fasting with devotion on the ninth day of both fortnights.
One should worship Durgā with faith by the name Aindrī,
who is seated upon Airāvata, radiant white, and in the form of a white bird.
Having devoutly fashioned [an image] out of gold, adorned with various ornaments,
and likewise [honored it] with various kinds of special flowers and diverse types of edible offerings.
Having thus worshipped Indrāṇī with the fragrances of yakṣakardama, incenses, agaru, and sandalwood, one should then feed a young girl.
Then, having fed the Brahmins and women according to his ability, he should eat while restraining his speech;
having performed his bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should consume the five products of the cow as food.
O lord of men, meditating thus upon the consort of Indra, one should sleep on the ground;
whoever, endowed with faith, should worship Durgā in this manner according to their ability.
O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Śrāvaṇa shall become an attendant of Indra, mounted upon Airāvata.
O Hero, devoted to the welfare of all beings, you should be intent on fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights, subsisting only on rice cooked with milk.
O King, one should worship Caṇḍikā according to the rules with devotion and faith;
one should always worship her by the name "Kaumārī."
Having devoutly fashioned an image of silver that is both formidable and destructive of sins,
one should worship it with karavīra flowers, perfumes, agaru, and sandalwood.
One should worship with the *mahāṅga* incense and also with sweetmeats (*modaka*).
"The *mahāṅga* incense" is that which has been described in the section on incense.
One should worship the young maiden with devotion, as well as women and Brahmins with devotion.
Restraining his speech, he should afterwards eat food prepared with bilva leaves;
thus, endowed with supreme faith, he should worship the Goddess.
That man who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Bhādrapada goes to the supreme abode where the Lord resides.
O Hero, eating milk-rice and black potherbs with faith,
one should always be intent on fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights.
O mighty-armed one, one should indeed worship the Vaiṣṇavī goddess with devotion— she who bears the conch, the discus, and the sword— with jasmine flowers and scents mixed with sandalwood.
One should fumigate with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and *sihlaka*.
One should offer as an oblation (*naivedya*) food filled with ghee according to one's capacity.
She is gratified by meat; therefore, young girls should be honored. Having consumed cow dung according to the rule, he should then eat while maintaining silence.
O lord of men, having gratified the twice-born and women according to his ability,
that man who thus constantly worships the Vaiṣṇavī with devotion—
O King, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āśvayuja is honored in the world of Viṣṇu, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Having become intent on fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights, one who has conquered the self and restrained the senses should eat only jaggery and rice.
O hero, having fashioned an auspicious image of Māheśvarī out of gold, one should then worship it and a bull with white flowers and unguents.
By the ritual slaughter of goats, buffaloes, and likewise rams,
one should gratify the Goddess according to the rules with offerings of flesh and blood.
O King, one should devoutly feed young maidens, Brahmins, and likewise women,
with various kinds of foods to be chewed and swallowed, as well as meats, according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped Durgā with bilva leaves and droṇaka flowers,
one should eat while restraining one's speech, purified by having subsisted on bilva leaves.
Having thus worshipped the consort of Maheśvara with devotion, O King,
one shall attain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and go to heaven.
Equal in splendor to the radiance of a twice-born’s body and in beauty to the flower-armed god of love,
he ascends the Puṣpaka vehicle and rejoices for eternal years.
O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika,
consuming milk-rice, speaking the truth, and having his senses subdued;
One should worship with faith the goddess Vārāhī, the bearer of the discus,
adorning her with garlands of lotuses and anointing her with saffron.
