One should offer black agallochum and storax as incense to the deity;
on the ninth day of both fortnights, one should offer sweetmeat balls with sugar as the food offering.
Having thus worshipped Vārāhī, one should then feed a young maiden and Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability; thereafter, one should eat while maintaining silence.
O Hero, having caused [the recipient] to eat sesame seeds, and having given and offered oblations according to one's ability,
and thus having worshipped Vārāhī, one shall attain heaven.
O King, having sported together with Viṣṇu and with the sporting gods and asuras,
the king shall return to earth and become a sovereign ruler of the whole world.
O King, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, constantly consuming *śaṣkulī* cakes, being self-controlled and having his senses subdued;
One should worship Cāmuṇḍā, the slayer of Muṇḍa, according to the rules and with devotion,
using blue lotuses, as well as lotuses and clusters of bilva leaves.
O King, with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and likewise with guggulu resin;
with many kinds of foods to chew and foods to eat, and repeatedly with various wines and meats.
Likewise, O hero, with blood, with various heads,
and from the piercing of the bodies of goats, buffaloes, and his own self;
On the ninth day of both fortnights, according to the rules and with devotion,
one should also feed young maidens, Brahmins, and women.
Having bathed with the five products of the cow and having consumed blood according to the prescribed rule,
one should then eat, O Indra among kings, using the earth as a vessel.
The man who thus constantly worships Cāmuṇḍā with devotion goes to the supreme abode, where that supreme power (kalā) resides.
Mounted upon a golden vehicle adorned with auspicious rows of banners,
he rejoices together with the deities for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Returning once more, O Great King, he becomes a king upon the earth,
resplendent with radiance and possessing a splendor like fire.
O hero, you are like the moon in splendor and like Bṛhaspati and Śukra in intelligence.
Thus ends the Upabhanavamī-vrata.
[283] [Now begins the Nāmanavamī-vrata.]
O hero, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, having especially observed the *nakta* fast, one should worship the goddess Durgā.
With bilva leaves, garlands, and droṇa flowers in every way,
with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, and with various kinds of foods and delicacies.
Practicing devotion to the Goddess, one should likewise perform her propitiation with excellent food, jewels, and sacrificed buffaloes and goats.
On the ninth day, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, as well as maidens,
other Brāhmaṇa women, and others, according to one's wealth and capacity.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should eat at night while remaining silent;
he who thus worships Durgā here, endowed with devotion, [attains the fruit].
Having observed a fast on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O King, he shall attain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and go to heaven.
O lord of men, the wise man who worships the Goddess with devotion on the ninth day with jasmine flowers, [should do so] under the name "Bhagavatī" itself.
Having fed the young girls, women, and Brahmins according to one's ability with camphor, agallochum incense, honey, and milk-rice;
Having cast cow-dung according to the rule, one should then eat while restraining one's speech;
and in this manner, a man should likewise worship you with devotion.
Having obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, that man goes to heaven;
O mighty-armed one, it is the same on a Puṣya day or on the ninth lunar day for one who has conquered his senses.
A person should worship the auspicious Tryambikā with these names,
using karavīra flowers and the filaments of saffron.
Having offered silhaka incense and an offering of meat cakes,
one should feed Brahmin maidens, women, and Brahmins according to one's ability.
Having consumed cow urine according to the prescribed rule, he should then eat while remaining silent;
whoever worships in this manner here shall obtain the merit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, O King, a wise man should worship Ambikā,
known by the name Sarvamaṅgalā, with jasmine and water-lily flowers.
O Bhārata, one should also offer incense known as *prabodha* or *guggulu*, as well as food offerings (*naivedya*), cakes, fish, and meat.
Having thus worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā according to the rules,
a man should also feed a young girl, as well as women and Brahmins, according to his ability.
O observer of noble vows, having duly sipped water for rinsing the horns,
one should eat while remaining silent and meditating upon Caṇḍikā.
Whoever worships Sarvamaṅgalā with such devotion according to the prescribed rite,
having obtained the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices, is glorified in Goloka.
O Indra among kings, one should always worship the Goddess with the name Caṇḍikā in the month of Phālguna;
one should honor the Blessed Lady with lotus flowers.
O Hero, one should worship with aloe-wood incense and also with *sihlaka*;
having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) of sweetmeats (*modaka*), as well as honey, meat, and milk.
Having fed those previously mentioned according to one's ability and according to the prescribed rule,
he who thus worships Caṇḍikā, the slayer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, in accordance with the ritual injunctions—
The fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice shall be a hundredfold;
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, the Blessed Āryā is remembered [as being present].
One should worship according to the prescribed rite with devotion using flowers of the *mudgaraka* plant;
one should also worship with incense, a profusion of blossoms, and *kāsāra*.
O King of kings, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Goddess by her name;
one should consume flower-water and thereafter eat while maintaining silence.
One should devoutly feed a maiden, as well as women and Brāhmaṇas;
by thus worshipping Ambikā here, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the beloved goddess Ambikā Umā;
having consumed water with kuśa grass and flowers, one should then eat while remaining restrained in speech.
O King, one should worship maidens, women, and Brahmins according to the prescribed rites,
with devotion, using *yūthikā* flowers, incense, and offerings.

With *balam* and the essence of perfumes and flavors, one should offer a sacrificial oblation for the glory of the essence of rice-milk porridge. Having thus worshipped the goddess Śrī, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Umā;
she is indeed celebrated by the name Karṇakoṭī and is also known as Lambakarṇā.
O King, one should worship according to the rite with *śamī* leaves and *kadamba* flowers,
and with incense mixed with camphor and *agaru* for those who bear skulls.
Having worshipped the Blessed Lady, one should then feed a young maiden,
as well as women and Brahmins according to one's ability, O lord of men.
Then, having consumed a leaf of the *śamī* tree, one should eat while maintaining silence;
by thus worshipping Mahākālī, one shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O Indra among kings, on the ninth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
a wise man should constantly worship Caṇḍamardinī by the name Nārāyaṇī.
O King, with red sesame seeds, bakula flowers, and kadamba flowers,
one should offer incense of guggulu mixed with ghee, as well as an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should then feed the young maidens,
as well as women and Brahmins, according to one's capacity and according to the prescribed rites, O King.
Having fed [the brahmins] and consumed clarified butter on the ninth day according to the rules, O King,
he who thus worships the Goddess shall go to the supreme state.
O King, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should always worship Candrikā according to the prescribed rites by the name Mahānandā.
O Bhārata, with white, red, and yellow flowers, as well as all kinds of blossoms,
and especially with guggulu incense mixed with camphor and agarwood.
Having thus worshipped Mahānandā according to the rules, O lord of men, with various kinds of foods to be chewed and swallowed, such as sweetmeats (modaka) and cakes (lopikā), and so forth;
A *lopikā* is a ball made of wheat flour.
One should worship the Virgin Goddess with devotion, as well as women and Brahmins;
having fed them, one should then consume a *bilva* fruit for the purification of the body.
Having made the ground his vessel, he should then eat while remaining silent;
having thus performed the worship, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the worship of Durgā,
offering them milk-rice mixed with honey and saturated with clarified butter.
Having fed a maiden, one should then give her a cow with six limbs;
"with six limbs" refers to a cow. That man who should practice this continuously for one year—
Listen with devotion to the meritorious fruit of his ninth name, which is called Nāmākhyā;
it grants liberation from all sins and bestows the fruit of all sovereign powers.
He shall dwell eternally in the city of Durgā and shall never return here again—
thus does one who performs this meritorious Navamī known by its name.
For having obtained his desires, he is indeed glorified in the world of Brahmā;
the sonless obtains sons, and the poor obtains wealth.
One who desires a daughter obtains a daughter; one who desires fame obtains fame.
Thus ends the Navamī-vow of the Name.
[Now begins the Rūpa-navamī-vow.]
Sumantu said: O lord of men, having fashioned a trident out of flour in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should prepare a silver vessel with a pericarp made of gold.
O Hero, having offered it with faith, let it be fully worshipped by the Blessed Lady;
whatever sin may have been committed even through desire, such as the killing of an embryo, shall be purified.
The Goddess certainly destroys all that by means of the gift of a trident;
[the donor], mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, is honored by gods and gandharvas.
O King, he who gives [this gift] while saying, "May Caṇḍikā be pleased with me," is honored in the heavenly world for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
[289] Forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of Durgā, fire-sacrifice, contentment, and the avoidance of theft.
This rule is established as common to all vows;
however, you shall also explain the specific vow for each month.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should offer the prepared paste of a swan to Brahmāṇī.
For more than a full hundred million years, he is honored in the world of Durgā.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should offer an elephant with four tusks, adorned with perfumes and garlands.
Having devoutly fashioned [an image] made of gold and placed it in a golden vessel,
one should offer it to Indrāṇī according to the prescribed rite, adorned with various gems.
The man who thus worships Indrāṇī with devotion and faith is honored in the world of Soma, mounted upon Airāvata.
Having fashioned an excellent golden ram during the month of Māgha, he is honored by gods and gandharvas for more than a full hundred million years.
Having placed [the offering] in a vessel made of gold, one should present it to Svāhā,
provided with various fragrances and adorned with various flowers.
Having offered [this] with devotion, a person is indeed glorified in the world of Agni,
having ascended a divine, auspicious celestial chariot adorned with garlands of banners.
Having returned to the earth, O King, he shall become a sovereign ruler of a mandala;
having fashioned an image of a peacock out of flour in the month of Phālguna, O King.
Having adorned her with perfumes and garlands, one should present her to the maiden;
having thus presented her according to the rite with devotion, one shall be seated upon a supreme celestial chariot.
[290] O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, he sports with the gods, the Gandharvas, and the high-souled Guha; he has fashioned a Garuda made of flour.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, O hero, one should present [the offering] to the Vaiṣṇava [deities],
adorned with various garlands, perfumes, and floral wreaths.
O mighty-armed one, having offered that [gift], one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu,
ascending a variegated vehicle adorned with clusters of various jewels.
O hero, having fashioned a necklace made of jewels, honored by the worlds, you shone as if blazing with splendor for more than a full hundred million years.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with offerings of perfumes and garlands,
and having presented these to Vārāhī here, one is glorified in the world of Indra.
O King of kings, having worshipped the deity and prostrated before him in the month of Vaiśākha, one shines with a splendor like fire for more than a hundred million years.
Having worshipped with devotion an image made entirely of copper, adorned with gold and jewels,
and with various kinds of saffron and guggulu incense;
Having offered it here to Cāmuṇḍā, one obtains the fruit of one's desires and goes to the supreme world where that Caṇḍikā resides.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with that of the Sun,
he inevitably returns to this world in due course and is born as a lord of men.
Having fashioned a tortoise out of flour, adorned with jewels, O hero— one who has many sons, great wealth, and who strikes fear into all enemies— [he becomes] a terror to all foes.
Having adorned her with garlands of flowers and sandalwood paste,
and having offered [the gift] with devotion to Vāruṇī, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Seated upon a magnificent celestial chariot resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon,
that lord of men sports for more than a hundred million years.
Having returned to earth, the king shall become a sovereign of a realm;
having fashioned a deer out of flour, adorned with jewels, in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Having worshipped it according to the rules with flowers, incense, and ointments, one should present a cow with golden horns and silver hooves to the Vāyavyas.
Having offered this, O mighty-armed one, he is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
likewise, O King, by making a very beautiful chariot out of flour.
O Lord of the Earth, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, it was endowed with many forms,
filled with divine garlands of flowers, and likewise adorned with rows of banners.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
and having presented these here to Kauberī, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
And having fashioned an image entirely made of gold, O Lord, in the month of Bhādrapada, one goes to the supreme abode worshipped by Goddess Durgā.
One should devotedly offer a buffalo of divine form, adorned with perfumes and garlands, to Bhagavatī, the goddess of the South, according to the prescribed ritual.
One should thus offer this with devotion; one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
And in the month of Āśvayuja, O hero, [one should offer] an auspicious bull made of clay.
Having prepared it, one should offer it with devotion to Māheśvarī according to the prescribed rite,
after having worshipped her according to the rite with garlands of bilva leaves.
Having prepared many kinds of foods and edibles made from *āśvinī* and wheat,
and having fashioned an auspicious image composed of flowers, adorned with various garments;
Mounted upon a variegated vehicle, he is honored in the world of Rudra;
for more than a hundred crores of kalpas, he dwells in heaven and sports there.
Accompanied by throngs of apsarases and sporting with the hosts of gods,
he comes at will to this world and becomes a king upon the earth.
O Hero, it is joined with the seven grains and all seeds, juices, and so forth; it is a powerful application, adorned with canopies and umbrellas.
And likewise, O King, having devoutly fashioned a silver mandala of the moon according to the prescribed rites, he honored it with many perfumes and garlands.
One should offer [an image] enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls to Rohiṇī;
listen to the fruit of the merit of him who performs this with devotion.
Whatever merit was described by the sages of old in the Vedas and Agamas, one shall obtain that merit multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt.
He goes to the supreme abode where that Caṇḍikā resides,
being praised by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and the leaders of the gaṇas.
For more than a hundred billion eons, he sports together with the deities;
having enjoyed desired pleasures in the worlds beginning with the realm of Indra.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of his merit, the lord of the earth once again became handsome and fortunate, by virtue of the constant granting of boons by Caṇḍikā.
And whatever desire men, women, or eunuchs have in mind when they worship the Goddess, they obtain all of that.
O Indra among kings, frequent houses made of clay, wood, stone, or likewise constructed with bricks, according to the extent of your wealth.
By giving a house equipped with all utensils and filled with all kinds of grain to the Blessed Lady, one shall attain all desires.
O King, he who thus performs this alone at night with devotion,
and observes the fast on the ninth day according to the prescribed rule, [attains the fruit].
O lord of men, by beholding the forms previously described,
one obtains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices.
Having obtained the fruit, O mighty-armed one, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā for thousands of millions of kalpas, being honored by gods and asuras.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of his merit,
that lord of the earth becomes once again an invincible king, a sovereign of the seven continents.
Thus ends the Rūpanavamī vow. [Now, the Rathanaṣamī vow:
Sumantu said:
O lord of men, having observed a fast on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship the goddess Durgā.
Having honored [the deity] with offerings of flowers, incense, and oblations, and having gratified the Brahmins,
he prepared the chariot adorned with various articles.
It was adorned with garlands of banners, umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors;
it was joined with lions and made beautiful by various flower garlands.
Having fashioned an image of Durgā made of gold, adorned with a seat upon the buffalo,
and having placed it in the middle of the chariot, one should worship her who possesses all the auspicious marks.
O King, having paraded that chariot along the royal highway on the ninth day amidst the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, one should lead it to the temple of Durgā.
[295] There, preceded by a vigil, the place was adorned with lamps and the like,
with various spectacles, O Hero, and with dancing children.
There, while worshipping Caṇḍikā, one should cause a vigil to be kept;
and at dawn, having performed the ceremonial bath for her and for her devotees in a splendid manner.
One should offer a chariot endowed with splendor to the Blessed Lady;
then, having eaten together with one's kinsmen and having prostrated before the Noble One, one should return home.
The vow known as the Navamī-ratha-vrata is the most excellent of all vows, the destroyer of all sins, and the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords—
all that in its entirety one shall obtain by observing the Navamī vow.
For more than a hundred crores of kalpas he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu;
returning again to earth, he shall become a sovereign king.
O lord of men, whoever, according to their ability, offers to the Blessed Lady a beautiful vessel made of ivory or wood, equipped with various utensils;
O King, having duly worshipped Caṇḍikā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
[one should give] as many pieces of fine silk and cotton cloth as there may be.
He who offers a bull marked with a trident to the Goddess shall be honored in the world of Durgā for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on its body.
Taking seven generations of his kin up to the seventh, he should go to the temple;
and he who [offers] a most beautiful cow with both faces to the Blessed Lady.
One shall obtain that same fruit as by giving the earth with its seven islands,
for as long as two feet or even half a head of the calf has emerged.
"In that case, the cow should be known as the earth; its donor would be a giver of the earth.
Thus ends the Rathana-vamī-vrata. [Now begins the Vara-navamī-vrata.]
O King, on the ninth day, one should subsist on flour for nine years;
then the auspicious Goddess, the bestower of all desires, will be pleased with him.
One who observes the vow for as long as one lives, refraining from eating food cooked by fire, shall be a granter of boons both in this world and the next; therein the fruit shall be unimpaired.
Thus ends the Vārānavamī-vrata [the Mahānavamī-vrata]:
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one who has conquered the senses and observes a fast, [should perform the rite].
O Hero, [it should be performed] in the month of Āśvayuja, in Kārttika, or in the month following Kārttika.
And during the Puṣya asterism, one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite with jasmine flowers;
one should offer guggulu as incense and sweet cakes made with jaggery as the food offering.
O King, one should recite the name of Durgā eight hundred times before [her image] during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, and the month following Caitra.
Likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, being devoted to fasting,
one should worship with jasmine, oleander, and bilva leaves.
One should offer incense made of agaru, karpūra, silhaka, and vṛṣaṇa,
as well as an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) and meat, to Maṅgalā.
O Bhārata, the name "Sarvamaṅgalanāmā" should be recited during the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and the month following Śrāvaṇa.
One should worship Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, with devotion,
using bilva leaves with their buds as well as śatapatrikā flowers.
With the incense of awakening alone, one should place sweetmeats as the food offering;
that man who thus worships Ambikā one by one, [attains his goal].
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, fasting and with senses subdued,
one obtains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations.
O Indra among kings, he attains the fruit [of his merit] and goes to the heavenly world,
having ascended a divine golden celestial chariot adorned with tinkling bells.
[298] Having thus sported, O Great King, one becomes a king upon the earth;
Durgā is worshipped on the first fast-breaking day, and Sarvamaṅgalā on the second.
O King, the third [form] is declared by the wise to be the Goddess Caṇḍikā;
first, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed for both bathing and consumption.

O mighty-armed King, [one should worship] with bilva leaves for the second month, and with honey and ghee for the third; thus month after month, O ruler of men, one should honor young maidens and Brahmins.
O King, one should feed [the guests] according to one's own capacity with various kinds of foods and edibles;
O ruler, at the conclusion of the fast, a great feast should be performed according to the prescribed rites.
Then, O Hero, one should worship Caṇḍikā with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
along with various spectacles and abundant sounds of Vedic chanting.
O lord of men, when the vow has been observed in solitude, one should especially honor it with stories recounting meritorious deeds and by making offerings to the reciter.
On the Mahānavamī day, O King, according to the prescribed rite, one should offer various kinds of foods and edibles,
having observed either a fast for nine nights or for three nights.
O Hero, by means of the previously described ritual, through the immolation of buffaloes and goats,
by feeding virgins, and by the satiation of Brahmins;
Whoever should thus worship each individual [deity] with this vow, by means of gifts of cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep, as well as garlands of bilva leaves and so forth;
O lord of men, through devotion to Durgā on the occasion known as Mahānavamī,
he goes to the supreme abode, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
[299] Wherein the Blessed Goddess stands before one while being worshipped;
thus ends the Mahānavamī vow. [Now begins the Ānandā-navamī vow.]
Sumantu said: O lord of the earth, Ānandā, Nandinī, Nandā, Mahānandā, and likewise another, the meritorious Navamī, are remembered as the great Pañcamī.
O Lord of the Earth, that ninth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna is known as Ānandā; it is considered highly meritorious and the remover of all sins.
Having taken a single meal on the fifth day, O King, and likewise a night-meal on the sixth,
one should take food not asked for on the seventh, and observe a fast on the following day.
O King, he who thus worships with devotion on the ninth day according to the rules,
fasting and honoring the Goddess, goes to the supreme state.
O Hero, one should adorn the Goddess with śrīkhaṇḍa, sandalwood, camphor, and likewise agallochum; and one should likewise offer incense made of agallochum.
One should worship with garlands of mallets as well as other flowers;
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation, along with *rasālā* and *modaka*.
O King, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are indeed recommended for bathing and consumption;
one should recite the name of the Goddess Aruṇābhā, the dispeller of fear.
Thus has been declared this first breaking of the fast, which destroys sin;
now hear about the second breaking of the fast, beginning after four months.
“Ādīyam” means the first. O mighty-armed one, one should feed Brāhmaṇa women and Brāhmaṇa maidens month after month on the ninth day, according to one’s capacity and according to the prescribed rule.
O Lord, one should worship the Blessed Lady in the month of Āṣāḍha, likewise in the month of Śrāvaṇa, in Bhādrapada, and similarly in the month of Āśvayuja.
Having taken a single meal on the fifth day, O King, and likewise a meal at night on the sixth,
one should take food not asked for on the seventh, and observe a fast on the following day.
Having fasted on the ninth day, one should worship Śivā according to the prescribed rite;
having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should likewise smear the Goddess with garlands of *jātī* flowers, with red sandalwood,
and with perfumes prepared from musk.
Buffalo ghee and guggulu incense are most highly honored;
as for the food offering, there should be jaggery cakes and sugar-coated sweets according to one's capacity.
Water from bilva leaves is prescribed for both bathing and consumption;
the name known as Durgā should be recited, which removes all fear of sin.
Having thus worshipped the Noble One and likewise having worshipped the Guru,
one should feed the maiden according to one's ability, as well as the Brahmins and women.
Thus, whoever worships with devotion according to their own means shall indeed ascend a lion-vehicle and proceed to the world of Brahmā.
[301] I shall describe the third fast, which removes all sins and is auspicious;
it is highly meritorious from the month of Kārttika onwards and increases the pleasure of Durgā.
One should worship the Goddess, who brings satisfaction to the world, with garlands made especially of various kinds of flowers, both those born on land and those born in water.
One should smear [the image] with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and fragrant substances;
likewise, one should worship Viṣṇu with offerings containing the essence of the moon and with bakula flowers.
Incense made from bilva and śirīṣa is recommended, as is guggulu mixed with ghee;
likewise, an oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds, and the consumption of sesame seeds is excellent.
One should recite the name of the Goddess, which destroys all sins—
an incomparable mantra called Aparājita that brings constant benefit to those who recite it.
In this manner, O mighty-armed one, he who observes the ninth lunar day with the Kṛcchrapāda penance month after month for the duration of a full year—
For having obtained sons, he is indeed glorified in the world of Brahmā;
thus ends the Ānandānavamī vow.
[Now, the Nandīnavamī Vrata:
Sumantu said: In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, whichever day it may be—
That highly meritorious ninth day is celebrated as Nandini.
But the man who, having fasted for three nights, worships the Goddess here,
attains the horse sacrifice in this world and is glorified in the realm of Viṣṇu.
Regarding the first breaking of the fast, I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍikā:
[one should perform it] with garlands of jasmine flowers and various clusters of blossoms.
One should worship Durgā, the destroyer of all demons, according to the prescribed rites at all times with various kinds of fragrant flowers mixed with camphor and agallochum.
One should smear [the image] according to one's ability and fumigate it with *sihlaka* resin;
likewise, one should offer food to be chewed, swallowed, licked, sucked, and drunk, according to one's means.
O mighty-armed one, one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) to the goddess Durgā;
likewise, having performed the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the recitation (japa) while meditating upon Ambikā.
Then, O hero, one should worship Durgā, the daughter of Śāṇḍilī, according to the prescribed rites;
and one should feed young maidens, Brahmins, and likewise women.
"One should eat while restraining one's speech, having first made the ground into a vessel.
Thus, O Hero, has this first breaking of the fast been described by me to you.
Listen to the second [chapter], O Indra among kings, as I speak it in brief:
in all the months, O King, one should be concentrated on Jyeṣṭhā during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
One should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite with various flowers, incenses,
clusters of *mudgara* flowers, and bunches of *jātī* blossoms.
O hero, one should worship the goddess Durgā with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
as well as with śrīveṣṭa, milk, milk-rice (pāyasa), and lotuses.
One should worship Caṇḍikā with devotion using *kuśa* grass, curd, and boiled rice;
furthermore, the wise man should recite her name, "Nārāyaṇī," at the three times of day.
One should consume consecrated cow dung together with dūrvā grass sprouts;
bathing with āmalaka fruits is recommended as it destroys all sins.
Or one should perform a bath with the five fragrances for the purification of the body;
O King, the observer of the vow who performs this on the ninth day [dedicated to] Nandinī.
The wise man is glorified in the heavenly world by means of the excellent moon-vehicle;
together with hosts of gods, he sports there for eternal years.
Returning once more, O mighty-armed one, he becomes a king upon the earth,
equal to Hari in valor and likewise equal to Hari in sovereign power.
Equal to Hari in splendor and to the ocean in profundity, he had many sons and great wealth; he was renowned and beloved by the king.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, one shall again attain heaven.
Thus ends the Nandinī-navamī-vrata. [Now begins the Nandā-navamī-vrata.]
Sumantu said:
That ninth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada which falls under the Uttarā-phalgunī asterism is known as Nandā; it is highly meritorious and proclaimed to be the destroyer of sins.
O joy of the Kurus, whoever worships Durgā there according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having eaten but a single meal on the seventh day and having fasted on the eighth,
one should worship Śivā according to the prescribed rite with *jātī* flowers, *kunda*, and *yūthī*.
One should visualize the Goddess standing upon dūrvā grass, fashioned according to her name,
[offering] dates, coconuts, flowers, and likewise āmalaka fruits.
O observer of noble vows, one should worship with the seven kinds of grain and oil-cake;
one should fumigate with pure curd, incense, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
Then, O King, one should keep a vigil at night before Nandā,
with various spectacles and abundant recitations of the Vedas.
O Lord, one should recite the mantra known as Nandā one hundred and eight times;
the mantra "known as Nandā" is *oṃ nandāyai namaḥ*.
Then, on the morning of the ninth day, having indeed worshipped Caṇḍikā—
Having gratified his gurus according to his ability, he should then feed a young maiden;
likewise in the month of Āśvayuja, in Kārttika, and in the month following Kārttika.
O Lord, one should worship the blessed goddess Nandā for four months;
O King, it is prescribed that one should bathe with water infused with kuśa grass and consume it as well.
Thus, O Hero, this first auspicious fast-breaking has been described;
now hear from me the second, which destroys sins, occurring in the month of Pauṣa.
One should worship Caṇḍikā here by the name Kanakanandinī,
adorned with various garlands and flowers, and anointed with saffron and aloe-wood.

Having bathed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), fasting and with senses subdued, [he should worship] with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as with agallochum incense.
Having worshipped Mahādevī, he sleeps on the ground at night;
then, on the ninth day, having worshipped Kanakanandinī according to the prescribed rites.
O son of Śāṇḍilī, having performed [the preliminary rites], one should then feed a young maiden;
thereafter, during the months beginning with Vaiśākha, one should worship Acyutā according to the prescribed rule.
O Bhārata, one should also smear [the image] with garlands of *mudgara* and *aśoka* flowers,
and with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
With incense mixed with agarwood, and with milk-rice,
one should recite the auspicious name "Acyuta," which removes all sins.
Having performed a bath with the water of *gorocanā* and the consumption of cow-dung,
and having observed a fast on the seventh lunar day, one should likewise worship the Imperishable One (*Acyuta*).
On the ninth day, one should feed young girls, Brahmins, and women according to one’s capacity;
O Lord, he who thus duly observes the Nandā Navamī.
One obtains the fruit of whatever single thing one has contemplated according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the Nandā-navamī.
Now, as for the Mahānandā-navamī: that ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, which is honored by the world, is called Mahānandā; it bestows all forms of bliss upon human beings.
Bathing, giving gifts, performing fire-offerings, and fasting—
all that is performed by men on this day is declared to be inexhaustible.
O Hero, one should worship the Blessed Nandā with garlands of white flowers,
as well as with blossoms and agallochum incense.

O Hero, having bathed with various kinds of modakas and diverse fruits, as well as with a paste of sesame seeds, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite.
For four months, one should worship the auspicious and divine goddess Nandā;
with devotion, one should feed young maidens, women, and likewise Brahmins.

O Hero, on the day of breaking the fast during the Jyeṣṭha and other months, one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite with clusters of jasmine and kadamba flowers, addressing her by the name Vindhyanivāsinī.

One should cause [the initiate] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); bathing with that very substance bestows merit. Likewise, one should offer milk-rice with honey and ghee, as well as excellent rice mixed with curd.
O observer of excellent vows, one should worship her with a smiling face during the months beginning with Kārttika,
using garlands of *kanda* flowers and *karavīra* blossoms.
One should worship with fragrances made from musk, with incense of agaru,
as well as with ghee-filled sweets, sugar-coated confections, and bilva fruits.
O lord of men, by bathing with the washing of a cow’s horn, one should worship;
O All-pervading Lord, one should worship the goddess Śvetamukhī with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
Whoever, having fasted, should thus worship Caṇḍikā for a year,
shall either attain all his desires or be glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having played together with the Brahmins, he becomes a king upon the earth;
endowed with an abundance of wealth and grain, he shall possess sons and renown.
Thus ends the Mahānandā-navamī. [Now, the Mahānavamī-vrata:
Sumantu said:
O lord of men, O hero, that ninth day of the bright fortnight in either the month of Māgha or Āśvayuja is Mahānavamī, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
O Hero, O Lord, whatever acts such as bathing and so forth are performed by men on that [day], all of that becomes inexhaustible; indeed, it likewise brings about spiritual success.
On the twelfth day, one should take a single meal; on the following day, one should observe the *nakta* fast.
On the fourteenth day, one should eat only what is unasked for; on the following day, there should be a complete fast.
In this manner, O Lord, the wise one should perform the arduous penance until the ninth day,
or else remain devoted to fasting for nine nights.
O lord of men, one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rites with bilva leaves;
likewise, O hero, one should worship her with droṇa flowers and jāti flowers.
Having devoutly constructed a temple for Durgā, adorned with various colors and the like,
filled with diverse jewels, and beautified by garlands of flowers.
Having thus constructed the divine abode of the Goddess in that very instant, it was filled with various bells and adorned with garlands of banners.
And likewise, O Hero, fashion a brand-new trident-shaped form indeed,
adorned with various kinds of foods and drinks, as well as sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
Having thus worshipped Durgā with dates, coconuts, and various other fruits, a person should then worship her together with the bull.
With *pūrikās*, *lipikās*, *khaṇḍaveṣṭas*, and *modakas*,
the wise should thus worship Durgā for four months.
Indeed, one should likewise perform the animal sacrifice with abundant liquor and meat,
and worship with the heads of buffaloes, goats, and rams.
Thus, O hero, this procedure for the first breaking of the fast has been told;
now I shall tell you, in brief, that of the second breaking of the fast as well.
And during the months beginning with Māgha, O King, one should worship Śivā according to the prescribed rites with various fragrant flowers and sweetmeats.
One should fumigate with jujube flowers and incense made of guggulu resin;
thereafter, one should feed the young girl many kinds of edible foods and delicacies.
And during the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhyas according to the rules, with devotion and faith, using various clusters of flowers.
One should likewise anoint [the image] with fragrant pastes and worship it with incense made of agallochum;
as well as sandalwood, saffron, costus, tagara, and silhaka.
O mighty-armed one, whoever worships Caṇḍikā with aṇḍaja, vṛṣaṇa, camphor, agallochum, mustaka, and black agallochum shall attain prosperity.
One should likewise worship with jaggery-rice, milk, and milk-rice;
one should devoutly feed a young maiden with milk-rice and clarified butter.
O descendant of Kuru, he who thus worships Durgā for a year shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus concludes the Mahānavamī vow.
Now follow the vows of the tenth day (Daśamī).
[The Universal Vow] In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states: Agastya said:
I shall now briefly describe another vow, that of the universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*),
by the proper performance of which a king may swiftly become a sovereign of the whole earth.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one who regularly eats only at night should always offer a pure oblation in the various directions.
“A pure offering” (*śuddhabali*) is an oblation for worship consisting of purifying substances.
One should likewise honor the twice-born with various flowers and edible foods, [praying]:
“May all you ladies be successful for me in birth after birth.”
Having spoken thus and offered the bali-oblation with a pure mind toward them,
one should then eat well-prepared curd-rice at midnight.
O King, for that monarch who performs this rite daily for a year— whether in the first half, the second half, or as he desires—
there shall be victory over all directions.
Thus ends the vow of the universal monarch.
Now follow the vows for a single meal.
In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states: Agastya said:
"On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should diligently observe the night-meal (nakta) according to the prescribed rule."
A wise person, however, should begin for a year from the start of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa.
That vow, desired for the sake of wealth, when performed, bestows riches.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"O best of sages, fasting on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is prescribed."
By worshipping Narasiṃha, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the vow of Ekādaśī. Now follow the vows of Dvādaśī; regarding these, Viṣṇu says: [49.1–8]

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva on the twelfth day with fine flowers, incense, ointments, lamps, food offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins. By performing this vow for a year, one becomes purified of sins. By performing it for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa. By performing it thus on the twelfth days of both fortnights for a year, one attains the heavenly world; by performing it for as long as one lives, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. The same applies to the fifteenth days. Likewise, by fasting on the new moon and the full moon, one attains the state of Brahman.
By attending upon Keśava as the embodiment of yoga, one shall attain greatness.
Thus ends the Dvādaśī-vrata.
[311] [Now begins the Matsya-dvādaśī-vrata.]
In the Varāha Purāṇa,
Satyatapas said:
"O Great Sage, who was it that performed this fast upon the earth?"
And what are those vows? You should tell this to me.
Durvāsas said: On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one who has restrained his self,
having bathed and performed the worship of the gods and the fire-ritual according to the rules, [should proceed].
Clad in clean garments and with a serene mind, having eaten well-prepared sacrificial food and other offerings,
one should walk five steps and then perform purification once more of the feet.
Having prepared a tooth-stick made from a milk-tree measuring eight finger-breadths,
one should then diligently rinse the mouth with water.
Having touched the sense-orifices with water and meditated for a long time upon Janārdana,
who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and wears yellow garments and a crown;
Having meditated upon the Lord with a serene countenance, endowed with all the primary marks,
who is Janārdana in the form of the Sun, one should take up water.
Having seen [the vessel], the person should then cause the *arghya* to be offered with water from his hands;
at that time, O great sage, he should utter these words.
Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat for two days on the following day; O Lotus-eyed One, O Acyuta, be my refuge.
Having spoken thus, he should then sleep there according to the prescribed rule at night in the presence of the God of gods, while muttering the mantra "Nārāyaṇāya."
Then, at the clear dawn, having gone to a river flowing to the ocean or another river,
or to a lake, he, with self-restraint, should take [water].
Having brought pure clay with this mantra, a person [should apply it], [reciting]:
"O Goddess, you are always the support and the nourishment of all beings."
By that truth, O Goddess Earth, deliver me from sin;
O Sun, the holy waters within the belly of the universe have been touched by your rays.
Since meritorious deeds arise from it, one should take earth from that place;
for all flavors, O Varuṇa, are eternally and always established in you.
"Having washed this earth, purify me without delay!"—
having thus propitiated the earth, the sun, and the water, one should touch oneself.
Having three times drawn a lotus in the water with the *śeṣamṛd* (remaining clay),
a person should then bathe properly according to the ritual procedure accompanied by mantras.
Having bathed and performed his necessary duties, he should again go to the temple;
there, having propitiated the supreme and auspicious Mahāyoga Nārāyaṇa.
Salutation to Keśava for the feet; to Dāmodara for the waist;
to Nṛsiṃha for the knees; and to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa for the chest.

[He should worship] the throat with "Salutation to the Lord Kaustubha," the chest with "Salutation to the Lord of Śrī," the arms with "Salutation to the Conqueror of the Three Worlds," and the head with "Salutation to the Soul of All."
To the holder of the chariot-wheel, a discus; to Śaṅkara, a lotus—“vārijam” meaning a conch; and to Gambhīra, a mace; to Śāntimūrti, a lotus.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa,
the wise man should again place four water-jars before Him.
Filled with water, adorned with garlands, smeared with white sandalwood paste,
covered with four vessels of sesame seeds, and containing precious gems within.
The four oceans are proclaimed to be the jars;
in their midst, one should place an auspicious seat provided with cloth.
And upon that, having prepared a vessel made of silver, gold, copper, or likewise wood— or, failing these, filled with water— one should then place it.
“From non-availability”: the meaning is that in the absence of gold and other such materials, one may even make [the image] out of wood.
Having fashioned Janārdana, the God, in the form of a fish made of gold, endowed with the limbs of the God of gods and adorned according to the Śruti and Smṛti.
There, having honored [the deity] according to the ritual rules with various kinds of foods, fruits, flowers, perfumes, incense, and mantras, it was made beautiful.
Just as the Vedas situated in the netherworld were recovered by you, O Lord,
in the form of a fish, even so, O Keśava, deliver me from this worldly existence.
Having recited this, one should cause a vigil to be held before it there,
according to the extent of one's wealth, until the clear dawn.
"According to the extent of one's wealth" means in accordance with one's available funds.
One should cause four water-pots to be given to four Brahmins;
one should give the eastern pot to a Bahvṛca (Rigvedin) and likewise the southern one to a Chandoga (Sāmavedin).
One should give the excellent western jar to one associated with the Yajurveda branch;
one may give the northern jar according to one's desire—this indeed is the prescribed rule.
[315] May the Ṛgveda be pleased in the east, the Sāmaveda in the south,
the Yajurveda in the west, and likewise the Atharvaveda in the north.
Having had jars prepared and covered with copper vessels containing sesame seeds,
he then gave that water-vessel to a Brahmin who had a family.
O highly fortunate one, he should give in this manner, and thereafter he should feed the most eminent Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa); after that, the man may eat at his own pleasure.
O Sage, he who performs this Dvādaśī once according to the prescribed rite should eat together with Brahmins, remaining silent and with his senses restrained.
He attains the world of Brahmā and remains there for that duration;
thereafter, at the time of Brahmā’s reabsorption, he who has remained there for a long time [is liberated].
In a future creation, he shall become a god known by the name Vairāja;
even the sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed here in this world [shall be purified].
Whether unintentionally or intentionally, those [merits] perish instantly;
one becomes poor in this world, or else a king who has fallen from his royal status.
Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rule, one becomes a lord of kings;
"lord of Me" (*meśvaraḥ*) means a lord of *lakṣmī*.
O auspicious lady, even a barren woman shall become so by this ritual procedure.
By fasting on that day, one shall have a most righteous son,
even if he has committed incest with a woman who should not be approached, whether knowingly or unknowingly.
By resorting to this procedure, he is liberated from that sin,
even though it was produced by many years of neglecting the performance of sacred rites.
By observing this fast even once with devotion, one attains the refinement of Vedic knowledge.
Moreover, O Great Sage, what is the use of saying more here? There is nothing that cannot be achieved.
Whether it be that which is to be attained or that which one does not perceive as evil,
this ritual procedure must not be given to one who is uninitiated nor to an atheist.
This should never be disclosed even to one who hates the gods or the Vedas;
it must be given to one devoted to the guru, for it destroys all sins.
In this very life, he who observes the fast according to the prescribed rule shall indeed obtain sovereignty, wealth, grain, and excellent women in various forms.
Thus concludes the Matsyadvādaśī vow.
[Now begins the Kūrmadvādaśī vow.
Dūrvāsas said:
On that meritorious twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
one should perform the rites such as bathing and so forth, having first made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as previously described.
Having performed the ritual of dismissal, O best of the twice-born, one should awaken Janārdana, the God of gods, on the night of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) with separate mantras.
First, one should worship the feet of Kūrma with "To Kūrma," and the hips of Hari with "To Nārāyaṇa," and the belly of Hari with "To Saṃkarṣaṇa."
The chest for Viśoka, and the throat for Bhava.
And [he worships] the two arms with "Salutation to Subāhu," the head with "Salutation to Viśāla," and the discus and conch with their own respective names,
using fragrant incense and perfumes.
With various kinds of offerings and diverse fruits.
Having worshipped the deity and placed the water-pot before him, its neck adorned with garlands and a blue lotus,
he should fill it with jewels as was done previously.
One should [fashion] the deity out of gold according to one's own capacity.
Having fashioned the ocean together with Mount Mandara in the form of a tortoise,
one should place it upon a copper vessel filled with clarified butter,
having first set it down atop a water jar.
On the following day, one should give to a Brahmin in this very manner.
On the following day, having fed the Brahmins and gratified them with sacrificial fees according to his ability, he should propitiate the God of gods,
Nārāyaṇa, in the form of the Tortoise. Afterwards—
And he himself should eat together with his circle of servants.
If this is done, the threefold evil is indeed destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
Having cast off the wheel of saṃsāra, one becomes pure.
But he attains the ancient world of Hari.
The sins accumulated over many previous births are destroyed through devotion;
moreover, one obtains the fruit described previously.
Nārāyaṇa, however, immediately attains satisfaction.
Thus ends the Kūrmadvādaśī vow. [Now begins the Varāhadvādaśī vow.
Durvāsas said:
O most righteous one, listen now to another meritorious account of the mountain Varāha on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
He who, whether knowing or unknowing, has committed an act of approaching one who should not be approached,
is liberated from that sin by resorting to this ritual procedure.
By fasting on this day with devotion even once, one may obtain the purification of the Veda, despite the omission of Vedic rites committed over many years.
Moreover, O most supreme upholder of dharma, what is the use of much speaking here?
One should simply perform the ritual bath according to the procedure previously described.
Having prepared [the offerings] and worshipped the Lord on the eleventh day, the wise man,
having honored Acyuta with flowers, food offerings, and perfumes, [should proceed].
Afterwards, one should place a jar filled with water in front of him;
[one should touch] the feet with "To Varāha" and the waist with "To Mādhava."
One should worship the belly with "to the Knower of the Field," the chest of Hari with "to the Universal Form," the throat with "to the All-Knowing One," and the head with "to the Lord of Creatures."
One should worship the two arms with "To Pradyumna," the Sudarśana discus with "To the Divine Weapon," and the conch with "To Him Born from Nectar"; this indeed is the procedure for the worship.
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place into that jar a vessel made of gold,
silver, or copper, according to his means and capacity.
Having established it filled with all types of seeds, the wise and discerning man should have a golden boar fashioned there according to his means.
Lifting the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and trees, with the tip of his tusk—
Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who had assumed the form of a boar.
Upon a vessel containing all seeds, which rests atop a jar filled with jewels,
one should place the supreme deity Hari, fashioned from gold.
One should place the Vaiṣṇava [liṅga] covered with a pair of white garments in a copper vessel and worship it with perfumes, flowers, various food offerings, and fruits.
Having constructed a pavilion of flowers, one should perform a vigil there;
at that place, the wise man should have the manifestation of Hari recited and should desire [the fruits thereof].
While he was being thus praised, at dawn when the sun had risen,
having bathed and become pure, he worshipped Hari and presented [the offering] to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should especially cause it to be given to one who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, of virtuous conduct, wise, devoted to Viṣṇu, and possessed of knowledge.
Listen now to the fruit that indeed accrues to one who, having given Hari in the form of a boar according to these prescribed rules, bestows him upon a Brāhmaṇa.
In this very life, one shall obtain good fortune, prosperity, luster, and indeed praise;
moreover, the wise man, the wealthy man, and the enjoyer of pleasures—even if childless—shall become possessed of sons.
Thus ends the Varāhadvādaśī vow.
Now follows the Narasiṃhadvādaśī.
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Phālguna, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
having fasted according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should invoke Hari.
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Narasiṃha," the belly with "to Govinda," the waist with "to Viśvabhuj," and likewise the chest with "to Aniruddha."
One should offer the throat to Śitikaṇṭha, the head to Piṅgakeśa,
the discus to Asuradhvaṃsana, and likewise the water-element to Toyātman.
Having thus worshipped the conch with perfumes, flowers, and fruits,
one should place the water-pot before it, covered with a pair of white cloths.
There, above that, one should fashion a golden Nṛsiṃha in a jeweled vessel—
either in gold according to one's means, or even in wood or bamboo.
Having placed it in a jar containing precious gems and having worshipped it there according to the prescribed rite,
one should present it on the twelfth lunar day to a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned.
O Great Sage, I shall now relate to you that fruit which was obtained in former times by the king named Vatsa when he had performed such deeds.
At the conclusion of his vow, the Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha was pleased with him and bestowed upon him a discus that causes the destruction of enemies in battle.
By means of that weapon, O best of kings, he himself conquered the kingdom;
established in his realm, the lord performed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
And at its conclusion, O best of men, one goes to the station known as the world of Brahmā;
this, O sage, is your auspicious Dvādaśī that removes all sins.
"Relate this with diligence; have faith as you desire.
Thus ends the Narasiṃha-dvādaśī. Now begins the Vāmana-dvādaśī vow.
Dūrvāsas said:
"In this very manner, O sage, having made a formal resolve on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the month of Caitra,
one should fast and with devotion worship Janārdana, the God of gods."
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Vāmana" and the hips with "To Viṣṇu";
the abdomen and the chest with "To Vāsudeva" and "To Saṃkarṣaṇa."

Having worshipped the throat with "Salutation to Viśvabhṛt," and the head with "Salutation to Vyomarūpin," and having worshipped the arms with "Salutation to Viśvajit," one should worship the conch and discus with their own names.
By this procedure, one should first place a pitcher with a gem within it, along with its pair, all around the God, the God of gods, the Lord of the universe.

Having first placed a pair of garments— a pair of cloths— and a golden Vāmana image, which has been fashioned according to one’s means, small in stature, and wearing a white sacred thread, upon the water-vessel, the wise man [should proceed].
One should place the water-pot at one's side, as well as the small umbrella and sandals;
and having set down the rosary, one should especially arrange the grass seat.
At dawn, one should cause that [image], equipped with these accessories, to be given to a Brahmin, while uttering:
"May Viṣṇu, in his short form, be pleased."
Combined with the name of the month and including the designation of the manifestation,
the injunction "may [he] be pleased" is proclaimed everywhere as the rule.

“By the common name” means by the names of Keśava and others associated with the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa. “Designating the manifestations” refers to [names such as] “the one in the form of a fish,” “the one in the form of a tortoise,” and so forth.
And it is heard in the Purāṇa: “In ancient times, King Haryaśva, the lord of the earth, being childless, performed austerities, that treasury of asceticism, desiring a son.”
O best of sages, while he was performing that sacrifice for the sake of a son,
the Lord arrived, endowed with the form of a brahmin.
He said to the king, "O King, what have you resolved? And the Brahmin replied to him, "It is for the sake of a son."
"O King, perform this very procedure with diligence.
Having spoken thus to the brahmin, he then vanished in an instant.
The king also fulfilled that purpose by giving the wealth obtained from the mantra to a wise, poor brahmin named Jyotirgarbha.
O Blessed One, just as you yourself became the son of Aditi though she was childless,
by that truth may a most excellent son be born to me as well.

“Vidhānam” means the ritual procedure for the Vāmana-dvādaśī vow. “Mantravit” means one who knows the mantras beginning with “yathāditer aputrāyāḥ. “Tam” refers to Vāmana. By this prescribed rite, O Sage, he became his son, renowned as Ugrāśva, a mighty universal monarch (cakravartin).
One without a son obtains sons; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom, and thereafter he shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Vāmana-dvādaśī vow.
[Now, the Jāmadagnya-dvādaśī vow.
Dūrvāsas said:

In the month of Vaiśākha, a man who has likewise made this resolve according to the prescribed rule should perform the ritual bath with clay in that same manner and then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, having propitiated Hari with devotion by means of these mantras,
the wise one [should worship] the feet for Jamadagnya and the belly for Sarvadhārin.
[326] To Madhusūdana, he offered the waist; to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa, the chest;
to the ender of the kṣatriyas, the arms; and to Maṇikaṇṭha, the throat.
Having thus worshipped the conch and discus with his own name, and the head bearing the cosmic egg,
the wise man should place a water-pot before it as previously described.
One should place it there, especially covered with a pair of cloths;
and upon that, one should install Hari using a vessel made of bamboo.
Having fashioned a golden image of Jamadagnya before him,
one should have that deity made with an axe in his right hand.
Having honored him with all kinds of perfumes as well as various types of flowers,
a devoted person should then perform a vigil before him.
At dawn, when the sun is clear, one should present it to a Brahmin:
"There was a highly fortunate king, Vīrasena, possessed of great strength."
In former times, that highly illustrious man, being childless, performed intense austerities;
while he was performing those formidable penances, the great sage Yājñavalkya [approached].
The great yogi came from afar to see him.
Rajovāca said:
"O twice-born one, how indeed shall I have a son with little effort?"
O Blessed One, please tell this out of affection to me who am bowed before you.
Thus addressed by that illustrious monarch, the Sage declared this twelfth day belonging to the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
For that king, desiring a son especially,
having fasted according to the prescribed rite, obtained as his son Nala, who was supremely righteous.
That he is even now celebrated in the world as the best of kings, Puṇyaśloka—
this indeed, O Great Sage, is the incidental fruit of this vow.
That a son is born endowed with wealth, learning, and supreme beauty—what is there to marvel at in this life? But hear from me concerning the next world.
Having dwelt for one kalpa in the world of Brahmā with hosts of apsarases, they sport there; then, in a subsequent creation, they are born as universal monarchs (cakravartins).
They live for thirty thousand kalpas; there is no doubt about this.
Thus ends the Jāmadagnya-dvādaśī-vrata. [Now begins the Rāghava-dvādaśī-vrata.]
Dūrvāsas said:
In the month of Jyeṣṭha as well, a man who observes the ritual procedure should likewise make his formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and worship the Supreme God with various kinds of auspicious flowers.
One should first worship the feet with "Oṃ, obeisance to Rāghava";
the hips with "to Trivikrama," and the belly with "to the one who sustains the universe."
He should worship the chest with "To Saṃvatsara," the throat with "And to Saṃvartaka," the two arms with "To the bearer of all weapons," and the two lotus-like hands with their own names.
Having worshipped the thousand-headed head of that Great Soul,
and having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should prepare a vessel of ghee.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual the golden images of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, covered as before with a pair of garments, one should indeed give them to a Brāhmaṇa at dawn.
These two should be given with a gracious mind by the Kāma-mantra and the Tatpuruṣa-mantra respectively;
they were formerly seen [and employed] by King Daśaratha when he was childless.
Vasiṣṭha, having come to the city on some occasion, spoke this very procedure to her who desired a son;
so did that twice-born one.
Having previously learned this secret, that king performed this [rite];
his son was born of himself, known as Rāma, the slayer of Madhu.
O great sage, Viṣṇu became fourfold out of complete satisfaction;
this which pertains to this world has been told, so now hear that which pertains to the next world.
Abiding in heaven, they enjoy divine pleasures for as long as ten Indras, numbering two by two;
when that time has passed, they return once more to the mortal world.
The king of kings becomes a performer of sacrifices.
“Ten and twice two” means fourteen.
The sins of that man perish,
and he attains his desires exactly as he wishes.
Having observed this very vow free from desire,
one attains that stable state of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the Rāghava-dvādaśī vow. [Now begins the Kṛṣṇa-dvādaśī vow.
Dūrvāsas said:
In the month of Āṣāḍha as well, having likewise made this resolution according to the rule,
a man should worship the boon-granting God with perfumes and flowers according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the feet with "To Vāsudeva," the waist with "And to Saṃkarṣaṇa," the shoulders for the destruction of sin with "To Aniruddha," and indeed the chest.
[330] One should offer the thighs to Cakrapāṇi, the arms likewise to Bhūpati;
one should offer the conch and discus by their own names, and the head indeed to Puruṣa.
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place a jar covered with cloth before it as previously described; then, he should place [the image] upon it.
Having worshipped that eternal Vāsudeva made of gold, with four limbs, according to the prescribed rite in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
As before, one should give to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and firm in his vows;
hear from me what merit belongs to one who is thus endowed with these observances.
Vāsudeva shall become the king, the increaser of the Yadu lineage;
Devakī was his wife, who observed vows identical to his own.
That virtuous woman, however, remained childless, being solely devoted to the duty toward her husband;
after a long time had passed, Nārada came to her home.
Honored with devotion by Vasudeva,
he who knows the dharma spoke these words to Devakī and Vasudeva.
Those two also performed this rite with devotion, endowed with faith;
Viṣṇu himself, pleased with them, indeed entered into the state of being their son.
Thus, this Dvādaśī is remembered as the remover of sins and the bestower of sons;
by fasting on this day, one shall obtain sons, knowledge, and wealth.
He restored the kingdom to one who had fallen from his throne and brought about the destruction of the sins of the sinful,
just as Keśava, moved by compassion, did for the Earth.
Upon death, he rejoices for an imperishable time in the beautiful city of Viṣṇu for thirty-six Manvantaras; thereafter, at the dissolution of time, he is born again.
In this world, he shall become a king for seventy thousand years;
as a donor accompanied by his sons, upon death, he shall attain nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇadvādaśī vow. [Now begins the Buddhadvādaśī vow.
Dūrvāsas said:
In this very way, having made a formal resolve on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should worship the Supreme God with offerings of perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the feet with "Salutation to the Buddha," the waist with "Salutation to Śrīdhara," the belly with "Salutation to Manobhava," and the chest with "Salutation to Saṃvatsara."
One should worship the waist with "To Sugrīva," and the two arms with "Viśvavāhana"; having worshipped the weapons as previously described, one should worship the head with "To the Supreme Self."
Having thus worshipped, the wise and discerning practitioner should then place a water jar; having fashioned that Buddha image out of gold, he should set it there.
Having thus worshipped that as well, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
previously, the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) was observed with fasting according to this very rule.
Śuddhodana himself became the Buddha, O Janārdana;
and endowed with sons and grandsons, he attained great prosperity.
Having enjoyed royal splendor, he then attained the supreme state.
Thus ends the Buddhadvādaśī vow.
[Now begins the Kalkidvādaśī vow.]
Dūrvāsas said:
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) and worship the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rule.
Homage be to Kalkin for the feet; to Hṛṣīkeśa for the waist;
to the one who destroys the barbarians for the thighs; and likewise to the embodiment of the world for the belly.
One should worship the throat with "To Śrīkaṇṭha," the two arms with "To Khaḍgapāṇi," the conch and discus with his own name, and likewise the head of Viśvamūrti.
Having thus worshipped, the wise man should place a water-pot before it as before;
likewise, he should have an image of the god Kalkin made of gold.
Having covered it with a pair of white garments and adorned it with perfumes and flowers,
one should present it at dawn to a brahmin who is most learned in the scriptures.
Formerly, there was a very powerful king named Viśāla in the city of Kāśī;
he observed the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and indeed became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Having sacrificed with various kinds of sacrifices, one may again attain nirvāṇa;
he is worshipped in the form of a fish by those desiring omniscience.
Hari is worshipped in the form of the Tortoise for the sake of uplifting his own lineage;
he is worshipped as the Boar by one submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
In the form of Narasiṃha, he appeared for those afflicted by the fear of all sins;
as Vāmana, for the purpose of deluding [Bali]; and as the son of Jamadagni, for the sake of wealth.
A wise man should worship the son of Daśaratha for the destruction of cruel enemies;
a learned man desiring sons should worship Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, without a doubt.
"One who desires wealth should sacrifice to Buddha Kalkin at the destruction of enemies.
Thus ends the Kalkidvādaśī vow.
[Now begins the Padmanābhadwādaśī vow.]
Dūrvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Āśvayuja, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should worship the eternal Lord Padmanābha.
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Padmanābha," the waist to "Padmayoni," the abdomen to "Sarvadeva," and the chest to "Puṣkarākṣa."
Likewise, one should worship the two arms for Avyaya as before, and worship the weapons;
having worshipped the head for Prabhava as before, one should place the water-pot in front.
Upon that [altar], one should place the golden image of the god Padmanābha;
having worshipped that very god in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should announce it to a Brāhmaṇa:
"In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a powerful king named Bhadrāśva."
Once, Agastya came to the house of that king, by whose name the region was known as Bhadrāśva.
He said, "I shall dwell in your house for five nights.
The king, bowing his head to him, replied, "Please stay."
He had a most beautiful wife named Kāntimatī;
seeing her thus endowed with beauty and splendor, Agastya [was struck].
And seeing her co-wives performing excellent work equal to hers, she said, "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! Excellent, excellent, [O Lord] regarding women and Śūdras!"
Having spoken thus, Agastya danced loudly in the presence of the king.
The king said:
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of your joy, by which you dance in this manner?"
Agastya said: "A certain queen of yours was indeed a maidservant of Haridatta, a Vaiśya, in the city of Vaidiśa; and you were her very husband."
A Śūdra named Viddha was his artisan;
there, in the month of Āśvayuja, on the twelfth day, he remained self-controlled and pure.
Having gone yourself to the abode of Viṣṇu and worshipped Hari with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
you should return to your own home, [entrusting] the two of you as guardians and protectors.
O Mahāmati, having stationed yourselves at the door for the purpose of lighting the lamps,
when he had departed, you two remained there lighting those lamps.
O best of kings, they spent the night without guile until dawn;
then, after a long time, both husband and wife passed away.
By that merit, you were born in the house of Priyavrata,
and this woman was born as his wife in a former life.
In the past, this supreme reward was obtained by you through your devotion when you lit a lamp belonging to another in the house of Hari.
Furthermore, the merit of one who, having worshipped Viṣṇu with his own wealth, lights a lamp,
cannot be calculated.
Thus ends the Padmanābha-dvādaśī vow.
[336] Now begins the Yogeśvara-dvādaśī vow.
Agastya said: Listen with devotion, O King, to how one may observe the Kārttika Ekādaśī according to the prescribed rule and thereby obtain the fruit of all [Ekādaśīs].
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the previously prescribed rule, one should likewise perform the bath;
then one should worship the stainless Lord Nārāyaṇa in reverse order.
One should worship the head of Hari with "Obeisance to the thousand-headed one," the two arms with "To Puruṣa," and the throat with "To the one of universal form."

One should worship the weapons with the mantra "to the one whose self is knowledge," the Śrīvatsa mark on the chest likewise with "to the one who devours the world," and the belly with "to the one of divine form."
The wise one, having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the forward order, should worship the waist with the thousand-footed [mantra] and the feet of the God.
One should worship all the limbs of Hari with the mantra "Namo Dāmodarāya.
Having thus worshipped according to the ritual procedure, one should place four jars before him.
One should place the Ratnagarbha images, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
their necks bound with garlands of flowers, and draped with white cloths.
O best of the twice-born, these four oceans have been fashioned from copper vessels filled with sesame seeds and gold.
In the center of that, according to the previously described procedure, one should place an image of Hari made of gold—
Yogeśvara, who follows the method of yoga, Ananta, and is clad in yellow garments.
Having honored him in this manner, one should perform a vigil there;
one should practice the Vaiṣṇava yoga and conquer Hari, the Lord of Yoga.
When a sixteen-spoked wheel has been fashioned with many colored powders,
having done this, one should bring five Brahmins at dawn.
Four water-pots should be given for the four [deities], and for the fifth,
one should devoutly and purely present a golden image of Yogeśvara.
What is given equally to a student of the Vedas becomes twofold when given to one who knows them;
however, when given to a teacher of the Pañcarātras, it becomes a thousandfold.
But for one who provides this ritual procedure together with its secret lore and its mantras,
what is given to him with devotion shall indeed become ten millionfold.
If a wise person, while the guru is present, should instead honor another who is nearby,
he falls into a miserable state, and whatever is given to him becomes fruitless.
When the guru is present, [the offering] is first given to him and afterwards to another;
for whether he is unlearned or learned, the guru is the god Janārdana.
Even if he stands on a wrong path, a teacher who stands on the path is indeed the supreme refuge;
yet that teacher who, having set out [on the path], deviates through delusion—
[338] He shall be cooked in hell for ten million eons; there is no doubt about this.
Having given in this manner according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Viṣṇu in accordance with reality.
Having given food to the Brahmins according to his capacity along with ritual fees,
Prajāpati indeed performed this Dharaṇī-vrata in ancient times.
In former times, the royal sage Yuvanāśva likewise obtained offspring and liberation through this very method in a secluded place, remaining devoted to Brahman.
Māndhātṛ obtained a son and the supreme, eternal Brahman;
likewise did Kṛtavīrya, the descendant of Haihaya and lord of men.
She obtained Kārtavīrya as her son and the supreme, eternal Brahman;
and Śakuntalā likewise, O great sage, having observed such a vow.
He obtained Śākuntala as his son, the son of Duṣyanta, a universal monarch (cakravartin); by this method, supreme universal sovereignty was attained.
In ancient times, this vow was also performed by Dharaṇī when she had sunk into the netherworld (pātāla);
therefore, it is called by the name Dharaṇīvratam.
When this earth-goddess had been completed, she was lifted up by Hari in the form of a boar; even today, being pleased, he supports her as a ship is supported upon the waters.
That best of men who hears this with devotion and who performs it shall be liberated from all sins and attain the same world as Viṣṇu.
How much more so these twelve, by whom Indra-hood was granted in the past?
Thus concludes the Yogeśvaradvādaśī vow.
[Now, the Bhartṛdvādaśī vow:
The Apsarases said: "O Blessed One, O son of Brahmā, O twice-born one, we desire husbands."
And tell us how Nārāyaṇa may become our husband.
Nārada said: Now I shall quickly tell you how one may obtain Hari himself as a husband— that bestower of boons— and how he grants the status of being one's spouse.
On that auspicious twelfth day of the bright fortnight in spring,
having fasted according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Hari together with Śrī.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods upon a couch provided with various coverings,
one should fashion an image of the Lord, the husband of Lakṣmī, out of silver and present it there.
Then, above that, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed with flowers;
and there he should cause a vigil to be observed with the sounds of dance and musical instruments.
One should place "to Manobhava" on the head, "to Anaṅga" on the hips,
"to Kāma" at the base of the arms, and having oneself occupied the belly, [one should assign the remaining parts].
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers— specifically with *mallikā* and *jāti* varieties— saying "To Manmatha" for the feet and "To Hari" for all other parts.
Thereafter, O King, having taken four beautiful stalks of sugarcane,
one should place them in the four directions in front of that deity.
Having done this, at dawn he should give it to a wise Brāhmaṇa who is proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) and possesses all his limbs intact.
Then Brahmins are to be fed, and one should complete this vow;
by virtue of this vow, Viṣṇu will certainly become your husband.
Without having offered me my salutation, you asked about the vow out of pride;
by means of that vow, O Lord of the Gods, you have obtained [me] as a beloved through your own conceit.
"At the end, there will be a removal by cowherds;
and he will become the divine husband of the future kalpas."
Thus ends the Bhartṛdvādaśī vow. [Now, the Śubhadvādaśī vow.
Agastya said:
Listen, O highly fortunate King, to this unsurpassed and auspicious vow, by which Viṣṇu is attained through that very auspiciousness; of this there is no doubt.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should first undertake the vow;
eating only one meal during the bright fortnight until the tenth day.
Then, having bathed at midday on the tenth day, one should worship Keśava;
having eaten, one with a pure mind should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as before for the twelfth day.
O King, having worshipped Hari with the mantra "Keśava," one who is self-restrained on the twelfth day should offer sesame seeds along with gold for his pleasure.
Having stayed there for that long, one should give barley to the twice-born;
