and with these [mantras], Hari is to be addressed during the gift-offering, the fire-oblation, and likewise the worship.
O best of kings, having likewise spent the four-month period in this manner,
one should again observe the fast from the month of Caitra onwards, being restrained and pure.
One should cause vessels of roasted flour mixed with gold to be given to the Brahmins;
likewise, one should worship Govinda during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
Having likewise spent those three months until the beginning of Kārttika, and having completed that year as well, being self-controlled and pure;
Having worshipped Hari with devotion according to the name of the month, the wise man,
with his senses restrained, should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with devotion on the twelfth lunar day.
O King, on the eleventh day, one should have a golden image of the earth fashioned according to one's ability,
complete with the seven netherworlds and the principal mountain ranges.
One should place it before Hari according to the procedure for the ritual placement of the elements (bhūvinyāsa),
covered with a pair of white cloths and provided with all the seed-syllables (bīja).
Having worshipped [the image] with the five jewels while reciting "O Priyadatta," the wise man should keep a vigil there; then, at dawn, he should again [feed] the twice-born.
Having addressed them by number, O King, according to their twenty-one names,
one should cause a cow and a bull to be given to each of them individually.
For each [deity], there was also a pair of garments, a single ring,
a golden bracelet, and an ear-ornament.
The king shall grant one village each to these [recipients] as a royal gift;
thereafter, he should cause a cow to be bestowed according to the extent of his available wealth.
Even a poor person, if unable to perform the rite in full, should do so according to his own capacity;
having fashioned the earth out of gold, he should likewise provide a pair of cows according to his means.
Then, having given a pair of garments according to one's financial capacity,
one should perform everything with gold alone in the event that a pair of cows is unavailable.
Having done this, on the following Kṛṣṇadvādaśī as well,
one should fashion an image of the earth out of silver, according to the extent of one's wealth and power.
One should likewise provide food for those Brahmins,
as well as sandals, wooden shoes, and an umbrella according to one's ability.
[343] May Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara, the God of gods, grant me this;
may the Lord Hari, whose form is the universe, be forever pleased with me.
Even in a thousand years, it would not be possible to fully describe the fruit that is obtained when giving and feeding are practiced in this manner.
O Lord of Men, that ruler who performs this meritorious and auspicious vow shall attain all prosperity and thereafter go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the vow of Śubhadvādaśī. [Now begins the vow for attaining Viṣṇu.
Varāha said:
Those men who indeed observe a fast on the twelfth day,
being entirely devoted to me, attain unto me alone.
Having observed the fast and then joining his palms in reverence,
he should gaze at the sun while uttering, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
For as many drops of water as fall from the joined palms,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
In the same way, on that twelfth day, having performed the ritual according to the rules with seasonal flowers, musk-scented substances, and incenses;
One should also hear of the destiny of whoever causes such ground to be prepared;
having placed flowers upon the head, one should recite this mantra:
Having uttered "Oṃ," the mantra is:

"O best of gods, O supporter of the earth, having taken these flowers with a well-disposed mind, may the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu be pleased with me. With this mantra, one should offer the flowers. The mantra for the incense is stated: "Oṃ, salutations to you, Viṣṇu; accept this manifest, fragrant incense for the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu. With this mantra, one should offer the perfumes.
And even without having heard the scriptures, whoever should cause me to be treated in this manner—
He shall go to my world and be born four-armed.
Śyāmāka, ṣaṣṭhika, and other wholesome foods along with their qualities;
likewise, śāli rice, barley-meal, and the pleasant meal of nīvāra grain.
But whoever, devoted to my ritual service, should consume these,
he shall bear the marks of the conch and the discus, and carry the plow, the mace, and the club.
Thus ends the Viṣṇuprāptidvādaśī vow. [Now, the Akhaṇḍavrata] according to the Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said: O Brahman, when, in the month of Āśvayuja, the lotus emerges from the navel of the Lord of the World,
it is exactly as this [lotus] of the God comes to be.
The beautiful kadamba tree stands at the tips of the fingers of Kandarpa;
by means of that kadamba, his supreme delight increases.
O Nārada, even for Maṇibhadra, the lord of the Yakṣas, a banyan tree appeared; indeed, he then took delight in it.
An auspicious *dhuttūra* shrub grew even within the heart of Maheśa;
by that means, it became the source of delight for the mind of Śarva.
In the same way, from the middle of his body was born the lordly emerald,
and from the glorious Viśvakarman, the Lord, came the thorny Khadira tree.
In the palm of Girijā’s hand, the kunda tree appears;
on the hand of the Lord of Gaṇas, the sindhuvāra flower shines.
To the right side of Yama is the Palāśa tree, and to the north-east is the Kṛṣṇa tree; from the Raudra fire was born the inexhaustible Kusūlaka, who causes agitation.
The Bandhujīva tree was born from Skanda, and the Aśvattha from Ravi; the Śamī tree grew from Kātyāyanī, and the Bilva from Lakṣmī, each held in her hand.
O Brahmin, from the serpents was born a great clump of reeds;
on the tail of Vāsuki it was very beautiful, while on his back it was dark green like dūrvā grass.
A green sandalwood tree has grown in the hearts of those to be converted;
thus, through that [tree], there may be delight for them all in that place.
On that auspicious and meritorious occasion which is the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (Śukla-ekādaśī),
one should properly worship Viṣṇu, by which the [sacrificial] portion is fully completed.
“By which the fragment is filled”: the meaning is that by means of which worship of Viṣṇu, the fragment—that which was incomplete with respect to dharma and so forth—becomes completely full.
[One should worship] with flowers, leaves, or even fruits endowed with fragrance and flavor, and with all medicinal herbs, as far as all that exists among stationary beings.
Ghee, sesame seeds, rice, barley, gold such as kanaka and the like,
gems, pearls, corals, and various kinds of garments.
And the flavors— sweet, pungent, sour, astringent, salty, and so forth—
as well as bitter things, should be offered, provided that they are indeed unbroken.
For the sake of that worship, it should be offered to the high-souled Keśava,
by which an unbroken full year is produced in the home.
O divine sage, having observed a fast on the second day,
one should undoubtedly bathe with that same bath by which one has indeed kept the year unbroken.
Anointment with either white mustard seeds or sesame seeds is prescribed by that same [text];
one should likewise perform the ritual bathing of Padmanābha with clarified butter.
O best of the twice-born, that very gift has been described according to one's capacity;
and worship with flowers should be performed, beginning from the feet up to Keśava.
One should burn various kinds of incense so that [the merit] may endure for a supreme year;
and one should worship that Teacher of the World with gold and garments.
Having worshipped Padmanābha, the Lord of the gods and teacher of the world, one should offer sacrificial foods (haviṣya) that are fresh, liquid, and fit for sucking.
Having understood this, O best of sages, O observer of excellent vows, [one should act] with this mantra:
"Homage be to the one who holds a lotus in his hand; homage indeed to the one whose womb is a lotus."
May dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa indeed be unimpaired for me;
O you whose eyes are like blooming lotus petals, may you likewise be unimpaired in every respect.
"O Keśava, may the religious duties of that being remain unimpaired. Having spoken thus, when the year is complete, he should observe a fast, with his senses subdued.
O Brahmin, one should indeed fulfill the vow completely regarding all matters;
when that vow has been performed, Mādhava is clearly pleased.
Furthermore, dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, and so forth, arise in an inexhaustible manner.
Thus ends the Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī vow [also known as Nāma-dvādaśī].

Having fasted from the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara with incense, garlands, wreaths, and other offerings. Having worshipped them and given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) while reciting their names, one partakes of all the fruits obtainable from the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Aptoryāma, Agniṣṭoma, Gomedha, Puruṣa, and Sautrāmaṇi sacrifices, as well as from the five great sacrifices and the fire-oblation (homa). This is attained through constant remembrance, worship, and the chanting of these names.
Thus ends the vow of the Twelve Names (Nāmadvādaśīvrata).
[The Śravaṇa-dvādaśī Vow] in the Vāmana Purāṇa. Premā said:
The twelfth day of the lunar fortnight known as Śravaṇa-dvādaśī occurs in the month of Bhādrapada; then, a certain city-dweller went there to bathe at the confluence.
There, too, I followed Airāvatī and Anaḍvalā, who were preceded by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, on account of my connection with their neighbors.
Having observed the fast on the eleventh day, pure and observant of the vow of purity,
he then [worshipped] the new cloud with the water from the confluence using a stream of water.
Having touched a clay vessel that is completely covered with cloth, filled with the water of the confluence, and indeed full of curd and rice;
He gave it to a pure Brahmin of foremost merit who had performed his duties;
this is the reason why that food was given along with water.
"That which was given returns day after day even at midday.
Thus concludes the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow [also known as the Vijaya-dvādaśī vow].
In the Āditya Purāṇa,
Bhānu said:
"O Brahmā, there is another Dvādaśī which is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism."
And when that [day] is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, it should be observed as a fast with great effort.
The twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism is proclaimed as Vijayā;
O Brahmin, it is only rarely obtained after a very long period of time.
That twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna which falls under the Puṣya asterism was declared by Viṣṇu himself in ancient times to be the Jayā-dvādaśī.
Whatever gift is given or austerity performed during that [lunar day] yields merit millions upon millions of times greater;
however, O Brahmin, when it occurs in the month of Śrāvaṇa, it may sometimes be like that of a Kṣatriya.
That lunar day is declared to be Vijayā; it should be observed as a fast according to the prescribed rules.
Having remained without food on the eleventh day, one should worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth day.
In a vessel made of silver or gold, or even one made of wood or bamboo,
having covered the vessel with unwashed, well-examined cloths;
Success shall be achieved through the paths born of the penis according to one's capacity,
using a *ḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds, or a *prastha*, a *kuḍava*, or the like of *bilva* fruits and other offerings.

In the absence [of sesame], the fruit [of the rite] is obtained with barley and wheat; it becomes equal to that of primary sesame through flowers, perfumes, fruits, and incense. One should worship Hari at the proper time.
With various kinds of offerings, including foods to be chewed and eaten, and rice with jaggery,
one should recite the mantra four times over, with devotion that is a hundred thousandfold superior.
One should keep a vigil there with the playing of musical instruments and dancing;
thus, observing these restraints on this day, when the morning has become clear, [one should proceed].
Or, out of devotion, he should cause it to be given with the best of his wealth along with gold;
the twice-born should give it according to the mantra to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the scriptures.
The knower of mantras receives the Brahmins with a mantra,
and likewise the donor, endowed with devotion, gives with a mantra.
“Vāmana is wise, generous, and established in material wealth; he is Vāmana himself. Indeed, it is by the grace of the Brāhmaṇa that he is truly Vāmana.
This is the mantra for receiving [the gift]. Now, the mantra for worship:
I worship the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Paraśurāma, and Kṛṣṇa; salutations, salutations!

Oṃ, one should offer salutation to Matsya at the feet; salutation to Kūrma at the knees; Oṃ, salutation to Varāha at the private parts; Oṃ, salutation to Nṛsiṃha at the navel; Oṃ, salutation to Vāmana at the chest; Oṃ, salutation to Rāma at the two arms; Oṃ, salutation to Rāma at the throat and the eyebrows; Oṃ, salutation to Kṛṣṇa at the head. All this—flowers, fruits, and food offerings (naivedya)—should be presented according to the prescribed method of worship. Having thus fasted on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) under the asterism of Śravaṇa, O best of Brahmins, one should take food consisting of *pṛṣadājya* (curd-butter mixture) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having first given to a Brahmin, one should afterwards eat oneself;
it is not for the sake of suffering, nor should one eat as much as one desires, nor is eating at night prescribed by rule.
O Brahmin, learn from me the merit that accrues upon the completion of the vow;
O best of Brahmins, it purifies one for seventy-one cycles of the four ages.
O Brahmin, for that long he sports at will in the imperishable city of Viṣṇu;
and having returned here at the end of time, he shall become a king of kings.
In the Tretā Yuga, the age of Dharma, he is born again and again;
O best of Brahmins, for ten births he is born in a beautiful city within the realm.
He shall be born into a great family, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
a donor of elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, an enjoyer of pleasures, and free from envy.
He shall become an enjoyer of the best of cities, performing sacrifices by the millions;
endowed with beauty and good fortune, he shall be long-lived and free from disease.
"Surrounded by sons and grandsons, may he live for a hundred autumns.
Thus ends the vow of Vijayā-dvādaśī.
[The Puṣyārka-dvādaśī-vrata] in the Devīpurāṇa:
"But by the fault mentioned in the mantra regarding the present [observance], one goes to hell."
Or rather, it is the resolve of one standing at the libation regarding the fulfillment of vows and the giving of gifts.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) coinciding with the Puṣya asterism and Sunday is meritorious and destroys all sins;
by whom was it performed, O Śakra, through the gift of a vessel of ghee?
To him, the giver, the God of gods, Janārdana,
appeared in person— drinking the mantra, clad in yellow garments, and four-armed.
Thus ends the Puṣyārkadvādaśī vow.
[352] [The Bhāgyarkṣadvādaśī vow]
Bṛhaspati said: How did that king, established in fortune, the sovereign superior to all the worlds,
attain divinity and go to the same realm as Viṣṇu?
"How was the Lord of All Gods, the Consort of Umā, pleased with him?
Brahmā said:
"That [twelfth lunar day] is named Bhāgyarkṣadvādaśī, and it bestows good fortune."
Having performed the worship of Hari there, having offered lotuses according to the prescribed rite,

O Sage, the self-controlled one should install both [images]— one complete with all auspicious marks, produced from an excellent tree, for Śaṅkara, and the other for the Supreme Person Hari— as the half-body of Śaṅkara.

“Harer arcā” means an image in the form of Hari-Hara. Regarding the phrase “śaṅkarārdhaṃ hareḥ” and so forth, the meaning is that one should install both forms of Hari-Hara, such that half of Śaṅkara belongs to Hari, the Puruṣa; thus, half of the image is Śiva and half is Viṣṇu.
Madhusūdana, when worshipped with devotion and all offerings within the twelve-syllable maṇḍala, [is pleased] by the clarified butter and the Cakrarāja.
The king was satisfied by that and thereby attained good fortune.
Regarding this, some say that the "King of Wheels" is the twelve-spoked wheel itself, known as the *Mahāsudarśana-mantra*.
O best of the twice-born, a boon was granted by the God of Gods when he was pleased:
From now on, my child, you shall become equal to me.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) falling on a fortunate constellation is indeed beyond counting;
one should perform its worship by having it conducted for the sake of Hari, who is worthy of worship within the sacrificial mandala.
Gold, cows, land, sesame seeds, and so forth should be given to the preceptor as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the extent of one's wealth; this purifies one from the ocean of hell.
Hari bestows fruit by the power of the fortune of the age (*yugabhāgyaprabhāveṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "by the power of the fortune of the age," it means by the power of the *karma*—the fortune—of the age, such as the Kṛta and so forth.
Just as even a single courtesan, having gone at the right time and to the right place, [obtains her reward].
O twice-born one, it attains all prosperity during the age of fortune;
likewise, O best of the twice-born, in the asterisms of Bhaga, Puṣya, and Vāsava.
One should know that [the results] are identical on the twelfth and the seventh lunar days.

“Bhāgya” is the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, presided over by Bhaga; “Pauṣṇa” is Revatī; and “Vāsava” is Dhaniṣṭhā. On these, the Lord of the Gods, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, is pleased.
Janārdana bestows sons, sovereignty,
and good fortune upon that mortal who performs the worship of Hari month after month.
In a lotus endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with every color,
Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, whose hand bears the discus, is pleased.
Thus ends the Bhāgyarkṣa-dvādaśī vow. [Now,
the Bhīma-dvādaśī vow] according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
Vāsudeva said:
If [the moon] should be on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the twelfth lunar days,
or even on other days or under other asterisms, one who is unable to fast completely [should do as follows].
Then, having fasted according to this rite on this meritorious day, the anniversary of Damayantī which destroys all sins, one shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
When the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha arrives,
one should perform an anointing with ghee and then carry out a bath with sesame seeds.
In the same manner, having worshipped Viṣṇu with "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," one should worship the feet with "To Kṛṣṇa" and the head with "Obeisance to the Soul of All."
One should worship the throat with "Salutation to Vaikuṇṭha," and the chest with "To the bearer of the Śrīvatsa";
likewise, one should worship [the arms] with "To the holder of the conch," "To the holder of the discus," "To the holder of the mace," and "To the Giver of Boons."
In this manner, all the arms of Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped in sequence;
the belly with "To Dāmodara," and the penis with "To Pañcaśara."
[355] Homage to the Lord of Good Fortune for the thighs; homage to the Sustainer of Beings for the knees; homage indeed to Nīla for the shanks; homage to the Creator of the Universe for the feet.
Salutation to the Goddess, salutation to Peace, salutation to Lakṣmī, salutation to Śrī;
salutation to Nourishment, salutation to Praise, and likewise salutation to Contentment and Prosperity.
Homage to the Lord of Birds, the winged one with the speed of the wind;
one should constantly worship Garuḍa, the destroyer of poison.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, Umāpati,
and Vināyaka with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of edible offerings;
Then, having restrained his speech and eaten kṛśara prepared with cow’s milk along with clarified butter, a man should go to Śatapatha.
Having taken a tooth-stick made of nyagrodha or else of khadira wood, the wise man, having sipped water, should clean his teeth while facing either the east or the north.

Manu said:
Is fasting or a vow sufficient to completely uproot the multitude of sorrows arising from separation from what is desired?
It brings about both worldly prosperity and liberation on this earth, and it is the destroyer of men's fear of cyclic existence.
Matsya said:
This which you have asked is dear to the world,

which is secret even among the Indras, Asuras, and Dānavas.
Nandikeśvara said:
The meritorious Viśokadvādaśī vow is observed in the month of Āśvayuja.
On the tenth day, the wise man, eating light food, should begin it according to the prescribed rules.
Facing either north or east, having first cleansed his teeth,

Salutation to Viśoka for the feet, and to Varada for the shanks;

"Salutation to Kandarpa for the secret parts; salutation to Mādhava for the waist;

Salutation to the lotus-navelled one for the navel; to the god of love for the heart; to Śrīdhara for the chest of the Lord; and salutation to the slayer of Madhu for his two hands.

The nose for the destruction of sorrow, the eyes for Vāsudeva,

One should worship with the words: "To Alakān Mādhava," "To Viśvarūpin," "Salutation to the Soul of All," and likewise, "Salutation to the Head."

“*Avarārdhyam*” means the minimum. Thus ends the Puṣya-vrata.
