In accordance with one's contemplation of the state of being, one shall obtain the fruit that is indeed real.
Thus ends the Brahma-Gāyatrī-Candra-Rohiṇī vow.
Now, regarding the monthly observances, the procedure for the Kārttika bath;
therein Viṣṇu says: [89.1–4]

The month of Kārttika has Agni as its presiding deity, and Agni is the mouth of all the gods. Therefore, one who bathes outdoors throughout the entire month of Kārttika, who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) only once [a day], becomes purified from the sins committed during the year. On this subject, there is a verse:

"One who bathes in the morning throughout the entire month of Kārttika, who has conquered his senses, who recites [the Gāyatrī], who eats sacrificial food, and who is self-controlled, is liberated from all sins."
Thus ends the procedure for the Kārttika bath. [The vow of eating only one meal a day] according to the Skanda Purāṇa.
He who passes a divine month subsisting on a single meal per day,
endowed with that deed, attains good fortune in every respect.
By performing it in the month of Pauṣa, one obtains many righteous sons;
and women who perform it in the month of Māgha obtain beloved husbands.
O best of men, one who constantly observes the practice of eating only once a day throughout the month of Phālguna should likewise pass the month of Caitra by eating only one meal a day.
That man who passes the month of Vaiśākha eating but a single meal a day shall be born handsome in a family abundant in wealth and grain.
That man who indeed observes the practice of eating but one meal during the month of Jyeṣṭha attains preeminence in the world; honored and possessed of wealth and grain, he prospers.
He who observes the practice of eating only one meal a day during the month of Āṣāḍha becomes the most excellent among his brothers and obtains abundant enjoyments.
Having attained honor, that man goes to his destination and obtains abundant desires,
even if he practices in this manner during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Having attained the position of commander-in-chief, he is reborn as one possessed of great strength—
he who likewise subsists on a single meal during the month of Āśvayuja.
Trade, agriculture,
and likewise herds of cattle bear fruit for him who observes the month of Kārttika by eating but one meal a day.
That best of men who passes his entire life eating but one meal a day attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Agni.
He who subsists on a single meal for a year shall go by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot to the world of Śakra.
Having become equal to a king, he traverses the earth like a lord of men.
In the Mahābhārata:
"He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with a single meal [per day]..."
But he who is born into a noble family and possesses [right] birth attains that state of Hari.
O son of Kuntī, he who passes the month of Pauṣa with a single meal becomes fortunate,
handsome, and a partaker of glory.
He who passes the month of Māgha eating but a single meal a day shall become illustrious,
possessed of kin, and attain greatness within his family.
He who passes the month of Bhagadaiva eating but one meal per day attains favor with women, and they become submissive to him.
He who passes the month of Caitra with a fixed regimen of eating only one meal a day is born into a great family, enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls.
Whether it be a man or a woman, he or she who, with senses subdued, observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Vaiśākha, shall attain preeminence among all living beings.
He who passes the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla subsisting on a single meal per day shall increase his kin; wherever he may be, he is joined with consecration.
Having remained diligent for the month of Āṣāḍha, subsisting on a single meal per day,
one is born with abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many sons.
He who, being disciplined, passes the month of Śrāvaṇa eating but one meal a day,
increases his kin and becomes endowed with empowerment wherever he may be.
The man who, during the month of Prauṣṭhapada, eats but once a day,
attains abundant wealth, prosperity, and incomparable sovereignty.
Likewise, he who passes the month of Āśvayuja eating but one meal a day will be born with progeny, great renown, and many sons.
The man who observes the practice of eating only once a day throughout the month of Kārttika becomes brave, highly fortunate, and indeed renowned.
Thus ends the vow of eating but once a day.
Now follows the Kāmavrata for women,
as described in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
The woman or man who passes the month of Kārttika eating but a single meal a day,
self-restrained by rules such as patience and non-violence, and remaining celibate;
One should respectfully offer to the Sun cooked rice mixed with jaggery,
along with *karavīra* flowers, *guggulu*, and clarified butter.
On the seventh or the eighth day, she should delight in fasting;
having bathed on both fortnights, she should be endowed with supreme faith.
In celestial palaces resembling sapphire that fulfill all desires,
a woman is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred yugas.
Therefore, having come to this world, she finds a husband according to her desire; [these qualities are:
forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, generosity, purity, and restraint of the senses.
Worship of the Sun, the fire-oblation, contentment, and the avoidance of theft—
this is the common duty that always abides in all vows.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should fashion a celestial chariot out of flour,
adorn it with perfumes and garlands, and offer it to the Sun-god.
In golden great vehicles accompanied by hosts of celestial nymphs,
he is honored in the world of the sun for eleven thousand years.
"With golden *gairikeya* [flowers]," meaning made of gold.
Having arrived in this world in due order, she shall obtain a king as her husband.
In the month of Pauṣa, however, having fashioned an image of Garuḍa, she should offer it to the Sun.
Having adorned the Sun, the foremost of the gods, with perfumes and garlands,
one should offer all of that into him while he is situated within a copper vessel.
On that Garuḍa,
by means of the Mahāpadmaka vehicle which wafts divine fragrances,
he is honored in the world of the sun for eleven thousand years.
Having thus attained in due course the world and a king as her desired husband,
she [should worship] in the month of Māgha one endowed with horses, adorned with lamps, jewels, and garlands.
Having joined him with the son of Piṣṭa,
he should bring him to the sanctuary by means of vehicles resembling great chariots, equipped with white horses.
For more than a full hundred thousand years, she is honored in the world of the Sun;
returning gradually to this world, she finds a husband according to her desire.
Having fashioned an image of the god made of flour in the month of Phālguna,
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should place it in the temple of the Sun.
In celestial chariots resembling the sun and filled with the sounds of song and instrumental music,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for eleven thousand years.
Having spent a moment in Caitra, adorned with perfumes and garlands, she returns to this world and finds a husband according to her desire.
Having placed it in a vessel as described, one should offer it to the Sun-god.
"As described" means made of copper.
[423] With celestial chariots resembling the autumnal moon and fulfilling all desires...
For more than a full hundred thousand years, one is honored in the world of the Sun;
then, upon the exhaustion of that karma, having returned here accompanied by sons and grandsons—
Having obtained her desired husband, she shall attain enjoyments that are very difficult to acquire.
[Having fashioned Mount Meru from a *piṣṭa* (flour) measure of rice;
“*taṇḍulāḍhakapiṣṭena*” means with rice.
Joined with the Nikṣubhā and Arka [mantras], adorned with all the elements,
endowed with various ornaments, and decorated with various garlands.
One should place [the image] endowed with all kinds of jewels in the abode of the Sun;
for this is the Mahāvyoma-vrata, which one should observe on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
He is honored in the world of the sun by means of various celestial palaces;
having gradually returned to this world, he sports upon the Mānasa forest.
Having fashioned a lotus with its pedestal out of flour in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship that "lotus"—
meaning a *padma*—
with vessels rich in fragrance and adorned with various garlands.
In celestial palaces resembling pure crystal that fulfill all desires,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred million years.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband;
and likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, she should offer a second, excellent lotus made of flour.
Having filled it with the essence of all seeds and endowed it with auspicious characteristics,
it was rich with the fragrance of *nāgakesara* flowers and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
O King, endowed with all enjoyments and traveling on great vehicles drawn by swans,
he is honored in the world of the clouds for more than a hundred million years.
Having reached this world in due course, she obtains a king as her husband.
Furthermore, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to the Sun;
[she shall travel] by means of vehicles that move at will and are adorned with various jewels.
For more than a full hundred million years, he is honored in the world of the Sun,
having attained various enjoyments endowed with many wonders.
Having reached this world in due course, she finds a king as her husband;
having then prepared an offering of rice in the sky during the month of Bhādrapada.
The celestial palace was rich with banners and cloths, adorned with various garlands,
visible even by the rays of the moon, and beautifully graced by magnificent great vehicles.
She is honored in the world of the sun for thousands of millions of years;
returning gradually to this world, she finds a king as her husband.
And having fashioned a vast mountain of grain in the month of Āśvayuja,
enriched with gold, garments, and perfumes, one should offer it before the Sun.
In various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles, endowed with excellent enjoyments,
she is honored in the world of the Sun for thousands of millions of years.
Having reached that world once more, she finds a king as her husband;
such is the vow for women according to their desire.
[The Nandā-vrata]
In the Devīpurāṇa,
Brahmā said:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim that which increases the prosperity of all."
O sinless one, by performing which [act] does one become a sovereign emperor in this world?
When the month of Nabhas has arrived, one who has conquered his senses should eat only at night,
bathe in the morning, constantly engage in sacred study, and be devoted to the fire-rituals.
O child, one should worship the Goddess with bilva, punnāga, and campaka flowers;
one should offer guggulu as incense and an offering of milk-rice cooked in ghee.
One should consume milk-rice, or curd-rice, or else vegetables and barley-gruel;
and one should perform the recitation of the mantra a thousand times, or else a hundred times.
One should worship the Goddess until the vow is fulfilled;
once the vow is complete, O child, one should likewise honor the Kalpācāryas and the twice-born.
One should feed and worship [the Brahmins] with devotion using gold, land, clothing, and grain;
however, O best of the twice-born, in the absence of wealth, the recitation of mantras (japa) should be performed.
But whoever should perform this with devotion shall also obtain a result equal to that;
for him there will be no disease, old age, or death, nor any fear arising from water.

O God, for the devotee, the imperishable fruit arises at the end. Herein are the mantra-words: *oṃ nande nandini sarvārthasādhini namaḥ*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). *oṃ nande hṛdayāya namaḥ*: this is the heart (*hṛdaya*). *oṃ nandini śirase namaḥ*: this is the head (*śiras*). *oṃ sarvāyai namaḥ*: this is the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *oṃ arthasādhini namaḥ*: this is the armor (*kavaca*). *oṃ trinetrāyai namaḥ*: this is the eye (*netra*). *oṃ namaḥ huṃ phaṭ*: this is the weapon (*astra*). *oṃ nandinī*: this is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
On the third and the fifth, on the fourth and the eighth days,
on the ninth, on the full moon day, and on the eleventh and the twelfth days.
On the sixth day, she herself, as the Mistress of Wealth (Vitteśā), should be worshipped especially;
and he who, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, offers a white bull dedicated to Nandā, [attains great merit].
He shall obtain the attainment of his desired wish and the eternal world of the Goddess.
In the month of Nabhasya, one should dedicate to her a cow accompanied by gold.
Having had his sins destroyed, he shall go to that imperishable realm of Nanda by fasting during the Navarātra of the month of Āśvina and subsisting on food obtained unasked.
Then, on the eighth day of the following month, having fashioned [an image] of the Goddess and worshipped her with golden flowers, jewels, garments, and various wonderful ornaments;
Gold should be given as a gift to Nandā for the attainment of heaven;
thus, with the multitude of his sins shaken off, he shall be endowed with all desires.
He indeed goes to that world where the goddess, the slayer of the enemies of the gods,
dwells for ten million eons, adorned by hosts of apsarases.
Having worshipped the Goddess with jasmine and white mustard seeds in the month of Kārttika, one rejoices, and upon returning, one shall become the sole sovereign on earth.
While giving food as a gift to a Brahmin, or even to maidens or women,
white garments should likewise be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One is indeed liberated from all sins, even those committed in other births;
such a yogi is born in this very life and attains the imperishable state in the hereafter.
Having bathed duly at the Mārga [tīrtha], one should likewise worship with saffron;
sacrificial food and ghee-filled cakes should be offered to the maidens and to the twice-born.
O child, one should feed and eat [these offerings] while wearing garments produced from the species of insects;
thus, one shall indeed attain all desires and be liberated from all sins.
In the month of Pauṣa, having propitiated the Goddess, one should worship her with garlands of lotuses;
one should offer cooked śāli rice as an oblation and, after feeding young girls, honor them with gifts.
Furthermore, a beautiful bed with yellow garments should be offered to the Goddess;
by this rite, the Goddess herself becomes pleased with him.
It bestows desired enjoyments and at the end leads one to its own city;
in the month of Māgha, one should worship the Goddess with devotion using garlands of *kuṭaja* flowers.
Likewise, they should be anointed with saffron together with camphor—
“together with camphor” meaning accompanied by musk—
and one should worship those maidens according to the rules as before.
With devotion and according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the twice-born and Caṇḍikā to be honored with milk-rice (pāyasa),
and one should cause sacrificial fees and oblations of sesame seeds to be offered according to one's capacity.
With his sins and misfortunes shaken off, endowed with all enjoyments, free from enemies,
and possessing many sons, he is born as the best of men.
At the end of the body, O King, one goes to the world of Nandinī, which is saluted by all the gods;
there is no doubt about this through this ritual procedure.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Goddess with garlands made of mango blossoms,
as well as with food offerings consisting of various edibles together with sugar and honey.
One should feed maidens and Brahmins, and give sacrificial fees and two white garments;
by this, one becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and goes to the world of the gods.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, one should worship the Goddess with *kiṃśuka* flowers;
sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍuka*) should be offered as food, and likewise, one should feed young girls.
And women should be initiated according to the ritual rule with red garments;
by this, one shall obtain all objects of desire without hesitation.
O child, one shall go to the world of the goddesses, where enjoyments are uninterrupted;
in the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the goddess with garlands made of karṇikāra flowers.
The food offering should consist of groats and sugar-candy; maidens should be fed and honored with gifts.
Auspicious gold and garments should be given to the best of the twice-born.
O child, one should propitiate the Goddess, who is unsurpassed among all the deities;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, however, Śaṅkarī is to be worshipped with red aśoka flowers and baskets.
Likewise, water-pots filled with scented water should be offered;
by this, the Goddess swiftly bestows the enjoyments associated with Varuṇa.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Goddess with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and petals;
one should indeed offer as an oblation rice cooked with sugar and barley-pudding.
O sinless one, you should feed young girls, women, and the twice-born, and likewise honor them with various gold ornaments, unguents, and the like, as well as sesame seeds, land, and pearls.
The Blessed Lady should be worshipped with one's power for the accomplishment of all desires and goals:
Nandā, Sunandā, Kanakā, Umā, Durgā, and Kṣamāvatī.
Gaurī, Yogīśvarī, Śvetā, Nārāyaṇī, Sutārakā, and Ambikā—
these are the names [of the goddesses] in successive order starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa.
O tiger among the Kurus, those men who rise and recite [this] become cleansed of sin and abound in wealth upon the earth.
O best of gods, these [names] constantly remind one on the road, in battle, and during afflictions by enemies that she is "Durgā" and "Caṇḍikā."
One should perform the most excellent of vows for half a month, or even a quarter,
or for a full month, beginning with the month of Śrāvaṇa and following the sequence thereafter.
Thus concludes the Nandā-vrata [the Nandā-pada-dvaya-vrata].
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the pada-vrata of the goddess Nandā.
By which high-souled one, O child, she will soon be pleased.

When the two sandals are made for one suffering from hemorrhoids, they should be worshipped with mangoes, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and bilva leaves according to one's ability and in accordance with the mantras.
Having worshipped the Goddess with devotion upon an altar or in images,
one should offer [the fruit] to a Brahmin who is my devotee or to virgins.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Durgā;
thereafter, O one of great wisdom, upon the exhaustion [of that merit], he becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas.
O best of kings, at the proper time, a man who has come here to this earth is born among the Brahmins; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the vow of the two feet of Nanda.
[The Trivikrama-vrata] is described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World or even the Sun-god,
he who eats one meal at night and offers the second to the Brāhmaṇas [is performing this vow].
One who performs this for the pleasure of the Sun during the month of Kārttika—
whether with effort in the first stage of life, or whether knowingly or unknowingly— shall attain [the fruit].
Therefore, one is liberated from committed sin; there is no doubt in this matter.
By this very procedure, a man [should act] in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Listen to me regarding the fruit obtained by that person who, having worshipped Him, offers a single meal to the Brahmins for the sake of pleasing the Blessed Lord.
O King, whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man in their middle age,
one shall be liberated from those various transgressions.
Having likewise observed the practice of eating only one meal a day, he who gives [food] to a Brahmin after worshipping the Sun in the month of Pauṣa is glorified.
O Lord of Men, he who performs this three-month vow is liberated from minor sins through the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
O King, in the second year one is liberated from minor offenses (upapātaka);
likewise, when it is performed in the third year, there is the destruction of even great sins (mahāpātaka).
This vow, when observed for three months by men and women alike,
bestows its fruit upon human beings after three years.

O King, by means of these three names of the God, even the threefold state resulting from three kinds of sins is established as being released within three months, though it would otherwise take three years.
Therefore, this vow is proclaimed as the Trivikrama;
it is the supreme means of propitiating the Sun-god and the pacifier of all sins.
Thus ends the Trivikrama-vrata. [431] [Now begins the Citrabhānupadadvaya-vrata.]
Brahmā said: O Kṛṣṇa, during the northern transit of the sun, one who has bathed with a restrained mind should bathe the god, the dispeller of darkness, with ghee, milk, and other such substances.
Having properly worshipped with offerings of beautiful garments, flowers, incense, and ointments, and likewise by means of the honoring of the Brahmins;
One who is devoted to the Sun should properly undertake the vow of two steps;
O lord of men, one should worship Citrabhānu at the time of bathing and likewise while eating.
Having eaten, and likewise while walking toward the fire,
while sleeping and while awake, he should always perform the fire-oblation as well as worship.
I shall perform the chanting of the names of Citrabhānu every day,
from this very day until the commencement of the southern solstice.
I shall always act in this way and I shall proclaim the Lord of the World;
likewise, I shall never speak an untruth or any harsh word against the Supreme Self.
Whether out of ignorance or through knowledge, I shall proclaim the Lord;
one should recite [the mantra] for Citrabhānu for exactly six months beyond this point.
Remembering him at the time of death, may I go to whatever destination he reaches;
may that same destination be mine, even if my death should occur within six months of this.
Therefore, I have here offered my very self to Bhāskara;
for even Brahmā, the Supreme Self, is ultimately composed of Citrabhānu.
O best of kings, that Sun-god, by remembering whom one attains the supreme goal upon bowing to him— whether at dawn, at evening, or at midday— is my ultimate refuge.
O King, within six months you have performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of vows;
O Lord of the World, refuge of all people, act accordingly.
"O Citrabhānu, my refuge comes from you according to the proper rule";
having uttered this, he performed the vow consisting of Citrabhānu for six months.
One should perform [the rites] for as long as it takes until the arrival of the southern solstice;
thereafter, one should offer propitiation to the Fire-god according to one's ability.
One should feed two Brahmins, both those born of the earth and those of the twice-born lineage, along with ritual fees;
likewise, one should recount the stories of the meritorious souls in the presence of the Sun.
O Supporter of the Earth, one should worship the reciter with devotion according to one's capacity;
O Kṛṣṇa, that man who thus causes this vow to be recited—
O tiger among gods, whatever woman is liberated from all sins—
if their death should occur within six months— [she attains that state].
One attains, without a doubt, that fruit which is said to result from fasting,
by one who is a true devotee constantly worshipping the two feet of Kṛṣṇa.
This vow to the pair of feet of Citrabhānu, which destroys all sin,
was proclaimed in ancient times by Bhānu to Kṛṣṇa when he inquired about it.
Thus concludes the vow of the two feet of Citrabhānu.
[Now follows the vow for the completion of the Saṃkrānti festival] therein, in the Matsya Purāṇa:
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall further describe the fruit of the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Saṃkrānti festival,
which is imperishable in the other world and bestows the fruits of all desires.
On the equinoxes and the solstices, one should observe the Saṃkrānti vow;
on the preceding day, having first cleansed the teeth, one should eat only a single meal.
On the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), bathing with sesame seeds is prescribed in the morning;
during the transit of the sun, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the ground with sandalwood paste.
One should fashion a lotus with its pericarp; upon it, one should invoke the Sun.
With "sandalwood"—meaning red sandalwood—one should then sequentially place Sūrya Āditya within the pericarp.
Homage to Yamārcis in the southern quarter, and homage to Ṛṅmaṇḍala;
homage to Savitṛ in the southwestern quarter, and again to Tapana in the western quarter.
Having assigned Bhaga in the northwest, one should worship him again and again;
one should always assign Mārtaṇḍa in the north and Viṣṇu in the northeast.
Then, one should worship upon the sacrificial ground with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and edible offerings;
and to a brahmin, one should give a water-pot along with a vessel of ghee and a golden object.
Having had a lotus made according to one's ability, one should offer it;
and with sandalwood water and flowers, one should place the *arghya* offering for the deity upon the ground.
Salutations to the All, who possesses all forms, whose abode is the All, the Self-born;
O Infinite One, salutations to the Creator, the Lord of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses.
By this procedure, one should perform everything month by month;
at the end of the year, a person should likewise perform it all twelve times.
At the end of the year, having worshipped the fire with ghee and milk-rice, as well as the most excellent of the twice-born,
he should [offer] jars again, each filled with twelve kinds of grain.
[He saw] those whose wombs were golden lotuses, covered with cloth and hair.
One should provide eight or seven milch cows that are well-behaved, equipped with golden muzzles, silver hooves, and cloths, along with bronze milking vessels.
Or even if he is unable to wear a garland and [fine] garments, he should still perform all four [restraints].
One afflicted by poverty should likewise offer a single tawny cow to an eminent Brāhmaṇa;
and one should give away the entire earth, including its golden ornaments.
Or else, it may be made of gold, silver, or even copper.
If one is unable [to provide the image made of flour], one should prepare it with sesame seeds and offer it together with a golden sun.
"With the remainder" means accompanied by the serpent Ananta. "Made of flour" (*paiṣṭī*) means consisting of ground meal (*piṣṭa*), and it should be provided with the seven continents.
A person should not practice stinginess regarding wealth in this matter;
by doing so, he goes downward—of this there is no doubt.
As long as the lords of men, headed by Mahendra,
and the earth together with its seven oceans shall remain here, so long shall he [remain] with the remainder of the hosts of Gandharvas.
O Nārada, he is honored in the vault of heaven.
Then, having attained the exhaustion of karma in this world,
he shall become a lord of elephants, endowed with noble lineage and good character; he shall possess a happy and unimpaired body and be accompanied by a wife.
He has many sons, and his feet are honored by kings.
Thus concludes the vow for the completion of the Saṃkrānti rite.
Now, the vows for the year.
[Now, the Sarasvata Vow: O King, you have asked well;
listen to the Sarasvata vow, by the mere recitation of which Sarasvatī is pleased in this world.
Whatever man devoted to me performs this unsurpassed vow,
he should perform it by first honoring a Brahmin at the beginning of that year.
Alternatively, on a Sunday, by means of the strength of the planets and lunar mansions,
one should feed the Brahmins milk-rice (pāyasa) after performing the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa-mantras.
Having given white garments along with gold according to one's ability,
one should worship Gāyatrī with devotion using white garlands and unguents.
O Goddess, grant such a boon that the Blessed One, the Grandfather of the world of Brahmā, may never remain apart from you.
O Goddess, may I not be deprived of all the Vedas and Shastras, nor of dance, song, and the like; likewise, may the Siddhis be mine.
O Sarasvatī, protect me with these eight forms: Lakṣmī, Medhā, Varā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Sṛṣṭi, Prabhā, and Mati.
Having thus worshipped Gāyatrī— who is adorned with the neck of a lute,
who possesses a water-pot, and who desires nourishment— with devotion using white flowers and unbroken rice grains.
Knowing the Dharma, one should eat in silence both morning and evening;
and on the fifth day of each fortnight, one should worship Chandavāsinī.
In the same manner, one should give a *prastha* measure of rice together with a vessel of clarified butter, milk, and gold, saying: "May Gāyatrī be pleased."
Likewise, one should practice silence during the twilight hours;
no food should be consumed in between for as long as thirteen months.
Upon the completion of the vow, one should give food prepared with sesame and rice,
a full water-pot, a pair of garments, and a beautiful cow to a Brahmin.
Furthermore, for the Goddess, [one should offer] a canopy with bells, accompanied by white eye-cloths,
sandalwood, a pair of garments, curd-rice, and a pinnacle.
Likewise, one should worship the teacher who instructs with devotion,
free from stinginess regarding wealth, using garments, garlands, and ointments.
Whoever performs the Sārasvata vow according to this procedure becomes possessed of learning, endowed with wealth, and blessed with prosperity.
Thus ends the Sārasvata-vrata. [Now follows the Phalatyāga-vrata] according to the Matsya-purāṇa.
Nindikeśvara said:
O Sage, the vow [should be observed] on the third lunar day in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
or else on the twelfth, the eighth, or even the fourteenth day.
O best of sages, one should begin during the bright fortnight after having performed the recitation by Brahmins,
even in months other than those [specifically forbidden], provided it be on an auspicious day.
One should worship the twice-born with milk-rice and sacrificial fees according to one's ability,
[offering] eighteen kinds of grains, excluding fruits and roots.
One should avoid [meat] for one year, except for medicinal purposes;
and one should have an image of Rudra made of gold, together with a bull and Dharmarāja.
The kūṣmāṇḍa, the mātuliṅga, the vṛntāka, and likewise the panasa; the āmrātaka and kapittha, the kāliṅga, and then the vāruka.
The bilva fruit, the aśvattha, the jujube, the citron, the plantain fruit,
the karmāra, the pomegranate, and sixteen silver [objects] according to one's capacity.
Radish, myrobalan, rose-apple, tamarind, karamarda,
takkola, cardamom, katunira, karira, kutaja, and shami.
One should devoutly fashion these sixteen fruits out of silver: the udumbara, the coconut, the grape, and the two types of bṛhatī.
One should prepare copper, the fruit of the *tāla* tree, and the fruit of the *agasti* tree,
as well as the fruit of the *piṇḍīraka*, the *kāśmarya*, and the tubers of the *sūraṇa*.
The bulbous root of the red *aluka*, the *kanaka*, the *abhīru*, and the *ciñcika*; likewise the fruit of the variegated creeper (*citravallī*) and the fruit of the *kūṭaśālmalī* tree.
A wise man should have these sixteen copper vessels made: one for village-grown grain, one for *niṣpāva* beans, one for *madhuka*, one for *vaṭa*, one for *iṅguda*, and one for *paṭola*.
Having prepared two water-pots upon grain, covered with cloth,
accompanied by two vessels of food, and provided with golden images of Rudra and the bull;
On an auspicious day, having honored a peaceful Brahmin who maintains a household and is accompanied by his wife, one should present [the gift] together with a cow.
Just as millions of gods dwell within all fruits,
so may devotion to Śiva arise in me through the vow of renouncing all fruits.
Just as Śiva and Dharma always bestow infinite fruits,
may they both grant me my boon by bestowing the fruit associated with that [practice].
Just as there may always be desires for fruits among the devotees of Śiva,
so may I obtain infinite fruit in birth after birth.
Just as I behold Śiva, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Padmajā without distinction,
so may the auspicious Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be ever the source of my welfare.
Having given all that and having adorned it with ornaments,
if one has the capacity, one should give a bed equipped with all necessary furnishings.
But one who is unable [to perform the full rite] should, according to the prescribed rule, offer only the aforementioned fruits,
as well as a pair of water-pitchers and two golden images of Śiva and Dharma.
Having given [the food] to the Brahmin, he should eat while restraining his speech and avoiding theft;
he should also feed other eminent Brahmins according to his ability.
Those who know the Vedas recognize this auspicious vow of renouncing all fruits as belonging to the devotees of the Lord, the Saura-Vaiṣṇava yogins.
And by women, O best of the twice-born, this should be performed according to their ability;
there is nothing superior to this, both in this world and in the next.
O best of sages, this vow yields infinite fruit:
as many atoms as there are in gold, copper, and silver;
O best of sages, for as many thousands of yugas as there are grains of powder produced from those fruits, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This shall always be for the livelihood of people among mankind, removing all their impurities;
and in future births, there shall be no sorrow of separation from one's children.
And he attains the abode cherished by the god Purandara.
Thus concludes the vow of the renunciation of fruits. Now follow the sixty vows, as described therein in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Vrataṣaṣṭika,
which was proclaimed by Rudra to the Goddess and which destroys even the greatest of sins.
1. Having performed the Devavrata vow for one year at night, one should give a golden discus and trident, along with two garments, to a brahmin who maintains a household together with a cow.
"Having bowed to Śiva and Rudra, one rejoices in the world of Śiva;
this is known as Devavrata, which destroys even the greatest sins."
2. He who, observing the Rudra-vow,
should pass a year eating but one meal a day and giving away a golden bull along with a cow made of sesame seeds, attains the abode of Śaṅkara.
This is called the Rudra-vrata, which destroys sin and sorrow.
3. The Nīla-vrata.
But he who, eating only on alternate nights, gives at the end of the year a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar, accompanied by a bull;
One attains that state of Viṣṇu through this auspicious Nīla-vrata.
In the Prīti-vrata, a man should avoid anointing his body for the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha.
He who gives food and utensils goes to the abode of Hari.
That which brings joy to men in the world is here called the Prītivrata.
Excluding the Gaurīvrata, he who, during the month of Madhu, [offers] curds, milk, ghee, and sugarcane—
"In spring," that is, in Caitra;
one should give fine garments together with vessels of flavorful liquids.
Having worshipped a Brahmin couple with the thought, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," this is known as the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows the world of Bhavānī. 6. The Kāma-vrata.
Having observed the *nakta* fast on the thirteenth day of the month of Puṣya and again in the spring (*madhu*),
one should give a golden *aśoka* tree ten finger-breadths in height, accompanied by sugarcane.
"Having given [this] together with a garment to a Brahmin, saying 'May Pradyumna be pleased,' one shall dwell in Viṣṇu’s city for a kalpa and then become free from sorrow once more, O King."
This is known as the Kāmavrata, which always destroys sorrow. As for the Śivavrata, which begins with the month of Āṣāḍha, one should avoid cutting one's nails.
And for four months, one should offer eggplants accompanied by jars of honey and clarified butter.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should present that golden [image] to a Brāhmaṇa.
"Beginning with Āṣāḍha" means starting from the month of Āṣāḍha; the meaning is that one should undertake the vow on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha.
One attains the world of Rudra; this is remembered as the Śiva-vrata.
8. He who avoids the *saumyavrata* during the late autumn (*hemanta*) and winter (*śiśira*),
and having offered three flowers on the full moon of Phālguna, as well as gold according to his ability;
One should give at the two times of day; may Śiva and Keśava be pleased. Having given, one goes to the supreme state; this is remembered as the Saumya-vrata.
9. Regarding the Saubhāgyavrata:
he who avoids salt on the third lunar day of the month of Phālguna shall, upon completion of the vow, give a bed and a house equipped with all furnishings.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased," one shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgyavrata.

10. A man should observe silence during the twilight prayers as part of the Sārasvata-vrata; at the conclusion of the year, he should offer a jar of ghee, a pair of garments, and a jar of sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa.
One attains the state of Sarasvatī, from which return is difficult to find;
this is that which is called Sārasvata, the bestower of beauty and knowledge.
11. The Saṃpadvrata: Having worshipped Lakṣmī, a man should observe a fast on the fifth lunar day. At the conclusion of the year, he should give a golden pitcher together with gold.
He indeed becomes possessed of fortune and attains the station of Viṣṇu birth after birth;
this is known as the Saṃpad-vrata, which eternally destroys all sins.
12. Having performed the vow of longevity (āyurvrata) with an ointment before Śambhu and Keśava,
one should further give a cow together with a water-pitcher for the duration of a year.
For ten thousand births one shall have a lifespan of a hundred years, and at the end, one shall attain the city of Śiva;
this is known as the Āyurvrata, which always destroys all evil.

13. Having prostrated before the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā at a single location, a man, restrained in speech and free from envy, should observe the Kīrtivrata by eating only one meal a day for one year.
At the conclusion of the vow, having honored a Brahmin couple along with three cows, one should give a golden tree; he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
This is known as the Kīrtivratam, which bestows the fruits of prosperity and fame.
14. It is the Somavrata; having performed a ceremonial bath with ghee for either Śambhu or Keśava, [one should proceed].
One should fashion a lotus with unbroken grains upon a circular mark made of cow dung.
At the end of the year, one should give a pure golden pitcher, eight finger-breadths in height, accompanied by a sesame-cow; such a person is honored in the world of Śiva.
“Samāṃ” means for a year. That which is to be given to the singer of the Sāmans is here called the Sāma-vrata.
15. The Vīra-vrata.
On the ninth day, having observed a single meal and having fed young girls according to one's ability, one should give a golden pitcher along with two garments.
Having given a golden lion to a Brahmin, one shall go to the city of Śiva;
for a hundred million births, he shall be handsome and unconquered by enemies.
This is called the Vīravratam, which bestows happiness upon women. As for the Pitṛvratam:
he who observes the vow of subsisting on milk alone on the fifteenth day (the full moon) throughout the month, [attains the aforementioned merit].
On the fifteenth day, that is, on the new moon,
one who performs the *śrāddha* at the end of the year should give five cows that have recently calved.
He who gives saffron-colored garments along with water-pots goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and delivers a hundred of his ancestors.
At the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings; this is remembered as the Pitṛvrata.
17. Furthermore, in the Ānandavrata, one should offer water unasked for during the four months beginning with Caitra.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-jar accompanied by food and clothing.
One who offers a vessel of sesame seeds and gold is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
at the end of the kalpa, he certainly becomes a lord of the earth—this is called the Ānanda-vrata.
18. Having performed the bath with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for the Lord for one year according to the vow of steadfastness (*dhṛtivrata*), [one should proceed].
At the end of the year, one should again give a cow accompanied by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

The "five nectars" (*pañcāmṛta*) are curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice. To the "Lord" (*vibhu*), that is Śaṅkara; one should give a conch shell to a Brahmin, and he attains the state of Śaṅkara.
At the end of the kalpa, he becomes a king. This is remembered as the *dhṛtivrata*.
19. Having avoided the vow of non-violence, a man who eats meat at the end of the year should become a giver of a cow;
likewise, he should give a golden deer, and he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The vow of non-violence (ahiṃsāvrata) has been described; by its power, one becomes a king at the end of the kalpa.
20. Regarding the Sūryavrata: having performed an ablution at dawn during the month of Māgha, one should worship a married couple.
Having fed them according to one's ability, one should honor them with garlands, garments, and ornaments.
One shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a kalpa; this is known as the Sūryavrata.
21. Regarding the Viṣṇuvrata:
during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should bathe in the morning.
Having given food to Brahmins on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should become a giver of cows.

He indeed goes to the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the vow of Viṣṇu (viṣṇuvrata). During the observance of the vow of conduct (śīlavrata), one should avoid milk and clarified butter for the duration of the entire year (ayana).
At its end, however, there should be garlands of flowers together with a cow made of ghee.
Having given ghee and milk-rice to a Brahmin, one goes to the city of Śiva;
this is known as the vow of good conduct (*śīlavrata*), which bestows health and the splendor of prosperity.
23. Regarding the vow of radiance (*dīptivrata*), a lamp for the twilight rites should be offered; one must avoid using oil for a full year.
At the end of the year, one should present a golden lamp, as well as a discus and a trident made of gold.
By giving a pair of garments to a brahmin, one becomes radiant in this world and attains the realm of Rudra; this is known as the Dīptivrata.

24. Having consumed barley-gruel with cow's urine on the third lunar day of the month beginning with Kārttika, one should observe the Rudra-vow at night for one year; at the end of the year, one should become a giver of a cow.
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa, and having returned, one shall become a king here;
this is known as the Rudra-vrata, which always brings about auspiciousness.
25. He who observes a firm vow should avoid perfumes and ointments during the month of Caitra;
yet, having given a conch shell filled with fragrance and two white garments to a Brahmin, he attains his goal.
One attains the station of Varuṇa; this is remembered as the Dṛḍhavratam.
26. In Vaiśākha, by avoiding flowers and salt, one who gives a cow performs the Kāntivratam.
Having performed a kalpa at Viṣṇupada and having remained there, one shall become a king in this world.
This is known as the Kāntivrata, which bestows the fruits of beauty and fame.
27. Regarding the Brahmavrata:
having fashioned a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) together with a heap of sesame seeds, [one should offer it].
Having observed the vow of sesame for three days, one should satisfy the fire and the virtuous brahmins.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments, he should say according to his capacity,
"May the Soul of the Universe be pleased," offering at least three palas of gold.
On an auspicious day, Brahmā goes to his lotus-bed and attains the state of no-return;
this is known as the Brahma-vow, which bestows the fruit of Nirvāṇa upon men.
28. He who gives away a "two-faced" cow (dhenu) accompanied by abundant gold,
and remains for one day observing the milk-vow (payovrata), goes to the supreme state.
This is known as the Dhenu-vrata, from which rebirth is difficult to attain.
29. Regarding the Kalpavṛkṣa-vrata: having observed the milk-vow for three days, one should [offer] a golden wish-fulfilling tree.
After the funeral pyre, one should offer rice grains together with a winnowing basket according to one's ability.
Having given this, one goes to the abode of Brahmā; this is known as the Kalpavṛkṣa-vrata.
30. As for the Bhīma-vrata: he who observes a month-long fast should give a beautiful cow to a Brahmin.
He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Bhīmavrata.
31. Having fashioned a golden image of the earth weighing more than twenty palas, one should perform the *dharāvratam* (earth-vow);
by subsisting on milk for a day, he is honored in the world of Rudra.
This is declared to be the *dharāvrata*, which follows one for seven hundred kalpas.
32. Regarding the *mahāvrata*, one should be a giver of a cow made of molasses (*guḍadhenu*) in either the month of Māgha or Caitra.
One who observes the Guḍavrata on the third lunar day is honored in Goloka.
This is called the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), which produces supreme bliss;
[447] 33. The Vow of Radiance (Prabhāvrata).
He who, observing a fast during the fortnight, gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin,
attains the world of Brahmā, being highly honored by gods and asuras.

At the end of the kalpa, one shall become a king of kings; this is known as the *prabhāva-vrata*. As for the *prāpti-vrata*, for one year, eating but a single meal a day, one should give food and a water-pot.
One shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Prāpti-vrata.
35. One who observes the Sugativrata should eat only at night on the eighth lunar days; at the end of the year, he should give a cow.
By this supreme Sugativrata, one goes to the abode of Indra.

36. Regarding the Vaiśvānara-vrata: he who provides fuel for the fire of a Brahmin during the four seasons beginning with the rainy season attains the supreme Brahman by the gift of a cow filled with clarified butter.
The vow known as Vaiśvānara destroys all sins. On the eleventh lunar day, one who observes the Kṛṣṇa-vow and eats only at night should offer a discus.
At the end of the month of Caitra, he shall attain the golden abode of Viṣṇu.

This is known as the Kṛṣṇavrata; it bestows a kingdom at the end of the kalpa. As for the Devīvrata, one who eats only milk-rice (pāyasa) should, at the conclusion of the year, give a cow together with a bull to a Brahmin.
One shall dwell in the world of Lakṣmī for a kalpa; this is known as the vow of the Goddess.
39. One who observes the Bhānu-vrata should eat only at night on the seventh lunar day and, at the end of the year, give a milch cow as a gift;
such a person attains the world of the Sun—this is remembered as the Bhānu-vrata.
40. Regarding the Vaināyaka-vrata:
on the fourth lunar day, one who observes the night-fast should, at the end of the year, offer a golden lotus.
This vow, named Vaināyaka, bestows the world of Śiva.
41. That man who, having renounced great fruits for four months, gives these [fruits] to a twice-born during the month of Kārttika together with a pair of cows, performs the Fruit-vow (phalavrata).
This is called the Fruit Vow (phalavrata); by it, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
"Great fruits" refer to those such as the *kūṣmāṇḍa* and the jackfruit (*panasa*).
42. The Solar Vow (sauravrata).
And he who, observing the fast on the seventh day at the end of the year, should give a golden lotus and cows according to his ability, together with vessels of gold and food.
This is called the Saura-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the world of the Sun.
43. As for the Vṛṣa-vrata, he who completes twelve Dvādaśīs by means of fasts, and then again—
A person should worship the Brahmins according to his capacity with cows, garments, and gold.
One attains the supreme state; this is remembered as the Vṛṣavrata.
At the conclusion of the Prājāpatyavrata, the giver of a cow should provide a meal according to his ability.
This is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite for Brahmins; it leads to the state of Śaṅkara.
The connection is: "food for the Brahmins. 45. Regarding the Tryambaka-vrata:
having eaten only at night on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], one who gives a pair of cows at the end of the year [attains the goal].
One attains the state of Śiva; this is remembered as the Traiyambaka [rite].
46. Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man as the Varavrata;
they call this the Varavrata, which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.
47. One who observes the Indra-vrata should sleep in the open air during the rainy season and, at its conclusion, give a milch cow as a gift;
he shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa. This is remembered as the Indra-vrata.
48. But that man who, observing the vows of moral conduct, eats food not cooked by fire on the third lunar day,
having given a cow as a gift, attains Śiva, from whom there is no return.
In this world, O Ānanda, this is remembered as the vow of moral conduct that brings joy to men: the Horse-vow consists of [offering] two palas of gold and a chariot yoked with a pair of horses.
49. The Horse-vow.
Gold weighing more than two palas and a chariot equipped with a pair of horses.
Having observed a fast, one who gives [this] shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas.

At the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings; this is known as the horse-vow (aśvavrata). Likewise, in the elephant-vow (karivrata), a man should give a golden chariot yoked with two elephants.
In the same way, after two palas have passed, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Having observed the fast, one should perform this rite known as the "Elephant Vow" (karivrata).
Alternatively, having completely renounced the "Happiness Vow" (sukhavratam), one should become a donor of cows at the conclusion of the year.
One attains lordship over the yakṣas; that is called the vow of happiness.
52. Having performed the Varuṇa-vrata by dwelling in the water at night, one should become a giver of a cow at dawn;
one attains the world of Varuṇa—this is called the Varuṇa-vrata.
53. He who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, known as the Moon-vow (candravrata), should offer a golden moon;
this is declared to be the Moon-vow, which bestows the fruit of the lunar world.
54. By performing the Rudra-vrata in the month of Jyeṣṭha, practicing the penance of five fires, and gifting a golden cow in the evening, one goes to heaven;
this is known as the Rudra-vrata for the sixth and thirteenth lunar days.
55. One should perform the Bhavānī-vrata once as a night-fast on the third lunar day at a temple of Śiva;
it is called the Bhavānī-vrata when, at the conclusion of the year, one gives a cow with devotion.
56. The Pavana-vrata:
in the month of Māgha, one should wear wet clothes; on the seventh lunar day, one should be a giver of cows.
Having dwelt in heaven for a kalpa, one shall become a king through the Pavana-vrata.
57. Having fasted for three nights, one should give a beautiful house on the full moon day of Phālguna;
this is known as the Dhāmavrata, by which one attains the world of Āditya.
58. He who, having fasted, worships a married couple with ornaments at the three junctions of the day according to the Indu-vrata,
attains liberation and other rewards such as those of the Indu-vrata.
59. Having undertaken the moon-vow (somavrata) on the second day of the bright fortnight, one should eat salt only for the duration of the moon’s phases;
at the conclusion of the year, by giving a cow to a Brahmin, he goes to the abode of Śiva.

At the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings; this is known as the Somavrata. Regarding the Viśvavrata: eating only one meal on the tenth day, at the end of the year, he should give ten cows.
And by giving a mountain of gold to a Brahmin, one shall become a sovereign lord.
This is called the Viśvavrata, which destroys great sins.
Thus end the sixty vows.
Now, regarding miscellaneous vows,
it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"He who remains without food on the eleventh day and eats on the twelfth day..."
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, that is indeed the great Vaiṣṇava vow.
Knowing this, O King, one destroys even most terrible sins by eating only at night on the thirteenth day; this is remembered as the "Dharma-vrata."
Starting from that time, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, and especially during the dark fortnight, the wise practitioner should undertake the Raudra vow.
O King, beginning from the month of Māgha for a full year,
one should observe the Indra-vrata on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight by eating only at night.
"O King, you have declared that the vow for the ancestors on the new moon day is the seed;
he who performs it thus for fifteen years [attains the goal]."
Who can state with certainty the fruit of lunar-day vows (tithivratas),
which equal thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecrations?
O Indra among kings, he has performed the sacrifices prescribed for the Kalpa;
yet, even a single vow, when constantly observed, destroys all his sins.
Furthermore, O King, that son of the best of men who should perform all of this in its entirety attains all the pure and stainless worlds.
[453] The Great Vows of Austerity in the Skanda Purāṇa.
O best of men, he who performs this for a single day and night for the Goddess obtains the beautiful fruit of ten gold pieces.
"Of gold" means "the fruit of the gift of gold.
That best of men who, month after month, observes a fast for a day and night,
being endowed with that deed, is freed from all evil.
He does not go to hell, nor does he see Yama; this is the truth.
Likewise: "He who performs the vow of fasting for three nights month after month,
having reached the world of Kubera, shall attain the supreme goal."
The man who, self-restrained and pure, eats on the fourth day,
attains the state of a Gandharva and rejoices in heaven like Śakra.
He who, unwearied, eats on the fifth day for every month,
being liberated from all sins, shall go to heaven with great splendor.
He who, being self-restrained and pure, always eats on the sixth day,
reaches the world of Varuṇa and attains the supreme state.
He who, having conquered the pairs of opposites and being firm in his vow, eats on the seventh day, attains the world of Āditya; he too shall find the great vow.
[454] “One who has conquered the pairs of opposites” means one who is patient with sufferings such as heat and cold.
He who eats on the eighth day, having conquered the pairs of opposites and being firm in his vow,
shall attain the world of Viṣṇu and become possessed of supreme splendor.
The man who, being self-restrained and pure, eats on the ninth day,
becomes dear to the Vasus and dwells together with them.
He who eats on the tenth day obtains the fruit of twelve days;
having become equal to the two Aśvins, he always blazes like the sun.
The "Twelve-Day" (Dvādaśāha) is a specific sacrificial rite.
However, that man who always eats on the eleventh day,
having reached the eleventh day [of mourning], shall attain the status of being a member of Rudra’s retinue.
O Goddess, that man who always eats on the twelfth day,
having reached the twelfth day [of the vow], is honored in the world of Śakra.
But the man who always eats on the thirteenth day shall dwell in the abode of Bhārgava, endowed with divine happiness.
By eating only on the fourteenth day and constantly passing the other days in fasting,
a man reaches the world of Tuṣita and becomes a Gaṇapati.
“Tauṣṭika” means divine.
He who passes half a month always indeed without sloth becomes equal to the king of the gods and remains in heaven.
But the wise man who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, passes a month [in this practice],
shall travel by means of a divine celestial chariot, accompanied by Apsarases.
She dwells in all the worlds for tens of millions of years;
thereafter, having attained the seat of Brahmā, she is highly honored by Brahmā himself.
O best of men, he dwells in the Brahma-world like Brahmā himself; as stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Having observed three-night fasts month after month for twelve years..."
One attains leadership of the assembly, free from rivals and without obstacles.
But that man who, for a full year, eats but once a day,
attains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
For ten thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world;
upon the exhaustion of that merit, having returned here, he attains greatness.
But he who, for a full year, eats only every fourth meal,
is constantly devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and has his senses restrained.
A man indeed attains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
for thirty thousand years he is glorified in heaven.

“He partakes of the fourth meal”: the meaning is that having fasted, he does not eat on the following day. “But for a year, O son of Kuntī, a man should spend his time at the sixth meal-time”; the words “he eats” are to be supplied after “at the sixth meal-time.”
A person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
He travels in a celestial chariot drawn by ruddy geese,
and he dwells in heaven for forty thousand years.
"O King,
the Blessed Aṅgiras has declared that for one who eats only once every fortnight for an entire year, it is equivalent to six months of fasting."
He shall dwell in heaven for sixty thousand years.
And he— “should eat,” meaning on every day in the second fortnight,
O Lord of the People— of lutes (*vīṇās*), lyres (*vallakīs*), and flutes (*veṇūs*).
He who is fast asleep is awakened by pleasant and sweet sounds;
he may drink milk here month after month for one year.
That best of men attains the abundant fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice;
he travels by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) yoked with lions, tigers, and other creatures.
A hundred celestial nymphs likewise delight that man,
and he rejoices in heaven for seventy thousand years.
"O tiger among men, no fasting is prescribed for more than a month.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me of that rule which can always be accomplished even by the poor."
Tell me that, O Grandfather, which is equal to these fruits of sacrifice.
Bhīṣma said: He who eats at dawn and likewise at evening, drinking nothing in between,
who is constantly devoted to non-violence and sacrifices to the fire;
"He should drink"—the word "even water" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He attains success in exactly six years; there is no doubt in this matter, provided he stays in the dwelling of celestial women that resounds with the sounds of dancing and singing.

He who eats a single meal continuously for three years shall dwell for a hundred million years in the world of Prajāpati, which resembles fire. "A hundred million" (padma) means one hundred times ten million.
One who always delights in his lawful wife shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
he who, on the second day, eats but a single meal [shall likewise obtain it].
He who, for twelve months, constantly offered oblations into the sacred fire and performed a sacrifice abounding in gold, dear to Vāsava.
Truthful in speech, generous in nature, devoted to Brahmanas, free from malice,
patient, self-controlled, and having conquered anger— one shall obtain whatever fruit [is gained by these virtues].
Then, in a celestial chariot resembling white light and marked with swans,
he shall dwell together with apsarases upon two perfected lotuses.
“When completed,” meaning when it is finished;
he who should eat a single meal on the third day,
constantly for twelve months, while indeed offering oblations into the fire (jātavedas).
One who is constantly devoted to the fire-ritual and always wakes up at the proper time obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
He shall always dwell in the world of the Seven Sages together with celestial nymphs;
they know that his stay there lasts for three padmas of years.
“Having stayed at this [place],
he who eats a single meal on the fourth day,
constantly for twelve months while offering oblations into the fire (jātavedas), [attains the goal].”
One obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and shall dwell in the world of Vāsava, as far as the edge of the ocean.
And he constantly observes the play of the king of the gods;
"the limit of the ocean" means the end of the specific enumeration of the oceans.
He who eats but a single meal on the fifth day—
Constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months,
he was free from greed, truthful, devoted to the Brahmins, and non-violent.
Free from envy and free from evil, one shall obtain the fruit of the twelve-day sacrifice:
a divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, marked with the sign of a swan.
One should ascend to a white house with a radiance equal to a garland of suns;
there are four revolutions and twelve lotuses of the balance.
And he dwells there happily for a duration measured by "arrows and fires.

"Āvartanas" refers to the Manvantaras; "tulāpadmas" refers to a measure of one hundred. "The measure of arrows and fires": arrows are five, fires are three. This measure also pertains specifically to the Manvantaras.
Furthermore, the sage who eats his meal on the sixth day...
Constantly for twelve months, indeed, offering oblations into the Jātavedas fire,
always bathing at the three periods of the day, practicing celibacy, and free from malice.
“The sage who has restrained his speech obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the *Gavam-medha* sacrifice;
likewise, having fallen asleep upon the limbs of an *apsaras*, he awakens.”
By the sound of anklets and the resonance of waist-bands,
thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of yugas passed away.
Likewise, there were eighteen lotuses and two banners,
as well as fifty thousand and one hundred bear skins.
One is glorified in the world of Brahmā for a duration equal to the measure of its hair.
"Patākā" refers to a specific numerical value.
He who eats but a single meal on the seventh day—
Constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas throughout the twelve months,
and protecting Sarasvatī, he should practice celibacy.
One should avoid the *sumana* flower, cosmetics, honey, and meat;
such a person goes to the world of the Maruts and to the world of Indra.
In each of those places, Siddhārtha is honored by celestial maidens;
that man obtains the fruit of a gift of much gold.

He rejoices in those worlds for a period exceeding all measure, guarding Sarasvatī—that is, restraining his speech—and using "varṇaka," such as saffron and other pigments. "Exceeding all measure" (atiguṇām) means surpassing all qualities; that is to say, it is immeasurable.
Furthermore, the man who eats on every eighth day for a full year—
Constantly devoted to the service of the gods and offering oblations into the sacred fire,
he obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
He ascends a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the color of a lotus;
there he finds women who are black, golden-complexioned, and likewise dark-hued.
One who, endowed with youth and beauty, eats [only] on the ninth day and on the following day for an entire year, attains [this], of this there is no doubt.
A person who constantly offers oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months indeed obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And that man obtains a celestial mansion radiant with the splendor of the lotus,
blazing with the brilliance of the sun and fire, and adorned with divine garlands.
He is led by the daughters of Rudra into the eternal intermediate space for eighteen thousand years and for an entire kalpa.
And he rejoices for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in those worlds,
who eats only after every ten days have passed throughout the year.
"Always," that is, for twelve months, indeed offering oblations into Jātavedas;
"gone" means having arrived.
Likewise,
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by dwelling in the abode of the daughters of Brahmā, which is enchanting to all beings.
And beautiful maidens always take pleasure with that man who,
when the eleventh day has arrived, consumes the sacrificial oblation (havis).
One who constantly offers oblations to the Jātavedas for twelve months should never desire another's wife, either in speech or even in thought.
One should not speak untruth even for the sake of one's mother or father;
one should approach Mahādeva, who is seated upon his celestial chariot and possesses great power.
Beautiful maidens with a golden luster lead him to that divine,
celestial, and enchanting heaven, the abode of the Rudras.
For immeasurable years, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon,
he remains for hundreds of thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of millions.
He who is honored by gods and dānavas should always bow down to Rudra;
he shall obtain well-being from him day after day.
He who, having reached the twelfth day, indeed consumes the sacrificial oblation,
while constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months;
He ascends a celestial palace that shines with the brilliance of twelve suns,
endowed with the eight great supernormal powers, and established in the Brahma-world.
Having reached a permanent dwelling crowded with men and women,
he who partakes of the sacrificial oblation when the thirteenth day has arrived—

By always [practicing] for twelve months, one indeed obtains the fruit of a divine sacrificial session (*devasattra*). A man shall accomplish the celestial chariot named Ratnapadmodaya; therein, he remains until the end of the age (*yugānta*) and even for an eon (*kalpa*), together with a ritual stake (*śaṅku*) and a banner (*patākā*).
Likewise, one may dwell for a yuta, an ayuta, a padma, and a samudra [of years].

“Śaṅkupatākā” and other such specific numbers [of aeons]. He is always praised by those celestial maidens, who are ever delighted by the songs and melodies of the Gandharvas and the sounds of kettledrums and conchs.
He who, when the fourteenth day arrives, eats the sacrificial oblation for twelve full months, shall indeed obtain the fruit of a great sacrifice.
Celestial maidens of indescribable age and form, beautifully adorned,
follow him from behind in celestial chariots, holding chowries.
And that man who dwells for a full year in that abode of celestial maidens, which is strewn with the sands of the Ganges, [attains his goal].
But he who, having conquered his senses, eats only one meal when the fortnight has passed,
and constantly offers oblations into the fire for twelve months;
He obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand *rājasūya* sacrifices;
he ascends a divine vehicle attended by swans and peacocks,
variegated with circles of sages and covered in gold.
It was adorned with excellent women resplendent with divine ornaments.
It had a single pillar, four gates, and seven stories;
it was most auspicious, adorned with thousands of victory banners and the sounds of singing.
He ascends a celestial chariot endowed with divine qualities and shall dwell there for a thousand yugas, riding upon a sword and an elephant.
He who, when the sixteenth day has arrived,
partakes of the sacrificial oblation (havis) for twelve full months, shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
He dwells eternally in the abodes of the daughters of Soma;
endowed with gentle fragrances, he is attended by hosts of apsarases.
Seated in a celestial chariot, he is indeed honored by beautiful and sweet-voiced women and served with all objects of sensual enjoyment;
for a hundred lotus-like eons, and even more than a hundred great eons, this is his fruit.
That man should also accomplish the four revolutions.
He who, having reached the seventeenth day, eats the sacrificial oblation,
constantly offering oblations into the Jātavedas for twelve full months.
He attains the realm of Varuṇa, or that of Indra, or even that of Rudra;
he goes to the realm of the Maruts, to that of Śukra, and indeed to the world of Brahmā.
There he is served with a seat by those of celestial appearance;
he also beholds the divine seer Viśvarūpa in the worlds of Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ.
“Bhūr-bhuvah” is the Brāhmaṇa.
O Lord, as long as both the moon and the sun move in the sky,
so long does that hero move, possessing the elixir of pure nectar.
On the eighteenth day, however, he should eat a single meal;
by doing so for twelve months, he indeed beholds the seven worlds.
He was followed from behind by chariots with joyful sounds,
mounted by celestial maidens who were radiant and adorned.
He himself ascends that supreme, divine celestial chariot;
there, for a thousand eons, he rejoices together with beautiful women.
He who eats only one meal on the nineteenth day shall enjoy the essence of nectar, which is like ambrosia and unsurpassed.
Indeed, for twelve months he constantly beholds the seven worlds;
he attains the supreme abode, frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
There, free from all affliction, wearing divine garments and endowed with splendor, he rejoices for a hundred times ten thousand years with the foremost women of the immortals.
Furthermore, he who eats but one meal on the twentieth day,
doing so for twelve full months while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire;
Abstaining from meat, observing celibacy, and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
he attains the stainless worlds of the Ādityas, which are under his control.
He is followed by Gandharvas and Apsarases, adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
in celestial golden chariots.
He who eats but one meal on the twenty-first day is indeed equal to one who offers oblations into the sacred fire for twelve months.
He goes to the divine world of Uśanas and to the world of Śakra;
he always delights in the pleasures of the Aśvins and the Maruts.
Unaware of sufferings,
seated upon his excellent celestial palace and attended by beautiful women, the lord sports like an immortal.
On the arrival of the twenty-second day, he who eats but a single meal,
constantly for twelve months while offering oblations into the sacred fire—
being steadfast, devoted to the path, truthful in speech, and free from malice— [attains the goal].
One attains the worlds of the Vasus, possessing a splendor equal to that of the sun.
Moving at will and subsisting on *svadhā*, he dwells in a magnificent celestial chariot;
adorned with divine ornaments, he delights in the company of divine maidens.
But he who eats only one meal on the twenty-third day,
always for twelve months, being moderate in diet and having his senses subdued;
He goes to the world of Vāyu, Uśanas, and Rudra;
moving at will and going wherever he desires, he is honored by hosts of apsarases.
Having ascended an excellent celestial mansion, adorned with divine ornaments, he rejoices with celestial maidens for the duration of many yugas.
Furthermore, he who eats but a single meal on the twenty-fourth day [attains this].
For he indeed, having offered oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months, [attained this].
Rejoicing, he shall dwell for a long time in the dwelling place of the Ādityas;
he delights with thousands and tens of thousands of celestial maidens.
He who eats but a single meal on the twenty-fifth day,
doing so consistently for twelve months, shall indeed ascend a magnificent celestial vehicle.
And he was followed from behind by chariots with joyful sounds,
mounted by celestial maidens upon bright, stainless, and auspicious silver vehicles.
There, indeed, for a thousand eons he delights, surrounded by hundreds of women,
and obtains the essence of nectar, unsurpassed and like unto immortality.
He who, for twelve months, always eats only one meal on every twenty-sixth day, being self-controlled and restricted in his diet;
Having conquered his senses and being free from passion, that fortunate man, while offering oblations into the sacred fire,
attains a state where he is honored by hosts of apsarases.
He attains the worlds of the seven Maruts and the Vasus,
and, being honored by Gandharvas and Apsarases, he rejoices.
For two thousand divine yugas with a divine mind,
he who eats but a single meal on the twenty-seventh day [attains this].
By constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months,
one obtains vast fruit and rejoices in the world of the gods.
Consuming nectar while dwelling there, he indeed remains satisfied and is highly honored;
sporting with women who delight the mind, he is intoxicated with joy.
He who,
with self subdued and senses conquered, performs this on the twenty-eighth day,
dwells happily indeed for three thousand yuga-kalpas and enjoys the vast fruit practiced by the celestial rishis.
Possessed of enjoyments and endowed with splendor, he was like a stainless god in heaven;
and women of exquisite beauty and great luster hurried toward him.
They delight their minds in a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun,
divine and endowed with all objects of desire, for hundreds of tens of thousands of kalpas.
On the twenty-ninth day, he who eats but a single meal,
remaining for twelve full months devoted to the vow of truth;
His worlds are auspicious and divine, endowed with the quality of celestial fragrance;
and there, auspicious women adorned with divine ornaments await him.
His words were delightful to the mind, sweet, and captivating with their excellent phrasing;
he was possessed of enjoyments, endowed with splendor, and possessed a radiance equal to that of Vaiśvānara.
With a divine body, he shone like an immortal god—
like one of the Vasus, the Maruts, the Sandhyās, or the Aśvins.
He goes to the worlds of the Rudras as well as to the world of Brahmā,
he who, being equanimous in soul, eats but one meal when a month has passed.
For twelve months, he shall indeed have access to the world of Brahmā;
glorious and captivating to all, his food shall consist of nectar and alkaline substances.
Endowed with splendor and a radiant body, he shines like the sun;
O lord of the earth, seated in his celestial chariot, he is accompanied by women who are his own.
He is constantly worshipped by the daughters of Rudras and devarṣis,
while he rains down upon Jambūdvīpa for a thousand years.
That many drops as fall from the surface of the sky constitute one year of the wise Brahmā’s world.
During the rainy season, he who possesses the splendor of an immortal dwells there for as long as it rains;

and so forth. The meaning is: in Jambūdvīpa, during the rainy season, for a thousand years, while the wise deity sends down rain, however many drops of water fall from the surface of the sky, for that many years he dwells in the world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, one who observes a month-long fast [attains] the supreme state himself after ten years.
Then, having attained the state of a great seer (maharṣi), he shall find his true course within his own body;
he is a sage, self-controlled, with anger conquered, and likewise with his genitals and belly subdued.
That man who, being self-restrained, offers oblations into the fire and practices the worship of the twilights,
thus eats [only once] for a month while observing many such observances.
And for him, whose conduct is characterized by non-existence and open space, his dwelling excels;
having gone to heaven in his own body, O King, he is like an immortal.
O King, having performed these fasts according to the prescribed rule, one enjoys merit in heaven as desired and shall go to the supreme goal.
Likewise: "If Vaiśyas or Śūdras, out of delusion, observe a fast for three nights or one night, no spiritual nourishment is found for them."
For a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the observance of skipping four meals is prescribed;
however, a fast of three nights has not been ordained by those who speak the Veda and know the Dharma.
“Nourishment” is the fruit.
For those who subsist on fruits and roots, sovereignty is the fruit; for those who subsist on leaves, heaven shall be attained.
One who subsists on milk goes to heaven, and through bathing, one becomes exceedingly wealthy.
One who is rich in cattle attains the path to heaven through vows of eating only herbs; those who subsist on grass attain it by fasting;
and women attain it by bathing at the three periods of the day. By subsisting on air alone, one obtains the merit of a sacrifice.
A king should bathe daily, while a twice-born man, reciting prayers at the two twilights, secures a kingdom with Indra; by fasting unto death, he attains the vault of heaven.
For those who sleep on the bare ground, houses and beds [are provided];
for those who wear garments of rags and bark, clothes and ornaments [are provided].
By the restraint of flavors, one finds good fortune in this world;
by the restraint of meat, one's offspring shall be long-lived.
He who observes the water-retreat shall become a lord of men.
"Pratisaṃhāra" means renunciation; "udavāsa" means dwelling in water. The speaker of truth, the best among men, rejoices together with the gods.
By abstaining from perfumes and garlands, one’s fame becomes abundant;
for those who maintain their hair and beard, their progeny becomes preeminent.
O King, by performing fasting, initiation,
or even ritual consecration for twelve years, one excels those who travel on heroic vehicles.

Thus ends the section on Vows (*vratakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, the chief minister for peace and war (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Govindacandra.
May there be auspicious prosperity.
